entries.section: 1. Righteousness and wisdom with faith

paragraphs.text: 1 Love righteousness, ye that be judges of the earth: think of the Lord with a good heart, and in simplicity of heart seek him. 2 For he will be found of them that tempt him not; and sheweth himself unto such as do not distrust him. 3 For froward thoughts separate from God: and his power, when it is tried, reproveth the unwise. 4 For into a malicious soul wisdom shall not enter; nor dwell in the body that is subject unto sin. 5 For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and remove from thoughts that are without understanding, and will not abide when unrighteousness cometh in.
Love righteousness, you who govern the earth, and think of the Lord with good thinking, and seek Him in the simplicity of your hearts. [1]

The wise man links the love of righteousness, good thinking about the Lord, and the seeking of the Lord. It is as though he opens the book with a call to three things: love, holy thinking and supplication.
By righteousness he means uprightness, or virtuous thought and diligent work.

The writer warns us against not thinking well or simply about God. Perhaps he means here not murmuring against the judgments of God, and not ignoring His divine providence and His hidden plan toward man, His beloved, because of His long-suffering toward the wicked and His allowing the righteous to undergo trials and afflictions.

The wise man looks at wisdom as not merely the enjoyment of temporal human experiences and the mental ability to act and manage affairs, but, while it sanctifies human experiences and the human mind, it is in essence the enjoyment of fellowship with the "wisdom of God", who is a divine hypostasis, dwelling in the soul and leading it in the divine way by a holy will. Through this understanding the wise man sees a strong relationship between wisdom, faith, righteousness and immortality, and on the other side between deprivation of wisdom, blasphemy, iniquity and eternal death.

There is no separation between wisdom and faith in God, the Almighty, the Maker of good things, nor between wisdom and walking in righteousness according to the will of God. For through this holy life the believer experiences the earnest of eternity and knows how to walk in life as a successful leader who governs the world. In the writer's speech with God he says: "Thou hast formed man through thy wisdom, that he should have dominion over the creatures which thou hast made, and order the world according to equity and righteousness, and execute judgment with an upright heart" (Wis 9:2-3)

* O the folly of those who seek God with these outward eyes, for God is seen only with the heart, as it is written in another place: "Seek him with a sincere (simple) heart" (Wis 1:1). For what is the pure heart but the sincere and simple heart? And as this light is not seen except with pure eyes, so God is not seen unless that which sees Him (that is, the heart) is pure.

* Do not give in to the thought of looking upon a bodily face, lest in your burning longing to see Him you prepare your bodily face to see Him, and so seek a (bodily) face in God. But if we conceive of God as spirit at least, without conceiving Him as bodily — this subject which was treated at length yesterday — if I have succeeded in removing that human image from your hearts, as from the temple of God, since the Apostle expresses his displeasure at those who "professing themselves to be wise, became fools, and changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man" (Rom 1:22-23). If this has entered into the depths of your thoughts and possessed your inner hearts, if you abhor this unbelief and keep for God His temple pure, if you want Him to come and make His dwelling in you, "think of the Lord with a good heart, and in simplicity of heart seek him" (Wis 1:1).

* Whoever desires to love God and takes care not to sin against Him must purify the upright intention of his heart from all duplicity. In this way he thinks of the Lord well and seeks Him in simplicity of heart (see Wis 1:1).

St. Augustine * The expression "the eyes of your heart" (Eph 1:18) points to those things that we cannot understand without perception and reasoning... For faith sees what is beyond the sight of bodily eyes. For bodily eyes exist not only in the head of the wise, but also in those who are not wise.
St. Jerome * The faithful are partakers in the divine wisdom.

Father Ambrosiaster * Where there are so many deceptions and so many errors of the wicked and the corrupt who murmur against wisdom, how greatly we need a pure, simple eye to find the way of wisdom! To flee from all these is to arrive at the full assurance of peace and at the dwelling of unchanging wisdom.

St. Augustine What is the sincere or simple heart but the pure heart, which seeks God not for a material or temporal aim, but for the sake of God Himself, wanting to possess Him and to live by Him and with Him forever?

He calls every leader, whether father or mother, or head or servant, indeed every believer, whatever his age or abilities, to love divine righteousness, and so to look at all things from a true perspective, that is, in the Lord.

entries.section: 1. Righteousness and wisdom with faith

paragraphs.text: For He reveals Himself to those who do not tempt Him, and appears to those who do not distrust Him. [2]

Whoever loves righteousness, thinks well of God and desires to enjoy God's dwelling in his heart, is prepared for God's revelation to him. For He appears to the believers who walk in righteousness and are earnest in enjoying the grace of the establishing of the Kingdom within them. But those who disbelieve in God, whether by inward unbelief or by speech or by conduct, darkness comes upon them, and they do not experience seeing God by faith in their hearts.

* He who has the pure heart sees God (Mt 5:8). But he who has not the pure heart does not see what others see. I think we must understand something like this concerning Christ also when He was seen in the flesh. For not everyone who cast his eyes upon Him was able to see Him. They saw His body, but they were not able to see Him as the Christ. But His disciples saw Him and beheld the greatness of His divinity.

entries.section: 1. Righteousness and wisdom with faith

paragraphs.text: Origen: For froward thoughts separate from God: and his power, when it is tried, reproveth the unwise. [3]

As he speaks of the love of divine righteousness and the pure, simple heart, and the appearing of God in it, he warns us against sin, especially thoughts of craftiness and deceit, for there is no fellowship between truth and falsehood, between divine love and deceit, between holiness and sin. The person who seeks sin and cherishes evil, the Spirit of God does not rest in him. By froward thoughts the soul draws away from God, because she cannot bear uprightness. But if the believer experiences the power of God, he challenges the unwise who oppose the divine truth.

What is the wisdom of God but the Way, the Truth and the Life? Wisdom keeps us from the crooked ways that destroy our lives, as the wise man says: "When wisdom entereth into thine heart, and knowledge is pleasant unto thy soul; discretion shall preserve thee, understanding shall keep thee: to deliver thee from the way of the evil man, from the man that speaketh froward things; who leave the paths of uprightness, to walk in the ways of darkness; who rejoice to do evil, and delight in the frowardness of the wicked; whose ways are crooked, and they froward in their paths" (Prov 2:10-15). It was also said of the wicked: "The way of peace they know not; and there is no judgment in their goings: they have made them crooked paths: whosoever goeth therein shall not know peace" (Isa 59:8).
* Walk with Him, and you will reach God. By Him you walk, and to Him you go.
Look to no other way by which you may go to Him.
Had He not deigned by His grace to become the Way, we would have remained in perpetual wandering.
I do not tell you to look for the way, for the Way itself has come to you; arise; walk.
* You hear the Lord praying; you learn to pray. He prayed for this reason, that He might teach you to pray.

* O sons of peace, sons of the one Catholic (universal) Church, go on your way, and sing as you keep watch. For travelers do so to keep their spirits high. Do you sing while you are on the way? I beseech you by the Way itself (Christ) on which you are walking, sing on the way, sing a new song.
Let no one sing the old songs, but the song of love for your (heavenly) homeland. Let no one sing the old. Behold, the way is new, and the traveler is new, and the song is new.

entries.section: 1. Righteousness and wisdom with faith

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine: Wisdom does not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in the body subject to sin. [4]
Here he personifies wisdom, as it is in (Prov 1:20-33; 8:1-36; 9:1-6; Job 28; Bar 3:9 - 4:4; Sir 24:1-21). She is a person, not separate from Him but one with Him, bearing the same divine attributes.

The Book of Wisdom did not adopt Platonic thought, as some have supposed, because it does not look at the body as evil. It does not ascribe sin here to the body, for it is a good creation (Wis 1:14); rather man uses the body to practice evil through the evil will.

St. Ambrose comments on what is written in the Book of Genesis about Abram (Abraham) entering into a covenant with God, where the Lord brought him forth abroad and said to him, Look now toward heaven (Gen 15:5).

* What then is the meaning of this expression: "He brought him forth abroad"? It is as though the prophet was led outside, so that he became outside the body, and saw the limitation of the body, which is his garment, and drank in the Holy Spirit, who showed a kind of condescension. So it is fitting for us also to go out from the borders of our temporal dwelling. We must cleanse the place in which our souls dwell from every defilement, and drive out every branch of evil if we wish to receive the spirit of wisdom, for "wisdom will not enter a wicked soul" (Wis 1:4).

St. Ambrose * He who desires to attain theoretical knowledge (contemplation of the divine things) must first follow practical (experiential) knowledge as far as possible, for this practical knowledge can be sought without the theoretical, but the theoretical is impossible to acquire without the practical. For there are certain fixed and ordered stages by which the humility of man ascends to the Most High... A man cannot fly to the second stage unless he begins with the first. In vain does a man strive to see God unless the traces of sin are removed from him, for "into a malicious soul wisdom shall not enter; nor dwell in the body that is subject unto sin. For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and remove from thoughts that are without understanding, and will not abide when unrighteousness cometh in" (see Wis 1:4-5).
Chromatius, the friend of both Rufinus and St. Jerome, comments on the saying of the Evangelist: "they besought him that he would depart out of their coasts" (Mt 8:34), saying:

* Such people are found also among us. For through unbelief they compel the Lord, the Savior of the world, to depart from the borders of their hearts, for according to the Holy Scripture: "The Holy Spirit does not enter a stubborn soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sin" (see Wis 1:4-5).

Father Chromatius * There is no way of attaining spiritual knowledge other than that way which the prophet described precisely, saying: "Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to goodness, plough for yourselves a ploughing, for it is time to seek the Lord until He comes and teaches you righteousness" (Hos 10:12). We must first sow in righteousness, that is, by works of righteousness we widen practical perfection. After that it behooves us to reap the hope of life, that is, by removing bodily sins we gather the fruits of the spiritual virtues. And thus we shall succeed in illuminating ourselves with the light of knowledge.

The psalmist also sees that this order must be followed by us, when he says: "Blessed are those who are blameless in the way, blessed are those who search out His testimonies" (Ps 119:1-2). For he does not say at first "Blessed are those who search out His testimonies" and afterward "Blessed are those who are blameless", but begins by saying "Blessed are those who are blameless", showing that a man cannot come to the examining of God's testimonies in a fitting manner unless he walks blamelessly in the way of Christ by his practical life.

entries.section: 1. Righteousness and wisdom with faith

paragraphs.text: Father Nestorius: For the Holy Spirit of discipline (the Disciplinarian) flees from deceit, and departs from foolish thoughts, and is put to flight (leaves man) when iniquity cometh in. [5]

The wise man calls the Spirit of God, whom he afterward describes as a lover of all men, the holy spirit of discipline. For there is no way to enjoy the spirit of wisdom and to grow in it without the fatherly divine discipline.
The Old Testament was preparing minds to come gradually to know the Holy Trinity, that we may realize His work of salvation, and the Book of Wisdom spoke of:
* God the Father, of whom it is fitting that we think well (Wis 1:2).

* Wisdom, as the hypostasis of Wisdom, or the Son, or the Word, who dwells in the holy soul (Wis 1:4). For wisdom is not merely an attribute, but a spirit that loves man (Wis 1:6), a judge who knows the hidden secrets of man (Wis 1:6) and who fills the world (Wis 1:7).
* The Holy Spirit (Wis 1:5).

* He who clings to the flock of Christ only through a bodily relationship with a deceitful heart cannot be said to be in the Church, and to be in the fellowship of the Spirit. For "the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit" (Wis 1:5).

St. Augustine In his book which St. Augustine sent to Vincentius Victor he assures him that, while he claims to be a member of the Catholic Church without accepting her faith, he is deceitful, and the Holy Spirit, who flees from the deceitful, departs from him.

entries.section: 2. Wisdom and love

paragraphs.text: 6 For the spirit of wisdom is a lover of man; so He will not acquit the blasphemer of what he has uttered, for God is a beholder of his reins, and a watcher of his heart who is not neglectful, and a hearer of his mouth.
Wisdom is a loving spirit, so He will not acquit the blasphemer for the words of his mouth, for God is a witness of his reins, and a true watcher of his heart, and a hearer of his tongue. [6]
Here he speaks of wisdom as a divine hypostasis, who is a spirit, a lover of mankind, and a judge who knows what goes on in the reins and hearts and what the tongues utter.

We are not surprised that, as the wise man announces that the Holy Spirit flees from the deceitful man and from him who has foolish thoughts, he begins with not acquitting the blasphemer of what he utters, and that He cares for every word that comes forth from man. God, who cares for man's salvation and sanctification that he may be prepared for the heavenly glory, is concerned with every word that issues from him. The mouth, like the heart, points to the sanctification of man in his practical life as in his inner life. No one will enjoy purity without the sanctification of the tongue as well as of the intention or inner will.
He speaks of the reins as the seat of the emotions, the hearts as the seat of thought, and the tongue as the seat of the inner life translated into words.
The wise man cares for the tongue, whether what it utters openly or what is in the inner intention.

* It is fitting that we understand the two reins as meaning the deep thoughts and the inner desires... I always look at the two reins as pointing to sense perception and sound thought... This is the custom of Holy Scripture when it intends to declare a hidden, secret and inward matter, saying: [O Searcher of the heart and the reins, O God] (see Ps 7:9).
St. Jerome

entries.section: 3. God's care for mankind

paragraphs.text: 7 For the Spirit of the Lord filleth the world: and that which containeth all things hath knowledge of the voice. 8 Therefore he that speaketh unrighteous things cannot be hid: neither shall vengeance, when it punisheth, pass by him. 9 For inquisition shall be made into the counsels of the ungodly: and the sound of his words shall come unto the Lord for the manifestation of his wicked deeds. 10 For the ear of jealousy heareth all things: and the noise of murmurings is not hid. 11 Therefore beware of murmuring, which is unprofitable; and refrain your tongue from backbiting: for there is no word so secret, that shall go for nought: and the mouth that belieth slayeth the soul.
The Spirit of the Lord fills the world, and He by whom all things are held together has knowledge of every word. [7]

In his speaking here of the Spirit of the Lord who fills the world, he does not declare this to affirm that He is present everywhere, as though God needed to reveal His attributes, but he says this to bear witness to God's care for all mankind and His embrace of it, for He is in all the world, "who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth". All things subsist by Him, and without Him they have no existence, and He knows every hidden word not to call them to account, but to reassure the wronged and urge the wicked to repentance.

* In this world there is the Son of God, and by Him the Holy Spirit, as the prophet says: "By the word of the Lord were the heavens made; and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth" (Ps 33:6). And in another place it was said in the same way: "The Spirit of the Lord filleth the world" (Wis 1:7). Hear also what Christ says to you: "Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world" (Mt 28:2). And concerning the Holy Spirit it was said: [I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and they shall prophesy] (see Joel 2:28).

* "The Spirit of the Lord filleth all creation" (see Wis 1:7), and "in him we live, and move, and have our being", as Paul said to the men of Athens (Acts 17:28). And also the saying: "Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the Lord" (Jer 23:24). For by power He is near to all things (Jer 23:23), so prayers do not ascend to a God afar off (Jer 23:23).

Origen * (The Holy Spirit) created all these; and He fills all by His essence, and contains all. He fills the world (Wis 1:7) with regard to His essence, and the world does not limit Him with regard to His power... He sanctifies (1 Cor 6:11) by His nature and is not sanctified... He measures and is not measured (Jn 3:34), He is partaken of (Rom 8:15) and does not partake, He fills (Wis 1:7) and is not filled, He contains and is not contained, He is taken as an inheritance (Eph 1:13-14), He is glorified (1 Cor 6:19-20), He is counted with the Father and the Son (Mt 28:19).

St. Gregory of Nazianzus * It is the Lord who fills all things, and this is also what we read concerning the Spirit: "The Spirit of the Lord filleth the world" (Wis 1:7). You find that it was said of those who accompanied the Apostles: "they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spake the word of God with boldness" (Acts 4:31).
Behold, you see that the Holy Spirit gives fullness and boldness. And this is what led the archangel to announce to Mary, saying: "The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee" (Lk 1:35).

entries.section: 3. God's care for mankind

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose: Therefore he that speaketh unrighteous things cannot be hid: neither shall vengeance, when it punisheth, pass by him. [8]

As the divine inspiration comments that the Spirit of God fills all the world, and has knowledge of every word that is spoken, and nothing is hidden from Him, this does not mean that He is a God who catches the mistakes of men, but that He is concerned with their sanctification, desiring them to be an icon of Him, affirming: "And ye shall be holy unto me: for I the Lord am holy" (Lev 20:26).

Our realization of God's exactness regarding our life and conduct and words, even our thoughts, is a sign of God's surpassing care for us. This drives us to enjoy the fear of the Lord, not the fear of slaves who dread meeting Him, but the fear of sons who will accept nothing but to be a spiritual icon of their heavenly Father.

By saying: "He that speaketh unrighteous things cannot be hid", he affirms that, although He is very long-suffering toward the unjust who insult their brethren and plot evil against them, they are not hidden from Him, and He will judge them if they do not turn back from their evils. So no one accused of injustice escapes divine justice except by resorting to the divine mercies through sincere repentance.

entries.section: 3. God's care for mankind

paragraphs.text: For inquisition shall be made into the intentions of the wicked, and the sound of his words shall come unto the Lord as proof of his iniquities. [9]
After speaking of the words of the blasphemer, he speaks here of the thoughts of the hypocrite, and another translation has "the unbeliever".

No one escapes the divine judgment, as the cruel unjust suppose, and also He will make known the hidden things in the day of the Lord, so the evil intentions of those who blaspheme against God will be exposed. The sound of their hidden intentions reaches the Lord and bears witness against them for their iniquities.

entries.section: 3. God's care for mankind

paragraphs.text: For the ear of jealousy heareth all things: and the noise of murmurings is not hid. [10]

Holy Scripture often speaks of the jealousy of God, for He is like the bridegroom who is jealous over his bride and will not accept that another occupy a place in her heart. As He gives her Himself, He asks that she give herself entirely to Him.

In His jealousy God's ear listens to every word that comes from His bride, for He desires to speak to her: "Let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely" (Song 2:14). He desires to see her face always cheerful and her tongue always thankful, therefore He warns her against murmuring.

He adds to the company of the unjust the murmurers who are discontented in their hearts, even if they do not utter a word. The unjust insult God through their injustice toward their brethren, and the murmurers insult God through their ingratitude to Him and their lack of thanks for His manifest and hidden care.

"Give thanks to God for His grace upon you, and bless the God of the ages, that He may come again and build up His dwelling in you, and restore to you all the captives, and you shall rejoice forever and ever" (Tob 13:12).
"Thy vows are upon me, O God: I will render thank offerings unto thee" (Ps 56:12).
"For the hope of the unthankful shall melt away as the winter's hoar frost, and shall run away as unprofitable water" (Wis 16:29)

"The voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride, the voice of them that shall say, Praise the Lord of hosts: for the Lord is good; for his mercy endureth for ever: and of them that shall bring the sacrifice of thanksgiving into the house of the Lord. For I will cause to return the captivity of the land, as at the first, saith the Lord" (Jer 33:11).

"Being enriched in every thing to all bountifulness, which causeth through us thanksgiving to God. For the administration of this service not only supplieth the want of the saints, but is abundant also by many thanksgivings unto God" (2 Cor 9:11).
* (The Gnostic) offers thanksgivings for his journey and blesses God at his departure, welcoming his dwelling in heaven.

entries.section: 3. God's care for mankind

paragraphs.text: St. Clement of Alexandria Therefore beware of murmuring, which is unprofitable; and refrain your tongue from backbiting: for there is no word so secret, that shall go for nought: and the mouth that belieth slayeth the soul. [11]

There is no sacrifice that man offers to God like the sacrifice of thanksgiving, for the backbone of worship is the Divine Liturgy, which is the sacrament of the Eucharist or the sacrament of thanksgiving, where the Church, priests and people, comes forward to offer to the Father the same unrepeated sacrifice of the Cross, to proclaim the divine salvation which gave her the right to enter heaven, to share with the heavenly beings the sacrifice of praise, thanksgiving and gratitude without ceasing.

The wise man warns us against murmuring which is unprofitable, for it deprives the soul of offering the sacrifice of thanksgiving. Murmuring is in fact the seal and confirmation that man has become wholly attached to the world and his heart has turned away from his heavenly Father, and he is no longer occupied with the eternal wedding prepared for him. "A wise servant will be served by free men, and a sensible man does not murmur" (Sir 10:28).
He also warns her against backbiting, that is, condemning others and slander.

The wise man affirms that God hears the hidden words of murmuring that issue from the heart, and cannot bear the false words of the tongue which slay the soul. He calls us to flee from the sins of the tongue, manifest and hidden, such as inward murmuring against God, slander against the brethren, and lying.

"The mouth that belieth slayeth the soul", for the tongue is the throne of life if it expresses man's inner fellowship with God, and the source of death if it behaves as the devil behaves, the liar and the father of liars.

* "Thou hatest all workers of iniquity: thou shalt destroy them that speak lies" (Ps 5:5-6)... He who does evil is hated by God; the liar is destroyed. Let us see which of the two is in the worse state, to be hated by God or to be destroyed. The man whom God hates is truly unhappy, for he lives in enmity with God, but he is still alive; as for the liar who is destroyed, he no longer exists. The man who lies is in a state more bitter than he who does iniquity.

* If someone slanders you, he does not harm you; you harm yourself if you slander others... If we have an enemy and think that we are doing something against him, all that we do is against ourselves. We revile him, we go here and there speaking of him with everyone. Do we think that we are harming him? We are doing nothing against him, but are killing ourselves, because we lie. "The mouth that belieth slayeth the soul" (Wis 1:11).

St. Jerome * The body speaks thus, so it is alive. But I ask whether the soul is also alive? Behold, the body speaks and so it is alive, but with what does it speak? As I said of the feet that they walk and so the body is alive. And then I asked, where do these feet walk? That I may understand whether the soul is also alive. So when I hear a man speaking I know that the body is alive, and I ask also with what he speaks, that I may know whether the soul is also alive. He speaks with falsehood. If so, then the soul is dead. How do we prove this? Let us ask the Truth Himself, who says: "The mouth that belieth slayeth the soul" (Wis 1:11). I ask: why did the soul die? I ask as I asked just now: why did the body die? Because its life, that is, the soul, has departed. Why did the soul die? Because God, its life, has left it.

* Of what mouth does he speak? This is a matter of question. In general, when Holy Scripture speaks of the mouth, it means the very seat of understanding in the heart, which is believed and judged. So he who lies in his heart accomplishes this by lying.

* "The mouth that belieth slayeth the soul" (Wis 1:11). And lest anyone think that this can be understood as excepting some liars, let him read in another place: "Thou shalt destroy them that speak lies" (Ps 5:6). In another place the Lord says with His own mouth: "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil" (Mt 5:37). Therefore the Apostle also, giving a commandment about putting off the old man, meaning by his name all sins, says immediately: "Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth" (Eph 4:25).

* That death which men fear in folly, while they do not fear sin, kills the body and not the soul, as the Lord teaches us in the Gospel. He urges us not to fear this death (Mt 10:28), but to fear the tongue that lies, and so kills the soul and not the body.

* The Apostle continues, saying: "It (the tongue) is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison" (Jas 3:8). He means that this member exceeds in the effect of its poisons the poisons of beasts and reptiles, for beasts may kill bodies, but the tongue kills the soul. "The mouth that belieth slayeth the soul" (Wis 1:11)... When the tongue of any man is tamed and humbled, he does not ascribe this to himself, but to the help of God and the mercies of His grace.

* Death for your body is its loss of life, and the death of your soul is its loss of life. The life of your body is your soul, and the life of your soul is God. When the body dies it loses the soul which is its life, and so the soul dies by losing God, its life.
St. Augustine * Beware of lying, for it drives the fear of God out of man.
* So every faithful son who wants to learn the form of purity must truly have in him nothing of the speech of falsehood.

St. Anba Anthony the Great * The soul has a discernment from its rational perception by which it knows the difference between truth and falsehood, as the mouth distinguishes between wine and vinegar even though they are alike in color, so the soul by rational perception knows the difference between spiritual gifts and satanic imaginations.

* Let us then call upon God with faith full of confidence, relying on His mercy, since we have His promises written, saying: "To him that knocketh it shall be opened" (Mt 7:8), and also: "I will dwell in them, and walk in them" (2 Cor 6:16). Men are drawn by myriads of cares, and trials darken their lives and force them to lie abundantly, even when they are bound by written contracts, so they are sometimes unable not to appear deceitful even if they wish. But God, who on the contrary does not lie, fulfills His promise to us by sending us the grace and the gift of the Holy Spirit (see Lk 11:13).

St. Macarius the Great * Let us reject the honor and dignities of the world that we may be rid of vainglory, and let us use the tongue in remembering God and the truth that we may be rid of lying, and let us love purity of heart and body that we may escape defilement, for all this surrounds the soul and restrains it when it leaves the body. So whoever is wise and acts wisely ought not to leave his soul without good works that he may be saved from that distress. Let us be diligent as far as our strength allows and our Lord will help our weakness, for He knows the misery of man, therefore He gave him repentance as long as he is in this body.

St. Abba Moses the Black * They also asked Abba John: "Who is the monk?" He said: "The monk is he who toils and labors and compels himself in everything, and does not act according to his own desire, and does not hold to his own word in anything. Also the monk ought not to say anything false, nor swear at all, nor be a listener to gossip nor a chatterer, nor murmur, nor judge anyone."
The Garden of the Monks

entries.section: 4. The slaying of the soul and the immortality of righteousness

paragraphs.text: 12 Do not be zealous for death in the error of your life, and do not draw upon yourselves destruction with the works of your hands: 13 for God made not death: neither hath he pleasure in the destruction of the living. 14 For he created all things, that they might have their being: and the generations of the world were healthful; and there is no poison of destruction in them, nor hath hades dominion upon the earth: 15 for righteousness is immortal.
Do not seek death by the error of your life, and do not bring destruction upon yourselves by the works of your hands. [12]

While the heavenly Bridegroom is jealous over His bride that she may enjoy eternal life, behold men seek death, and make a covenant with it, and ally themselves with it as its party, having exchanged eternal life for death, light for darkness, and God for the devil.
In folly they think of the devil, their enemy and the destroyer of their life, as a friend to them, although he prepares for them the poison of death in sin.

entries.section: 4. The slaying of the soul and the immortality of righteousness

paragraphs.text: For God made not death: neither hath he pleasure in the destruction of the living. [13]

It is clear that the writer does not mean here bodily death but spiritual death, the second death (Rev 2:11; 21:8), where the soul is separated from God, and bodily death where the soul is separated from the body. For God, the Creator of the soul and the body, did not create them to die, and did not give mankind life to destroy it.

* Truly death was not part of man's nature, but became natural, because God did not establish death in the beginning, but offered it as a remedy. Let us then take care lest the opposite appear to us. For if death were good, why was it written that "God made not death" (Wis 1:14), except that it entered the world through the evil of men?

St. Ambrose * For God's purpose in His creation is not that man should perish but that he should live forever, and this purpose still remains the same, and when He sees that His goodness shines in us, even with a slight spark of good will, He kindles it as though it came out of the hard flint of our hearts. He stirs it up and tends it and strengthens it by His breath, who "will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth" (1 Tim 2:4). For "even so it is not the will of your Father which is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish" (Mt 18:14)...

God is true and does not lie, when He swears, saying: "As I live, saith the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel?" (Ezek 33:11). He does not want any of His little ones to perish, so how are we not blasphemers if we imagine that He does not want all men to be saved but only some of them?!

Those who perish perish against His will, and He testifies against each one of them day by day, saying: "Turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die?" (Ezek 33:11). And also: "how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!" (Mt 23:37), "Why then is this people of Jerusalem slidden back by a perpetual backsliding? they hold fast deceit, they refuse to return" (Jer 5:8).

So the grace of Christ is present at hand every day, and as it wills that "all men should be saved, and come unto the knowledge of the truth", it calls all without exception, saying: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mt 11:28).

For if He did not call all but only some, the result would be that all are burdened with the original (ancestral) sins and the actual sins, otherwise the following saying would not be true: "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God" (Rom 3:23), and we would not believe that death has passed upon all men (Rom 5:12). And since those who perish perish against the will of God, therefore we can say that God is not the maker of death, according to the testimony of Holy Scripture which says: "For God made not death: neither hath he pleasure in the destruction of the living" (Wis 1:13).

Father Cheremon * We are sons; let us hasten to the Father (Lk 15:20). Let us not fear because we have squandered the inheritance of spiritual honor in order to obtain earthly pleasures (Lk 15:13). For since the Father gave the Son the treasure that is His, the wealth of faith will not be without profit (Rom 4:14). Although He has given all, He still possesses all, and loses nothing of what He gives. Do not fear that perhaps He will not receive you, for the Lord has no pleasure in the destruction of the living (Wis 1:13), for when He meets you on the way, He falls upon your neck, for the Lord raises up those who fall. He receives you, that is, He gives you the earnest of godliness and love.

St. Ambrose * In another place I said: "God seeks the death of no one". This is explained thus: man brought death upon himself by forsaking God, so he who does not return to God brings death upon himself, as it is written: "For God made not death" (Wis 1:13).

* "God made not death" (Wis 1:13), although it is written in another place: "Death and life are from the Lord God" (Sir 11:14). The punishment of evildoers, which is from God, is counted an evil to the evildoers, but it is counted among the good works that belong to God, for it is just that evildoers be punished, and all that is of justice is certainly good.

entries.section: 4. The slaying of the soul and the immortality of righteousness

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine For He created all things that they might have being, and the generations of the world were healed, and there is no deadly poison in them, nor dominion of death upon the earth. [14]

The wise man's view of death did not stop at the soul's departure from the body, but was the deprivation of man as a whole from God, the source of life and immortality. God did not create man to die, but for immortality (Wis 1:14), but by practicing sin in craftiness he brought death with his hands and his words, and entered with it into a covenant instead of entering into a covenant with God (Wis 1:16). God asks that there be no death for all men, but this deadly poison was breathed in by the ancient serpent, the devil.
* If there is anything poisonous in us, it is God who created it, but we ourselves have brought evil and sins upon ourselves.

entries.section: 4. The slaying of the soul and the immortality of righteousness

paragraphs.text: Origen: For righteousness is immortal. [15]

The wise man always links the inner life with the outward conduct. By "the error of life" he means acquiring death through the hidden sins in the heart, and destruction is drawn by the works of the hand, that is, the outward conduct. If iniquity entered us into death through the envy of the devil, the righteousness of God restores us to immortality. By immortality he means here infinite existence with God and the enjoyment of the blessed heavenly life.

entries.section: 5. Blasphemers and the covenant with death

paragraphs.text: 16 But the hypocrites called death to them with their hands and their words. They thought it a friend, and wasted away, and made a covenant with it, because they are worthy to be of its party.
But the wicked called death by their works and their words, counted it a friend and wasted away, and made a covenant with it, because they are worthy to be of its party. [16]

Perhaps he refers here to Adam and Eve, for Eve entered into conversation with the ancient serpent and made a covenant with it, and she and her husband became in alliance with it, as of its party. The prophet Isaiah says: "Because ye have said, We have made a covenant with death, and with hell are we at agreement" (Isa 28:15).
The writer considers the practical conduct of the wicked as a friendly talk with death and entering into a covenant with it.
When the righteous speak of death, they mean by it the death of the soul, for this is what they fear. But the wicked speak of the death of the body, and this is what they dread.

The faithful, the sons of Abraham according to the Spirit, enter into a covenant and pact of friendship with God, but the unbelievers make a covenant and alliance with death as an inseparable friend. Just as God is the portion of the righteous believer and they are His portion (Ps 16:5; 73:25; 119:57; Deut 32:9; 2 Kgs 11:17; 2:12), so the ungrateful are the portion of death, and death is their portion; they are of its party, belonging to it by the corruption and evil of their will.
Let me possess You, that I may possess immortality
* You have come to us, O Holy and Righteous One, and our heart is kindled with longing for righteousness.
Our eyes were fixed on You, so we began to seek You in the simplicity of a good heart!
We saw You, so our thoughts were sanctified by You, and our tongue was opened to seek You!
* What do we seek but to possess You, for by You we become kings, O King of kings, and by You we enjoy the uprightness that is Yours, O only Holy One!
Our heart will not turn from You to the right or to the left, but in simplicity we see You and enjoy fellowship with You.
* We do not want to see You here with our bodily eyes!
Wash our inner eyes that in simplicity of heart we may see You.
Grant us purity of heart that we may enjoy beholding You.
Remove from us all malice, that we may not walk in crooked ways, but that You may be our only Way, for You are the Way, the Truth and the Life.
Let me walk by You and go to You, O wonderful Way!
* Sanctify me completely, sanctify my soul and my body, that my soul may not bear a spirit of malice, nor my body be enslaved to lusts.
Sanctify me, that I may be made worthy to walk according to Your will, O divine Wisdom!
Sanctify my reins and my heart and my tongue, that I may become wholly consecrated for the sake of Your Kingdom.
* Your Holy Spirit fills the whole world, seeks nearness to every person, spreads His love over every individual, wanting all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
Let Your Spirit give me the life of fullness, and grant me the power of hope, opening the gates of heaven before me, and let Him fly with me to the divine embrace.
* Your Holy Spirit knows the intentions of the heart and the hidden words.

He is long-suffering toward the slanderers and the unjust, waiting for their repentance that they may enjoy the divine mercies, so that He rejoices over them, even those who fell under their injustice.
* Shine Your light upon me, and no trace of murmuring will remain in my heart.
Instead of murmuring there come forth hidden offerings of thanksgiving and unceasing praises of the heart.
Receive them as sacrifices of thanksgiving, and be pleased with them, O heavenly Bridegroom.
* You created me longing to live forever, but the enemy of good, by his envy, brought death into the world.
And in my folly I received death as a friend to me, I entered with it into a covenant, and became of its party.
Who can tear up this covenant but Your precious covenant?
Who can free me from sonship to the devil but sonship to God, Your Father!
Reign over me, O Resurrection and Life, and death will not be able to creep in to me.
You are my resurrection and my immortal life.

entries.section: 1. Their gloomy view of life

paragraphs.text: 1 For in the error of their thoughts they said within themselves: "Our life is short and wretched, and there is no remedy for the death of man, and it was never known that any man returned from Hades.
For they (the wicked) thought wrongly, and said to one another:
"Our life is short and tedious, and there is no remedy for the end of man, and it was never known that any man returned from the grave. [1]

It is clear that the writer is Solomon the Wise, for until his time they had not heard of a dead person rising, whereas in the days of Elijah and also Elisha, the first raised the son of the widow after his crying to the Lord (1 Kgs 17:20-22), and the dead man who touched the bones of the prophet Elisha rose (2 Kgs 13:21).
Someone may say: Was this not the view of righteous Job, who cursed the day in which he was born (Job 3)?

Far apart is Job's speech about the shortness of life from the speech of the wicked, for although Job was greatly embittered by the weight of trials and the accusations of his friends and their enmity toward him, and he longed for death, yet he often hoped for the just divine judgment and for the resurrection from the dead. But the wicked in their gloomy view of life denied the resurrection.

The shortness of life is something no one can deny, but the righteous looks at his life as a bridge to cross over to eternity with joy and gladness, while the wicked is crushed by the darkness in his heart, so despair dominates him, and instead of preparing for eternal life by enjoying the righteousness of Christ, he walks in a spirit of selfishness.

The divine Word became incarnate, and walked the way of our temporal life, and accepted death in the prime of His youth, that by His resurrection we may hope for the resurrection, and according to the shortness of our life on the earth as a joyful divine gift.

St. Augustine sees that the Lord Christ appeared to the Apostles after His resurrection for no purpose but to confirm the resurrection of the body. [He wished to teach us nothing but that we must believe in the resurrection of the dead.]

* Truly our faith in the resurrection of our Lord from the dead and His ascension into the heavens supports our faith with a great hope. For this doctrine shows us strongly how He of His own will, He who has the power to lift up His life, laid it down for our sake. How great is the confidence which the hope of the believers inspires when they realize the greatness of the things He endured for the sake of men who were not yet believers! When it was expected that He would come from heaven as Judge of the living and the dead, the negligent were in great terror, but when they consecrated their lives with great striving they were filled with longing for Him, walking in a holy life instead of fearing His coming because of the evil of their life.

* It is a sure hope... it has already become present and we have acquired it in practice; our future life has now been accomplished in our Head and Mediator who rose from the dead, the man Jesus Christ.

St. Augustine * If you believe that Christ has risen from the dead, you must believe that you also have risen with Him in like manner. And if you believe that He sits at the right hand of the Father in the heavens, you must believe that you are no longer henceforth in the earthly scene, but in the heavenly. And if you believe that you have died with Christ, you must believe that you shall live with Him. And if you believe that Christ is dead to sin and alive to God, you also must be dead to sin and alive to God.

This is because the man who (sets his mind on things above) shows his faith in Him who raised Jesus from the dead. And as for this man, "his faith is counted for righteousness". For if we have risen with Christ, who is the Righteousness, and walk in newness of life, and live according to righteousness, then Christ has risen for us, that we may be justified.. since we have taken on a new life after the likeness of His resurrection."
Origen * Thinking that is not simple causes a man to lose his hope in the last coming of the Lord (the Parousia), which drives him to evil conduct.

St. Clement of Rome * He appeared to put an end to the sins of the Jews, and that we may be saved through the Heir, the Lord Jesus, who was prepared to come into the world, and by His coming save our souls that walk in the ravines of death and are given over to the evil way.
The Epistle of Barnabas

entries.section: 2. A life at the mercy of the winds

paragraphs.text: 2 For we are born at all adventure: and we shall be hereafter as though we had never been: for the breath in our nostrils is as smoke, and speech a spark from the movement of our heart: 3 which being extinguished, our body shall be turned into ashes, and our spirit shall vanish as the soft air, and our life shall pass away as the trace of a cloud, and shall be dispersed as a mist, that is driven away with the beams of the sun, and overcome with the heat thereof. 4 And after a while our name shall be forgotten, and no man shall have our works in remembrance.
We were born by chance, and hereafter we shall be as though we had never been, for the breath in our nostrils is smoke, and speech is a spark from the beating of our hearts. [2]

The wicked in their conduct embrace a practical atheism, looking at man's life as the offspring of sheer chance, with no place in their minds for God's plan, and looking at bodily death as the end of life, with no other life and no resurrection.

The wicked view life as the enjoyment of pleasures and temporal merriment, for unbelief destroys all hope in men, so they feel their existence as though it were nonexistence; their spirits are not from God but are smoke that quickly vanishes never to return, and their bodies turn into ashes scattered as by the winds.

One of the most important points in Origen's eschatological thought is his understanding of the Christian hope in the resurrection. In the preface to his book De Principiis he mentioned among the teachings defined in the preaching of the Church the faith that the soul has its own substance and life, which continues after death, to experience reward or punishment for its conduct, and expects that a time will come for the resurrection from the dead. He also spoke afterward in the same work of the resurrection of the body, and holds that this body will rise a spiritual body, quite different in its form from what it is at present.

In the final chapter of the book he demonstrated in a positive manner the immortality of the soul, reckoning it evil that what is in man in the likeness of God, such as the human mind, could perish entirely.

entries.section: 2. A life at the mercy of the winds

paragraphs.text: When it is extinguished, the body shall be turned into ashes, and the spirit shall vanish as the empty air [3]

These are the thoughts that the wicked turn into philosophies, whose aim is to justify man's practicing evils without restraint. Many philosophers believed in the complete annihilation of the body and soul.

When man isolates himself from God he sees himself trivial, of no value, like nothingness, but in God he sees himself the object of the love of the Creator of heaven and earth, who set him as a ruler to govern the world in righteousness and holiness, and he sees himself the very dear son of his heavenly Father.
* (Christ) is the word of truth, the word of incorruption, who renews the human person by raising him to the truth. He urges us to the salvation that abolishes corruption and takes away death.

St. Clement of Alexandria Origen spoke clearly that anyone who despises the resurrection of the dead as the Church believes has no hope in Christ, unless he believes that the soul lives and is refreshed and does not receive this body in the resurrection but a body of an exalted kind. However, the Fathers of the Church affirm that the risen body is the same body that struggled with the soul in this world, but it bears a glorious nature fitting for eternal life.

* It is fitting that we do not doubt that our mortal body will rise again at the end of the world... This is the Christian faith, this is the faith of the Catholic Church, this is the apostolic faith.

St. Augustine * Just as the kingdom of darkness and sin remains hidden in the soul until the day of resurrection, when the bodies of sinners are overwhelmed by the darkness now hidden in the soul, so the kingdom of light and the heavenly image, Jesus Christ, now shines secretly within the soul and reigns in the souls of the saints. He is hidden from the eyes of men, but the eyes of the soul alone behold Christ truly until the day of resurrection comes, when the body also will be flooded with the light of the Lord and glorified by it, that light which is now hidden in the soul of man.

* Just as the fire that burned on the altar in Jerusalem was buried in a pit during the period of the captivity, and when peace came and the captives returned to Jerusalem this same fire was renewed and burned as it had before the captivity (2 Macc 1:18-33), so now the heavenly fire works in this body which we are used to, this body which in its dissolution (by death) turns into stench, and renews this body and raises it after it has decayed. For the inner fire that now dwells in the heart will then be revealed from outside and accomplish the resurrection of the body.

entries.section: 2. A life at the mercy of the winds

paragraphs.text: St. Macarius the Great And our name shall be forgotten in time, and no man shall have our works in remembrance, and our life shall pass away as the trace of a cloud, and shall be dispersed as a mist, that is driven away with the beams of the sun, and overcome with the heat thereof. [4]

The wicked unbelievers see their life as a mist driven away by the ray of the sun, then condensed by the heat of the sun, turning into water that falls on the earth, and the earth drinks it and it has no more existence. With the passing of the life, which the wicked liken to a cloud that passes so that the sun appears, they believe that not even a remembrance remains for man among the coming generations. The wicked man sees no difference between the portion of the wicked and the righteous after death.

Holy Scripture affirms: "The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot" (Prov 10:7). And the Lord gives a promise to the righteous: "Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off" (Isa 56:5). Such a promise has no place in the thought or in the heart of the wicked.

entries.section: 3. Their goal is temporal pleasure

paragraphs.text: 5 For our life is a shadow that passeth away; and after our end there is no returning: for it is sealed up, so that no man cometh again. 6 Come on therefore, let us enjoy the good things that are present, and let us speedily use the creatures while we are in youth, 7 let us fill ourselves with costly wine and ointments, and let no flower of the spring pass by us: 8 let us crown ourselves with rosebuds before they be withered, and let there be no meadow through which our pleasure doth not pass. 9 Let none of us go without his part of our voluptuousness: let us leave tokens of our joyfulness in every place: for this is our portion, and our lot is this.
For our days are the passing of a very shadow, and our end has no returning, because it is sealed, so that no man cometh again. [5]

The wicked see that their life passes like a shadow, and here they do not mean merely the shortness of temporal life, but its total vanishing into nothing, formed like a shadow out of nothing and ending in nothing, which drives them to immerse themselves in pleasures. But the Apostle James, when he says: "For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away" (Jas 4:4), by its vanishing in this world we enjoy a new, eternal life, so he adds: "Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin" (Jas 4:17). The wicked's sense of the shortness of life corrupts them, and the righteous's sense of it drives them to greater striving.

In great despair the wicked believe in the shortness of life, where there is no escape from death and no return from the grave. But the righteous, as they believe in the surpassing providence of God and His plan, realize that "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven" (Eccl 3:1), so life is not the offspring of chance, and events do not come to pass without divine management. The wise man realizes that his creation is a divine gift, and that his life has a glorious mission that fulfills God's plan toward him.

entries.section: 3. Their goal is temporal pleasure

paragraphs.text: Come on therefore, let us enjoy the good things that are present, and let us make use of creation with the ardor of youth. [6]

The wicked focus on present good things, or temporal pleasures, instead of eternal glories. As though their short life were an opportunity to make use of creation by every means in the ardor of youth, that is, like those who have strength and power, enjoying good things before old age and weakness come.

entries.section: 3. Their goal is temporal pleasure

paragraphs.text: Let us be drunk with costly wine and perfumes, and let not the flower of spring pass by us. [7]

Although they realize that temporal things are temporary and passing, yet because they feel that they are on their way to nothingness and that there is no immortality for man, there is no room for striving for the holy life in the Lord, but luxury and pleasure are their enjoyment before corruption comes, whether to matter or to themselves. Their joy is poured out in pleasure. But the believer perceives the love of God the Creator in the beautiful world He brought into being for him, yet finds his enjoyment in offering thanks to the Creator for His gifts, and not in enslavement to matter. He cherishes the exercise of the freedom that was granted him, so he remains always master of matter and not its slave.
St. Clement of Alexandria says that food is not a goal that we desire, but a means of life, so the Word of God, not the desire for food, leads us to the enjoyment of eternity.
* Food is not to be our chief concern, nor our enjoyment and aim in life, but a means for our life, which the Lord, the "Word", arranges to lead us to eternity...
They did not realize that God gave His creature man food and drink that he may live and continue in life, and not for pleasure...

We were created not to eat and drink but to consecrate ourselves to the knowledge of God.. for the belly of the wicked is never satisfied (Prov 13:5), for it is filled with an appetite that is not satisfied and not quenched.

* We must have a kind of discernment with regard to food, so that food is simple, very ordinary, suitable for simple children.. it prepares for a life that stands on two essentials, health and strength. This accords with food being simple and uncomplicated, so that it is easy to digest, makes the body light and agile, and brings growth and health.
The wretched art of cookery spoils the taste, as happens in the art of making sweets and pastries.

The human body gains no benefit from extravagance in kinds of food; on the contrary, those who use the minimum of food are stronger and healthier and more honorable and dignified, so we see servants healthier than their masters, and peasants sounder in body than the owners of estates.

* The philosophers are wiser than the rich, for they do not bury the mind under heaps of food, nor deceive themselves with pleasures and enjoyments, but the feast of love "agape" `agapy is in the heavenly food, and in the feast of the mind and sound thinking...
The glutton is like one who buries his mind in his belly.

St. Clement of Alexandria As for drunkenness with wine and putting wreaths of flowers on the heads, they were among the pagan rites, connected with the practice of abominations and the worship of idols.

entries.section: 3. Their goal is temporal pleasure

paragraphs.text: And let us crown ourselves with rosebuds before they be withered. [8]

Theaters and arenas were usually used for celebrations of the pagan gods or of the ruler or emperor as a god, and they had their own rites, such as lighting torches and putting wreaths of flowers on their heads. Some Christians in the first centuries, because of the simple or the weak in faith, were compelled to refuse the use of flowers, not because they are unclean, but because they were associated with the worship of Satan and idols. Yet the martyr Justin (110-165) says:

[Everything that is born as the inviolable gift of God cannot be violated by a human act (even if it is used in pagan rites). In any case, we abstain from using them lest anyone think that we submit to the demons for whose sake wine is drunk, or that we are ashamed of our religion.

Certainly the flowers of spring are delightful to us, for we choose the spring rose and the lily and other flowers of very joyful colors and fragrant scent, and we use them, whether each one by itself, or we scatter their petals, or weave them together as wreaths with which we adorn our necks.]
And Minucius Felix (second or third century) says that flowers are useful for the sense of smell, for the nose receives a sweet fragrance.

St. Clement of Alexandria says: [Those who have been taught by the Logos refrain from wearing wreaths (of flowers). For they consider that it is not necessary to bind their minds which are in their heads, not because the wreath is a symbol of the life of unrestrained drunkenness, but because it is associated with paganism.]
Let none of us be without a share in our revelry.

entries.section: 3. Their goal is temporal pleasure

paragraphs.text: Let us leave in every place tokens of our rejoicing, for this is our portion, and this is our lot. [9]

For nothing occupies them but a life of revelry or noisy carousing (revelry) and wantonness (wanton). They invite their relatives and friends to share in these dissolute parties, looking at it as life itself and gladness, and that this is the portion of the joyful man. Without it life is counted as death, without taste.

entries.section: 4. Their law is the law of the jungle

paragraphs.text: 10 Let us oppress the poor righteous man, let us not spare the widow, nor reverence the ancient gray hairs of the aged of many days. 11 Let our strength be the law of justice: for that which is feeble is found to be nothing worth.
Let us oppress the poor righteous man, and let us not spare the widow, nor reverence the gray hairs of the aged of many days. [10]
The wicked in their dissolution want to silence the voice of wisdom and justice; they oppose the wise and do not care for the experience of prudent elders.

The wicked's loss of hope in immortality does not drive them to pleasure only, but they find their enjoyment in plundering others, even the poor and the widows and the aged. They have lost the feeling of love and tenderness, so their law became injustice and robbery, caring nothing for the needs of the poor, or the bitterness of soul of the widow, or the weakness of the aged. They saw that it was their right to exercise power, and that in this conduct there is justice.

By withdrawing from God, the source of love and tenderness and the practical model of sound values and principles, they lost every feeling and emotion, and their inner balances were upset; they became more hideous than beasts of prey moved by instinct and lust, which are cruel with violence without knowing it.

entries.section: 4. Their law is the law of the jungle

paragraphs.text: But let our strength be the law of justice: for that which is feeble is found to be nothing worth. [11]

The law of the wicked and their principle is not the law of God but the law of force, as being above truth. Their law is the law of the jungle. They see in love, long-suffering and endurance weakness and servility unbecoming to them.

* O you who are exalted and proud and arrogant, remember death, which will destroy your loftiness and dissolve your members and loosen the joints and bring corruption on the body in all its forms. By death the exalted are brought low, and the violent and cruel are buried in its darkness...

O you greedy plunderers who rob your companions, remember death, and do not multiply your sins. For in that place sinners do not repent, and he who robbed the possessions of his fellow does not even own his own money, but goes to the place where wealth is not used, and becomes nothing, his dignity passes away from him, and his sins remain to stand against him on the day of judgment.
St. Aphrahat

entries.section: 5. Their hatred of the righteous

paragraphs.text: 12 Therefore let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is grievous to us, and is contrary to our doings: he upbraideth us with our offending the Law, and objecteth to our infamy the transgressings of our way of life. 13 He professeth to have the knowledge of God: and he calleth himself the son of the Lord. 14 He was made a reprover of our thoughts. 15 He is grievous unto us even to behold: for his life is not like other men's, his ways are of another fashion. 16 We are esteemed of him as counterfeits: he abstaineth from our ways as from filthiness: he pronounceth the end of the just to be blessed, and maketh his boast that God is his father. 17 Let us see if his words be true: and let us prove what shall happen in the end of him. 18 For if the just man be the son of God, he will help him, and deliver him from the hand of his enemies.
Let us lie in wait for the righteous, for he troubles us, opposes our works, and blames us for our transgressions of the Law, and accuses us of being unfaithful to our teaching. [12]

The wicked did not stop at being absorbed in lusts and using violence and injustice even with the poor and needy, but they try to entrap the righteous and set snares and traps for them, because they refuse fellowship with them in their evils, and because they rebuke them for their wrong behavior, if not by words then by the conduct of the righteous. Thus the sight of the righteous becomes exceedingly grievous to them, because he rebukes them.

Some see that these expressions carry clear prophecies about our Lord Jesus Christ, the Righteous, who by His conduct as by His teachings rebuked the scribes and Pharisees, and they could not bear Him, but lay in wait to kill Him and be rid of Him by the Cross.

It is strange that the wicked do not bear the righteous even after his death, for his memory remains rebuking them. This happened with the Lord Christ even after His death and resurrection, for the Jewish leaders could not hear the name of Jesus, and the accusation directed against the Christians was the accusation of the Name. And the cries of the leaders against them were that they bring this Name upon them.

The divine light shining in the life of the righteous is not borne by the darkness lurking in the hearts of the wicked. The world in its darkness does not receive the light, and as the Lord Christ said in His farewell prayer about His disciples: "the world hath hated them, because they are not of the world" (Jn 17:14).

St. Ambrose sees that Joseph found his brethren in Dothan (Gen 37:17), which means "abandonment", and thus they represent the souls that forsake God and do not wish to come to Him to find rest in Him (Mt 11:28). These, when they saw Joseph coming from afar, rose up against him and wanted to kill him (Gen 37:28). They rose up while he was far from them; so also when the Lord Christ came to His own to draw near to them they rejected Him and planned His killing, saying what is stated in the Book of Wisdom: "Let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is grievous to us" (Wis 2:12).
* Let us flee from the peace of the wicked, for they plot against the righteous man. They gather together to press upon him who is righteous.

St. Ambrose * As the thoughts of the Jews were to do the Lord an injustice... they forgot that they were bringing wrath upon themselves, therefore the Lord wept over them (by the mouth of the prophet), saying: "Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?" (Ps 2:1).
Truly vain is the thinking of the Jews, for they think death against Life, and devise unreasonable things against the Word of the Father!
And he who now looks at their dispersion and the ruin of their city says: "Woe unto them, for they have devised evil against themselves"..

This is good, my brethren, for since they sinned against Holy Scripture they did not know that "He that diggeth a pit shall fall into it; and whoso breaketh down a wall, a serpent shall bite him" (Eccl 10:8).

Pope Athanasius the Apostolic * They bound Jesus and brought Him to the house of the high priest. Do you want to know how this too was written beforehand? Isaiah says: [Woe unto their souls! for they have rewarded evil unto themselves, saying, Let us bind the righteous; because he is closed to us] (see Isa 3:9; Wis 2:12). Yes, woe unto their souls.

That you may see how this is: Isaiah was sawn asunder, and afterward the people were set right. Jeremiah was cast into a pit of mire, but the wound of the Jews was healed, for their iniquities were few because they were directed against a man. But when the Jews sinned against God made man it was said: "Woe unto their souls... Let us bind the righteous!"

Was He not able to set Himself free?! Someone may say: He who loosed Lazarus from the bands of death on the fourth day, and set Paul free from the iron fetters of prison, was He not able to set Himself free?
The angels stood ready saying: "Let us break their bands asunder" (Ps 2:3), but they held back, because their Master willed to accept this.
He was led to the court before the elders. And this is a testimony of that: "The Lord will enter into judgment with the ancients of his people, and the princes thereof" (Isa 3:14).

entries.section: 5. Their hatred of the righteous

paragraphs.text: St. Cyril of Jerusalem He professeth to have the knowledge of God: and he calleth himself the son of the Lord. [13]

Since Jesus the Righteous rebuked the Jews in many places (Mt 25; Jn 8), and revealed to them their sickness, they did not bear this world but sought to kill Him, "because he not only had broken the sabbath, but said also that God was his Father, making himself equal with God" (Jn 5:18).

entries.section: 5. Their hatred of the righteous

paragraphs.text: He became a reproach to our thoughts. [14]

St. John Chrysostom sees that God does not separate the righteous from the wicked, but allows them to mingle together for the benefit of both sides. The wicked look at the righteous, and the righteousness of the righteous rebukes them, and on the other side this is counted a gain for the righteous in that they are a cause for the repentance of some of the wicked.
Even the sight of him is grievous to us.

entries.section: 5. Their hatred of the righteous

paragraphs.text: For his life is not like the life of others, and his ways are different. [15]
He became strange in their eyes, for righteousness is to them weakness and cowardice, and violence and plunder are strength and chivalry. Good became evil in their eyes, and evil good.

* There is a benefit for the wicked in mingling with the good, for they feel confusion, and are ashamed, and are put to shame in their presence. For even if they do not abstain from evil, they do not dare to do what they do in secret. And this is no small matter, that they do not commit transgression openly. The life of others becomes an accuser of the evil of those. Hear at least what is said of the righteous man: "He became a danger to us, even his appearance" (Wis 2:14). It is no small beginning of reform through torment in the presence of (the righteous man).
* The thief hates the light.

The mere looking at the righteous man is hateful to sinners. "Even his appearance is grievous to us" (Wis 2:15). For they cannot bear his splendor, like diseased eyes that cannot bear the rays of the sun.
But to many it is grievous not only to see him but even to hear of him.
St. John Chrysostom We are esteemed of him as counterfeits, and he avoids our ways as he avoids uncleanness.

entries.section: 5. Their hatred of the righteous

paragraphs.text: He pronounceth the end of the righteous to be blessed, and maketh his boast that God is his father. [16]

It is not fitting for the righteous to despise sinners, nor to condemn them, although he does not accept their evils and does not walk in their ways. It is not fitting for him to insult them even by his looks, but to be gentle with them and love them in the Lord, seeking their salvation. But the wicked, knowing the corruption of their ways and the righteous man's refusal to walk with them in the same way, realize that he is teaching them that their way is vain and false, and that he avoids their ways because he blesses the end of the righteous and cherishes the spirit of sonship to God, this spirit which the rich grace of God gave him in the waters of Baptism.
But what is the reaction of the wicked who persist in their evil? They say:

entries.section: 5. Their hatred of the righteous

paragraphs.text: Let us see whether his words are true, and let us prove what shall happen in the end of him. [17]
Instead of imitating the righteous, they mock them, as they mocked the Holy Righteous One, the only-begotten Son of God.

entries.section: 6. Opposition to the righteous even unto death

paragraphs.text: 19 Let us examine him with despitefulness and torture, that we may know his meekness, and prove his patience. 20 Let us condemn him with a shameful death: for he shall be visited, as he saith.
For if the righteous man be the son of God, he will help him, and deliver him from the hand of his enemies. [18]

The wicked cherish their brute strength and think that there is no power able to stand before them, not even God Himself. And as they wrong the righteous they mock him, saying: "If the righteous be the son of God, let him help him and deliver him from the hand of his enemies". Thus they challenge God Himself, whether He is able to deliver the righteous from their hands.

Here is a clear prophecy about the Lord Christ, when they mocked Him, so that the two thieves said: "He saved others; himself he cannot save". And it was said of Him: "If he be the Son of God, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him". They did not realize that by the Cross the Lord Christ triumphed over Satan, and by His death trampled death, and saved all mankind that it might triumph and be crowned by Him.
Let us examine him with despitefulness and torture, that we may know his meekness and prove his patience. [19]

This challenge was present between Satan, personally or through his party which entered into covenant with him, and God in the persons of His believers among the men of the Old and New Testaments, and it reached its peak at the coming of His only-begotten Son, for the enemy of good thought that he was able to be rid of Him completely by the Cross, as the enemy was ignorant of His humility and His plan for the salvation of the world. And this challenge remains between the world which lies in the wicked one and the Church of God, increasing until it reaches its peak with the coming of the Antichrist in the last days, when the enemy of good realizes that his end has come very near.

entries.section: 6. Opposition to the righteous even unto death

paragraphs.text: Let us condemn him with a shameful death: for he shall be visited, according to his words". [20]

Both St. Augustine and Origen see that the wicked condemn the Righteous One, our Lord Jesus, to a shameful death, that is, the Cross, and did not realize that by the Cross He was at the peak of glory through His love and humility.
* Behold, we see this prophecy (Wis 2:12-21) in the form of a longing and a prayer fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

St. Augustine * He was glorified when He came to the Cross and when He endured death. Do you want to know that He was glorified? He Himself said: "Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee" (Jn 17:1). Bearing the Cross was glory to Him, but His glory was not in a beautiful appearance but in humility. For it was said of Him: [He humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross] (see Phil 2:8). And the prophet prophesied of this, saying: "Let us condemn him with a shameful death" (Wis 2:20). And Isaiah says of Him: "From oppression and from judgment he was taken" (Isa 53:8).

Origen And as the enemy wished to be rid of the Lord Christ by the Cross, so he does not cease to strive to kill the believers and destroy them from their birth. Origen comments on the statement: "And Pharaoh charged all his people, saying, Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river, and every daughter ye shall save alive" (Ex 2:22), saying:

[Do you see what the ruler of this world commands his servants? He commands to steal our children and cast them into the river, and to set snares continually from their birth. He commands to attack them from the moment they begin to touch the breasts of the Church and asks to tear them away from her and pursue them until the waves of the world swallow them...

Consider the danger that threatens you from your birth, or rather from your new birth, that is, immediately from your receiving Baptism... For Jesus was led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil (Mt 4:1).

This is Pharaoh's command to his people concerning the children of the Hebrews, that is, to attack them and prey on them at the moment of their birth and drown them... But Christ conquered that He might open to you the way of victory; He conquered while fasting that you also may realize how to cast out this kind by fasting and prayer (Mk 9:29).]

entries.section: 7. Their denial of immortality

paragraphs.text: 21 Such things they did imagine, and were deceived: for their own wickedness hath blinded them. 22 As for the mysteries of God, they knew them not: neither hoped they for the wages of righteousness, nor discerned a reward for blameless souls. 23 For God created man to be immortal, and made him to be an image of his own eternity. 24 Nevertheless through envy of the devil came death into the world: 25 and they that do hold of his side do find it.
Thus they reasoned, but they were deceived, for their wickedness blinded them. [21]
Their pride prevents them from reviewing themselves, so they remained fixed in ignorance, error and spiritual blindness.

Their immersion in evil blinded them from seeing the wisdom of God in His long-suffering, giving them an opportunity for repentance, and how He proves the righteous by their enduring sufferings that they may receive crowns of glory in heaven. They did not realize the power working in the life of the children of God, which gives them peace in the midst of tribulations and a sense of God's presence with them, so that they rejoice and exult in the midst of sufferings.

* These flourish in the happiness of this world, and perish by the power of God. It is not that while they flourish they perish by the same thing; for they flourish for a time and perish eternally. They flourish in unreal good things, and perish in real torments.

entries.section: 7. Their denial of immortality

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine For they knew not the mysteries of God, neither hoped for the wages of righteousness, nor estimated the honor of the souls that are blameless. [22]

The wicked do not know the mysteries of God, that is, His wisdom and purposes toward man, since they do not experience them in their lives. Neither do they care about what is stated in the Law about the recompense of the righteous and the destruction of the wicked. They did not know, or ignored, what is stated in the Book of Genesis about man, that he is the image of God, and was created in His likeness (Gen 1:27). Since they do not taste the earnest of heaven here, they have no portion with the righteous in the eternal glory, and do not even believe in it.
* Those who consent to iniquity have no portion among the immortal.

entries.section: 7. Their denial of immortality

paragraphs.text: St. Anthony the Great For God created man for immortality, and made him the image of His own eternity. [23]

* God was not content to create us out of nothing, but He also granted us by the grace of the Word the possibility of living according to God, but men turned their faces away from eternal things, and by the counsel of Satan turned to the works of natural corruption, and became themselves the cause of the corruption of death that befell them.
