She sets man up as a wise lord, able to act with power and wisdom, in holiness and righteousness. However great man's perfection and gifts and abilities and resources may be, without divine wisdom man is counted as nothing.

* Wisdom must be sought from God alone and not from philosophers or astrologers. God gives wisdom like a spring whose waters will not cease, and waters everyone who enters by it; but the wisdom of philosophers and other human agencies is not given generously, and soon dries up.

Hilary of Arles. * What blessing does that man not possess who seeks this wisdom and receives it from the Lord? This gives you understanding. What a grace this is; for if this wisdom were from ourselves it would not be from above, and we would not ask it from God who created us.

entries.section: 2. The need for divine wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine. For I am thy servant and the son of thine handmaid, a weak man and short-lived, with little understanding of judgment and laws. [5]

King Solomon confesses that he is a servant of the Lord and the son of His handmaid; what he receives from God is by His free grace and generous love, and not by personal merit. In the spirit of humility the king declares his inability to accomplish his mission with which God entrusted him, for his days are short and his understanding little, he has no knowledge nor learning nor experience, so he is in need of the grace of God, the giver of wisdom and understanding and insight.
* The weak in the flesh, who being wise in the world forsake their knowledge... become as children of their own free will, and so learn the wisdom that is not acquired by the toil of study.
St. Isaac the Syrian. * God grants wisdom that we may understand it as is fitting.

Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus. * Those who wish to return to their first rank will not be able to do so except by humility. For pride was the cause of the fall at the beginning from heaven. And so whoever lacks deep humility from all his heart and mind and spirit and body does not inherit the kingdom of God.

entries.section: 2. The need for divine wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Anthony the Great. For though one be perfect among the children of men, yet if thy wisdom be not with him, he shall be counted as nothing. [6]

Solomon realized that the feeling of self-sufficiency and not hungering and thirsting for God deprives man of every divine spiritual gift, even if he appears in the eyes of men successful and good and perfect.

* Everything that a person has through natural creation, when he exercises it, he receives what is through the grace of God. Thus he has an abundance and comes to be in a stronger state in what he has. This is not only with regard to wisdom, but in every good thing we must reflect upon the words of Solomon: "For though a man be perfect among the children of men, and thy wisdom be not with him, he shall be counted as nothing.

Origen. * The man who is wise by the standards of the world is in truth very ignorant, because he does not put away corrupt teaching. A little learning is a dangerous thing, for it makes those who possess it unwilling to learn more. The unlearned are more ready to learn; they are not so ignorant as those who think themselves wise.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 3. Every person has a mission

paragraphs.text: 7 Thou hast chosen me to be a king of thy people, and a judge of thy sons and daughters, 8 and hast commanded me to build a temple upon thy holy mount, and an altar in the city of thy dwelling, a resemblance of the holy tabernacle which thou hast prepared from the beginning.
Thou hast chosen me to be a king of thy people, and a judge of thy sons and daughters. [7]

Solomon prayed and received, for along with his realization of God's surpassing resources, and his need to enjoy God's wisdom and grace, he also realized that he has a special, distinct mission that will not be accomplished by human resources, but by the grace of God ready to work. For besides the general mission to which every man is committed, every person has a special mission, which it befits him to recognize in order to accomplish it according to God's plan and divine good pleasure. So Solomon was set up as king over the people of God for a mission according to God's plan.

entries.section: 3. Every person has a mission

paragraphs.text: And hast commanded me to build a temple upon thy holy mount, and an altar in thy dwelling place, a resemblance of the holy tabernacle, which thou hast prepared from the beginning. [8]

It was not possible for Moses the prophet to set up the tabernacle of the testimony according to his own human thought, but he set it up according to the pattern which the Lord showed him in heaven, that it might be an icon of heaven. For it is said: "Who serve unto the example and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was admonished of God when he was about to make the tabernacle: for, See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount" (Heb 8:5).

And now it was not in Solomon's mind to build the holy temple identical to the tent of meeting, but according to the holy tabernacle which God had prepared from the beginning, that is, the one existing in heaven.
This is the mission of every true believer, to set up by the Holy Spirit of God and divine wisdom a temple for the Lord after the likeness of heaven itself. As Holy Scripture says:
"Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" (1 Cor 3:16).
"If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are" (1 Cor 3:17).
"What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?" (1 Cor 6:19).

"Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God: and I will write upon him my new name" (Rev 3:12).
"He that sitteth on the throne shall dwell among them" (Rev 7:15).

* Everyone whom the Word of God leads to strive together in the way of godliness is a precious stone in the one great temple of God. Therefore Peter the Apostle says: "Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ" (1 Pet 2:5). And Paul the Apostle also says: "And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone" (Eph 2:20). Something similar is also found by a hidden allusion in that passage of Isaiah in which he addresses Jerusalem: "Behold, I will build thy stones with antimony, and lay thy foundations with sapphires, and make thy pinnacles rubies, and thy gates of carbuncle stones, and all thy borders of precious stones, and all thy children shall be taught of the Lord, and great shall be the peace of thy children" (Isa 54:11-14).
So among the righteous there are some who are antimony, and some who are sapphire, and others carbuncle, or precious stones, that is, there are in them all kinds for choosing.
Origen

entries.section: 4. A second cry for wisdom

paragraphs.text: 9 With thee is wisdom, which knoweth thy works, and which was present when thou madest the world, and knoweth what is pleasing in thine eyes, and what is right in thy commandments. 10 O send her out of thy holy heavens, and send her from the throne of thy glory, that being present she may labour with me, and I may know what is pleasing unto thee. 11 For she knoweth and understandeth all things, and she shall be to me a prudent guide in my doings, and preserve me by her glory. 12 So shall my works be acceptable, and I shall judge thy people with justice, and shall be worthy of my father's throne. 13 For what man is he that can know the counsel of God? or who can discern what the Lord willeth? 14 For the thoughts of men are hesitant, and our insights are not firm. 15 For the corruptible body presseth down the soul, and the earthly dwelling weigheth down the mind that is full of cares. 16 And hardly do we picture the things that are upon earth, and with toil do we perceive the things that are before us: but the things that are in the heavens, who hath searched them out?
With thee is wisdom, which knoweth thy works, and was present when thou madest the world, and knoweth what is pleasing in thine eyes, and what is right according to thy commandments. [9]

Solomon the wise looks toward the divine throne and sees the divine hypostasis of wisdom seated upon it, the object of the Father's delight and good pleasure. It is as though he had already heard the voice of the heavenly Father during the baptism of the Lord Christ as well as during His transfiguration: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Mt 3:17; 17:5; Mk 1:11; Lk 3:22; 2 Pet 1:17).

Solomon realized man's inability to be an object of the Father's delight, after he chose disobedience of his own will, and in pride accepted the counsel of the devil instead of believing the divine promises.
Solomon longed to acquire the divine wisdom and to be hidden in Him, so that through Him he might become an object of the Father's delight, and Solomon himself also take delight in God.

Holy Scripture has expressed the mutual delight between God and man in Jesus Christ the Crucified, who offered reconciliation between the Father and man. For this reason it is often said of the burnt offering, the symbol of the Cross: "it is a burnt offering unto the LORD: it is a sweet savour, an offering made by fire unto the LORD" (Ex 29:18; cf. Ex 29:15, 41; Lev 1:9, 17, etc.). This is about God's delight in us in Christ, the object of His delight. As for our side, it is said: "The fear of the Lord is glory, and boasting, and gladness, and a crown of rejoicing" (Sir 1:11). "The service keeps the heart, and justifies it, and gives gladness and joy" (Sir 1:18).

This is what drove Solomon toward seeking wisdom, since through the hypostasis of wisdom he becomes an object of God's delight, and himself enjoys delight and joy. The son of Sirach says of wisdom: "Whoever loves her loves life, and they that seek to her early shall be filled with joy. He that holdeth her fast shall inherit glory, and wheresoever she entereth, there is the blessing of the Lord" (Sir 4:12-13).
* Make us happy, O my God, in our occupation with You, so that we do not lose You.
* I say, happy is he who possesses God.

entries.section: 4. A second cry for wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine. O send her out of thy holy heavens, and send her from the throne of thy glory, that being present she may stand by me and labour with me, and I may know what is pleasing unto thee. [10]

Solomon was longing for the coming of the Lord Christ, the heavenly Word. He asks that the wisdom of God come down from the holy heavens, to carry him to heaven and bestow upon him the holy life. And that He be sent from the throne of glory, to bring him in to the throne.
The wisdom of God came to stand at our side against the devil, and to work in us and by us and with us, and to disclose to us the Father's delight in us.
* James (Jas 1:6) shows that the foundation of all human wisdom is faith. Here he attacks Simon the Magician, who asked the two Apostles to give him the Holy Spirit, and did not ask to receive faith.
Hilary of Arles. * Today "the carpenter's son"... made for Himself a living ladder, setting its base upon the earth, and its head rose toward heaven, and upon it God rests.

It is she whose image Jacob contemplated (Gen 28:12); by her God came down in His steadfastness, or rather bowed down in condescension, and "shewed himself upon earth, and conversed with men" (Bar 3:38).

Father John of Damascus. * How does God take the wise in their own craftiness? (Job 5:13) By showing them, while they think they are able to work without God, that they rather have need of Him. They enter into distress until they show themselves to be less than fishermen and the unlearned, and where they cannot work without their wisdom.

entries.section: 4. A second cry for wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom. For she knoweth and understandeth all things, and shall lead me wisely in my doings, and preserve me by her glory. [11]

Who knoweth the Father but the Son, and he to whom the Son reveals Him? The Son, "Wisdom," alone is able to disclose to us the divine mysteries, and to give us our understanding, and to take us by the hands to lead us to heavenly glory, keeping us from the evil enemy.
* Spiritual wisdom is the cause of every perfect work. This is the heavenly wisdom, and when we are strengthened by it we can do everything perfectly.

Theophylact. * It is right for us to be there in the presence of God in the heavens, we who kept the lesson while we were on earth, and went there to heaven to be in the love of God the Father, whom we knew while on earth, and because God the Word the Holy One made all things and taught us and teaches us all things, and He trains us in all good things.

entries.section: 4. A second cry for wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Clement of Alexandria. So shall my works be acceptable, and I shall judge thy people righteously, and shall be worthy of my father's throne. [12]
Without the Lord Christ our works will not be accepted, nor will our mission be accomplished.
* Do you also concede this, that Christ is "the power of God, and the wisdom of God"? You answer: "We concede this."

Listen then: "The spirit of the righteous is the seat of wisdom" (Wis 1). Yes, for what is the seat of God but the place where He dwells? And where does God dwell but in His temple? "For the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are" (1 Cor 3:17).
Be watchful in your reception of God. "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth" (Jn 4:24).
Let the ark of the covenant enter your hearts, and let Dagon fall, if you will" (1 Sam 5:3).
Listen now. And learn to long for God. Be ready to learn how to see God. For He says: "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God."

entries.section: 4. A second cry for wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine. For what man is he that can know the counsel of God? or who can conceive what the will of the Lord is? [13]
Our Christ declares in us the divine will, and gives us the ability to carry it out in practice.

* If I am not mistaken, it is not mentioned anywhere that He (Jesus Christ) prayed with His disciples. In every place He prayed alone, because human prayers cannot take hold of the counsels of God (Wis 9:13; Isa 40:13), and no one can share in the inner mysteries of Christ.

entries.section: 4. A second cry for wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose. For the thoughts of mortal men are miserable, and our considerations are not firm [14]

Solomon the wise confesses that he is in need of the divine wisdom, who declares the will of the Father and fulfills it in us, and even gives us steadfastness in Him, so that our thoughts are not like a storm at the mercy of the winds, nor our longings and thoughts wavering.

* The psalmist sings: "Come ye unto him, and be enlightened: and your faces shall not be ashamed" (Ps 34:5). We draw near to God by faith, and faith is the work of the spirit and not of the body. But since we do not know what degree of perfection the spiritual body attains, for we are speaking here of a matter in which we have no experience, but on the responsibility of Holy Scripture we do not speak in a definite manner, we must have recourse to the words of the Book of Wisdom: "The thoughts of men are hesitant, and our considerations are not firm" (Wis 9:14).

entries.section: 4. A second cry for wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine. For the corruptible body presseth down the soul, and the earthly tabernacle weigheth down the mind that is full of cares. [15]

Origen sees that those who love God with all their souls and desire to be united with Him draw themselves away from the weight of the (lusts of the) body and all material things, praying with the Apostle Paul: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" (Rom 7:24). They groan in this tabernacle (that of the body), being burdened with the corruptible body (2 Cor 5:4).

* Why then do we hesitate and doubt to put off the corruptible man who hinders us and weighs down the soul, the earthly tabernacle that fills the mind with many cares, so that we may be freed from our bonds, and turn back from the stormy waves that are the lot of flesh and blood? For by this we enjoy Christ Jesus, the rest that accompanies blessedness, and contemplate in Him in His fullness the life-giving Word. And as we feed on Him we perceive the manifold wisdom in Him, and are sealed with the very truth, and our minds are enlightened with the light of true knowledge that does not grow dim, and we enjoy the sight of those things which are seen by the eyes enlightened by the commandment of the Lord (Ps 19:8; Eph 1:18).

Origen. * We were told by the prophet to rend our hearts and not our garments (Joel 2:13), which we can do when we remember that we ourselves often sin at least in thought if not in deed. For the earthly tabernacle represents the mind full of cares (Wis 9:15), and our earth does not cease to produce thorns and thistles for us. We are unable to eat our bread unless we toil with effort and the sweat of our brow.

Father Fulgentius. * Even if our dust is to some extent bound to evil, and the earthly tabernacle presses down upon the soul that flies to the heights (Wis 9:15), which was created to soar on high; yet let the image be washed from defilement and lift up the body that is its partner in the yoke, lifting it up on the two wings of the mind.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus. * We must not ascribe deviation in the wandering of the heart to human nature or to its Creator, for Holy Scripture says truly: "God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions" (Eccl 7:29). The difference of thoughts depends upon ourselves, for good thought draws near to those who know it and the sensible man finds it. So whatever is subject to our discernment and our work we can attain, and if we do not attain it this is due to our laziness and neglect and not to a fault in our nature.

If this matter were not within our power the Lord would not have rebuked the Pharisees, saying: "Wherefore think ye evil in your hearts?" (Mt 9:4). Nor would the prophet have been commissioned to say: "put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes" (Isa 1:16), "How long shall thy vain thoughts lodge within thee?" (Jer 4:14), nor would the kind of our thoughts have been considered on the Day of Judgment, since God threatens through Isaiah, saying: "And I will recompense their works and their thoughts" (Isa 66:18). It would not be right to recompense or punish according to the testimony of our thoughts in that dreadful and deadly examination, since the blessed Apostle says: "their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another. In the day when God shall judge the secrets of men according to my gospel" (Rom 2:15-16).

Father Serenus. * Shall we be young or old when we rise? If we die young (as children) and rise young, we shall need nurses in the resurrection. In any case, if we die young and rise old, then the dead do not rise at all; they will be changed into new beings.

Will there be distinction of sex in the world to come? Or will there be no such distinction? If the distinction continues there will be marriage and bodily relations and the begetting of children. If it does not continue, then the bodies that will rise will not be themselves. It is said: "The earthly tabernacle weigheth down the mind that is full of cares" (Wis 9:15). But the bodies that we have in heaven will be refined and spiritual, as the Apostle says: "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body" (1 Cor 15:44).

St. Jerome. * Share with me in my labor, for you see what I have undertaken, and who I am who have undertaken it. You see what I desire to speak about, and where and what my condition is except that I am in [the corruptible body that weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling that weighs down the mind full of many cares (cf. Wis 9:15). Therefore I strip my thought of the many things, and gather it in the one God, the indivisible Trinity, so that I may be able to see something to speak about. Let them know that in that [body (which) weighs down the soul] I am able to say "Unto thee, O LORD, do I lift up my soul" (Ps 25:1) LXX (that I may be able to speak to you of things worthy of the subject). May the Lord help me and lift up my soul with me. For I am very weak in relation to Him, and He is very mighty in relation to me."

* (The righteous) who have died have truly been stripped of the corruptible body that weighs down the soul (Wis 9:15). But they still await the redemption of their bodies (Rom 8:23), where their bodies rest in hope (Acts 2:26), but have not yet shone with the incorruption that is to come.
* Let us bear in mind that in this body that weighs down the soul (Wis 9:15) we live a miserable life.

* We are men who carry a body, which walks in this life; and although we have been born again of the seed of the word of God, yet in Christ we have been renewed in such a way that we have still not been completely delivered from Adam. For truly the mortal and corruptible part weighs down the soul (Wis 9:15), showing itself to be present, and declaring that it is from Adam, but what is spiritual in us and raises up the soul is the gift of God and of His mercy, who sent His only-begotten Son to share our death and lead us to His immortality.

* Let us lift up our souls to God, and not against God, for it is said: "Unto thee, O LORD, do I lift up my soul" (Ps 25:1). Let us lift them up with His help, for they are heavy. And what is the cause of their heaviness? Because the corruptible body weighs down the soul (Wis 9:15), and the earthly tabernacle presses upon it, and it is occupied with many things.
* Since we are burdened with such a very heavy load, under which we groan, how shall I lift up my soul unless He lifts it up with me, He who gave Himself for me?

* On one side our corruptible body is a weight upon our souls, and on the other the cause of this hindrance is not in the nature and essence of the body. Therefore, since we know its corruption, we do not desire to be unclothed of the body but rather that it put on its incorruption. In the immortal life we shall have a body, but it will no longer be a weight since it will no longer be corruptible... We have been weighed down, then, by this corruptible body. But since we know that this state of weight is not from the nature and essence of the body but from its corruption, we therefore do not desire to be rid of it but to put it on with its incorruption. Then there will be a body, but it will no longer be a weight because it will no longer be corruptible.
* This body that is dead because of sin lives, which is without doubt corruptible and is a weight upon the soul (Wis 9:13).
* The word "corruptible" was added to show that the soul is weighed down not by any body whatever, but by the body that has come to this state through the fruit of sin.

* If every sin is evil, who can resist? We answer: The nature of man is good and at the same time also able to be freed from evil. For this reason we pray earnestly: "deliver us from evil" (Mt 6:13). This deliverance is not fully accomplished as long as the soul is weighed down by the body that hastens toward corruption (Wis 9:15). In any case, this process is accomplished by grace through faith, so that it is said: [O death, where is thy struggle? O death, where is thy sting? The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law] (cf. 1 Cor 15:55-56).

* The prayer of the whole City of God, while she is in a state of exile, cries out to God with the mouth of all her members: "Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors" (Mt 6:12). This prayer is effective not for those who have a dead faith without works (Jas 2:17), but for those whose faith worketh by love (Gal 5:6). For they, though subject to God, are weighed down by the corruptible body (Wis 9:15), so long as it is mortal, and it has not complete authority over vice. For this reason the righteous need this prayer. For although they exercise authority, the vices do not submit without resistance.

St. Augustine. St. Augustine fears that the believer may fall into despair when he is fought with a fleshly lust or a carnal thought that weighs upon the soul, for as long as man is in this world the corruptible body remains resisting, but there is a great difference between resistance and surrender.

* Although every crime is a sin, not every sin is a crime. Thus we say that the life of the saints may be free from crime, but as John the Apostle says: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 Jn 1:8). But even crimes themselves, however great, can be forgiven in the Holy Church, and there is no despair of God's mercy for those who truly repent, each according to the measure of his sin.

entries.section: 4. A second cry for wisdom

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine. And hardly do we guess at things that are upon earth, and with difficulty do we find the things that are before us: but the things that are in the heavens, who can discover? [16]

With difficulty man can come to know some of the secrets of the visible world, and yet he still stands on the shore of the ocean of knowledge, so how can he come to know the secrets of the heavenly God and the heavenly things? Does he not need the divine wisdom to declare by Himself concerning Himself and His Father and His Holy Spirit?

* While the seraphim are not able even to behold God, who does not reveal Himself to them except as a condescension on His part according to their weakness, we see men who dare to picture in their minds the very nature which the seraphim are unable to comprehend. They claim that they are able to look upon it clearly and without limits. Tremble, O heavens, and be astonished, O earth".

* "Truly God is incomprehensible and cannot be approached, even for these orders. For this reason He condescends to appear in the manner recorded in the Revelation. God, who is not bounded by place and does not sit upon a throne... out of His love for us appears seated on a throne with the heavenly powers surrounding Him.

When He appeared on the throne and these powers surrounded Him, these powers could not behold Him nor bear to look at the brightness of His light, so they covered their eyes with their wings, and they had nothing left but to praise and sing with hymns full of glory and holy trembling, and songs bearing witness to the holiness of Him who sits upon the throne."
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 5. A third cry

paragraphs.text: 17 And thy counsel who hath known, except thou give wisdom, and send thy Holy Spirit from above? 18 For so the ways of them which are upon the earth were set straight, and men were taught the things that are pleasing unto thee, 19 and by wisdom were saved all that pleased thee, O Lord, from the beginning.
And who hath known thy counsel, except thou give wisdom, and send thy Holy Spirit from on high? [17]
Our Christ, who loved us even unto death so as to save us and bring us into union with Him, offers us on the night of His passion another Comforter, saying:

"But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you" (Jn 14:16-18, 26).
"But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me" (Jn 15:26).

"Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak: and he will shew you things to come. He shall glorify me: for he shall receive of mine, and shall shew it unto you" (Jn 16:13-14).

* A man does not have wisdom and understanding and counsel and fortitude and knowledge and godliness and the fear of God unless he receives the spirit of wisdom and understanding and counsel and fortitude and knowledge and godliness and the fear of God, according to the saying of the Apostle (2 Tim 1:7; Isa 11:2-3).

* This is the wisdom that tames the tongue, descending from above (Jas 3:17), and does not spring from a human heart. Would anyone dare to snatch it away from the grace of God and, in the conceit of pride, put it under the authority of man?
St. Augustine. * Wisdom is given not through a book that one learns, but through the enlightenment of the Holy Spirit.

Father Ambrosiaster. * When the soul is united with the Comforter Spirit in ineffable intimacy, and is wholly mingled with the Spirit, it is counted worthy to become itself spirit, and in its mingling with Him it then becomes wholly light and eye and joy and rest and gladness and love and compassion and goodness and tender mercies.

entries.section: 5. A third cry

paragraphs.text: St. Macarius the Great. So the ways of them which live upon the earth were set straight, and men were taught what pleaseth thee, and by wisdom they received salvation." [18]

We were in need of the incarnation of God, the Son the Word, the Second Hypostasis, that the incarnate God might come forward, in the depths of His love for me, bearing death for me in His body. And though the mind is unable to comprehend the depths of God's love for him... God the Word becomes flesh, He who fills all with His divinity!! God the Word becomes incarnate to suffer and bear shame!!

* If they had given thanks to God who gave this wisdom, they would not have ascribed anything to themselves. For this reason the Lord gave them up to the lusts of their hearts and they did what is not fitting.

St. Augustine. * "We have peace with God" (Rom 5:1), through our Lord Jesus Christ who reconciled us with God through the sacrifice of His blood... Christ came to destroy the enemies, and to make peace, and to reconcile us with God from whom we had been separated by the barrier of evil that we set up by our sins.
Origen
Let me acquire You, O You who sit upon the throne
* I cry out to You, O Father of the fathers.
You want to make of me a father who loves all mankind.
You want to pour Your mercy into me, that I may become merciful through You, O Lord of mercy.
You wish to give me wisdom and understanding, O my Creator!
* You created me to rule the world in holiness and righteousness.
Sanctify me and I shall be sanctified, and I shall long to see the whole world sanctified to You.
Justify me and I shall be justified, and I shall not cease from prayer and constant work, until all are justified by You.
You did not create man a slave but free.
You created him that his heart might open with love to all mankind.
He rules, not by domination nor by commands, but by largeness of heart and by giving and bestowing!
* When I look around me, I long to love every person without exception.
But who can give largeness to my heart except You?
I lift the eyes of my heart to Your throne, and I am filled with honor, and I realize Your pride in me, I feel that I am a son among Your sons!
You lift me from the dust to heaven.
You raise me from weakness to strength, * I confess to You that I am weak, and my days are few and numbered.
And my understanding of things is feeble.
But there is no place in me for faintheartedness.
For I am Your servant and the son of Your handmaid.
You carry me in Your hands to Your bosom.
You give me surpassing resources from Yourself!
* My soul praises You, who have chosen me for Yourself!
You have granted me to surrender to You my whole being, so that You make of me a holy temple, even my body becomes a spiritual tabernacle!
You created me for a mission from You.
Make known to me: what do You want me to do?
Lead me all the way by Your wisdom.
Without You I shall not know how to begin!
Without You I shall not continue in the work!
Without You I shall not reach the end!
* Sanctify my mind, that I may know Your will.
And sanctify my will, that it may be in harmony with Your will.
Work in me, that everything that does not please You may flee from me!
And let not the enemy of good be able to lead me astray, nor the love of the world to seduce me, nor the lusts of the flesh to break my spirit, nor the earthly tabernacle to weigh me down with cares.
* I cry out to You, O divine Wisdom, shine upon me with Your light, that my soul may be enlightened and perceive Your mysteries.
The doors of heaven will open before me, and I shall enjoy the sight of You.
You carry me to You, and I shall enjoy the fellowship of glory.
To You belongs salvation, O Savior of the world!

entries.section: 1. The role of wisdom in the life of Adam

paragraphs.text: 1 She preserved the first-formed father of the world, when he was created alone, 2 and delivered him out of his fall, and gave him strength to have dominion over all things.
It was she who watched over the first one formed, the father of the world, after he was created alone, and delivered him from his fall. [1]

It is difficult to perceive the role of divine wisdom in protecting Adam while he was in the garden of Eden, but Adam's giving of names to the animals for the first time, without enjoying the experiences of predecessors (Gen 2:18-20), requires great wisdom and authority. Moreover, when Adam fell because of his disobedience, God did not forsake him but took up his cause, and the wisdom of God offered him the way of salvation.

* When Adam transgressed the commandment of God and obeyed the wicked serpent, he became sold, or sold himself, to Satan, and the soul, that sensible creation which God fashioned in His own image, was clothed with the soul of the wicked one like a garment. Therefore the Apostle says: "Having spoiled principalities and powers, he triumphed over them in the cross" (Col 2:15), and this is the purpose for which the Lord came (into the world), that He might cast them out and recover His house and His temple, that is, man.

St. Macarius the Great. * He loosed Adam, the chief of the captives, from his bond, for the Savior heard the voice of the prisoner, and came down and rescued him from under the earth, that He might raise him to the height of heaven.

St. Jacob of Serugh. As for his being "alone," perhaps it means that he is the only one whom God created from the dust and breathed into him the breath of life, while Eve came from his side, and their children were born of them. Or perhaps it means that he is unique, given authority over all creatures (Gen 1:26-28; Wis 9:2-3).: Some think that Adam, when he was alone, before the creation of Eve, who played her part in his temptation.

entries.section: 1. The role of wisdom in the life of Adam

paragraphs.text: And gave him strength to have dominion over all things. [2]

St. Gregory of Nyssa looks upon man as a unique being, the object of God's surpassing love, whom He created, alone among all, in His image and likeness. He set him up as king... therefore He did not form him until after the creation of the whole world, as a royal palace for the beloved king, man! He created him to bear witness to Him by sharing His goodness, so that he bears fellowship in the divine attributes, especially love and holiness... as He also gave him authority. And when he fell by his own will, and chose evil, which is not the work of God but the absence of virtue, He did not leave him, but the divine Word came incarnate to restore to him his first image, and to bring him into sonship to God, and to return to him his paradisal state... He is the goal of God's work of salvation.
* All the world is well-ordered and awaits man; issue Your command, O working power, that he may come and take possession of his dominion.
* He placed over his head a lock of hair like a crown, that he might be known by his creatures to be a king.

* (Adam) stood alone as the image of [the Son], full of beauty, and the creatures feared the image and obeyed it; the likeness of the Son appeared in the heir who was formed, and the heights and the depths and all creatures submitted to him, the new Christ; Adam, who became an image of the Son, stood in the world, and all the world knelt and worshiped him.

The light longed for him, because the image of light was pictured on his face, and heaven rejoiced and its light hastened to serve him, the sea was glad and prepared its fishes to present to him, and the earth was pleased and knelt and worshiped with its trees, the sun and the moon offered him their rays, and by their rising they were adorning the new Lord, the new reptiles and what is in the waters, and the birds flying in the air, were worshiping him in pairs and pairs, and boasting of him, all the beasts and animals and the kinds that came to be bowed the shoulder to put the yoke on their necks, the possessions came before the owner in choirs and choirs, and companies and companies, and throngs and throngs, and pairs and pairs, they came worshiping, and full of trust and love, and the head of the wild beasts was bowed to submit to him, there was pictured on Adam the great image of divinity, and as soon as the world saw him all of it submitted to him, all the kinds of beasts and animals came forward, and worshiped him, and he set his seal upon his possessions.
St. Jacob of Serugh

entries.section: 2. The role of wisdom in the life of Abel

paragraphs.text: 3 But when the unrighteous man departed from her in his anger, he perished in the fury in which he murdered his brother.
But when the unrighteous man departed from her in his anger, he perished in the fury with which he killed his brother. [3]
By the "unrighteous man" he means Cain (Gen 4:8-13), for because of his injustice to his brother and his shedding his blood he died spiritually (perished).
Cain's offering was rejected because of the impurity of his heart, and when Cain abandoned wisdom he was defeated by his anger, and brought upon his life misery and wretchedness.

In unwisdom Cain despised the life of his brother Abel, and behold, he despises God Himself in his speaking with Him. For every sin aimed at our brothers drives us to sin against God Himself. And as St. John Chrysostom says:

[Let none of us despise another, for this is an evil work that teaches us to make light of God Himself. In truth, if one scorns another, he scorns God, who commanded us to show every concern for others. Cain despised his brother, and at once made light of God.]

* You know, my dear, that the sign of an offering accepted by God is the descent of fire from heaven and the burning of the offering. When Abel and Cain offered their offerings together, the living fire that ministers before God (Ps 104:4) came down and consumed the pure sacrifice of Abel, while it did not touch the impure sacrifice of Cain. Thus Abel knew the acceptance of his offering and Cain the rejection of his offering. The fruits of Cain's heart were afterward made known when he was tested and his heart was found full of deceit, when he killed his brother, so that what he conceived in his mind his hands brought forth. But the purity of Abel's heart was the foundation of his prayer.

St. Aphrahat the Persian Sage. Cain committed a most hideous crime, and yet if he had sought the wisdom of God it would have removed his folly from him and he would have offered a repentance that would save him, as St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian says.

* God appeared to Cain with gentleness, so that if he repented the sin of murder that his fingers committed would be pardoned by the contrition of his lips. If he did not repent, a bitter sentence would fall upon him, in keeping with his wicked folly.
St. Ephrem the Syrian

entries.section: 3. Its role in the life of Noah

paragraphs.text: 4 And when the flood overwhelmed the earth because of him, wisdom again saved it, guiding the righteous man in a vessel of mean wood.
And when the flood overwhelmed the earth because of him, wisdom again saved it.
Guiding the righteous man by a paltry piece of wood. [4]
The righteous man here is Noah, who escaped the flood by the ark.

For the first time Holy Scripture mentions that the flood was a result of the evil that multiplied on the earth because of Cain, and that God preserved the world for the sake of righteous Noah and his family by means of a mean wood, that is, the ark, as a symbol of the Cross, the sign of shame and disgrace and curse among the Jews.

He attributes the flood to the unrighteous "Cain," since he reckons him an example, which the wicked imitated in the days of Noah. In Josephus the Jewish historian it is said that the wicked are the sons of Cain according to Jewish tradition, though this does not appear in Holy Scripture.

Attributing the flood to the sin of Cain seems to be a kind of exaggeration, but the writer looks to the hideousness of this sin together with God's long-suffering toward the descendants of Cain, and when the measure was full the flood came.

If the wicked, because they did not enjoy the divine wisdom, were corrupted in their evils and exposed to the flood, then Noah in contrast held fast to the wisdom of God, and so enjoyed the symbol of the Cross and the Church, that is, the ark, and was saved from destruction.

* That ark was a sign of the Church, the bride of Christ, which is His holy congregation, just as the ark was joined one part to another by Christ from many races and countries and tongues. Christ gathered them to faith in Him, and made all one by His Spirit, gathered together by His love and their keeping of His commandments like the gathering of the wood of the ship one to another by nailing and the laying on of pitch. Likewise the fear of Christ and His love in the assembly of believers who fear and love Him, and one another, and their being nailed together by spiritual love, and their union together by keeping the commandments, so that all may be one ark, one body of Christ. Each of them, as God has given him of the gifts, serves another who has not received them... God told Noah to lay on pitch inside and outside, that is, that love be within their hearts toward one another, cleansing their outside by their services and care and consolation of one another, nailed together with the nails of the fear of the Lord, and love covers them from the entry of Satan to them, as the pitch protects the ship from the entry of water.

And as the planks of the ship cannot be joined one to another except by nails, so the congregation cannot be gathered in harmony one with another except by the fear of Christ our God... And because the Church believes in the Trinity, he pointed to the mention of the Trinity in the ship, repeating on every side the three decks and the height of three hundred and thirty cubits.
St. Ephrem the Syrian

entries.section: 4. Its role in the life of Abraham

paragraphs.text: And when the nations conspired in evil and were put to shame together, it is she who knew the righteous man, and kept him blameless before God, 5 It is she who, when the multitude of the nations agreed together in evil, found the righteous man and preserved him for God without blemish, and kept his inward parts deaf toward his son.
And kept him stronger than his tender affection for his son. [5]

He refers here to the Babylonians who joined together to build the tower of Babel for fear that the flood would be repeated, so that they might escape it. They look to God as an enemy, and so wisdom turned aside from them, and they thought they were able to flee from God. They dealt with the matter by human wisdom instead of the divine wisdom that calls us to flee from the divine wrath by throwing ourselves into the bosom of God and enjoying His mercy through repentance. Their deprivation of wisdom drove them to shame, where their tongues were confused, and they were scattered in the world (Gen 11).

* The peoples and multitudes applauded with one opinion to begin the work of iniquity with a hard heart: Come, let us take possession of the land, and dwell in it with might, like a gathered host lest it be scattered over the lands, let us hold to one another lest we be lost in the countries. Let us become one people and not be called peoples on the earth, let us build a village that the flood will not overcome, and let us erect a building that the waves will not sweep away, let us begin with a work that the rivers will not pierce, and let us make a fortress that can deliver from the flood, let us build a tower such that if the waters come out upon the earth and strike it, their waves will not overthrow it, let us lay a foundation such that if the great sea opens it will not break it or harm it with the strong waves, let us make sure and build something new that will not fall, and if the deep opens it will not reach it, and by skill let us build a great fortress in the name of the dreadful might and let us go up to heaven, let us go up and be neighbors of the sun in its high place and let our dwelling be by it and near it, let us go up and settle in the course in which the moon works, and look upon the changing of the seasons as they revolve, come let us go up to the stars of light in their courses, and come let us make for ourselves a name more famous than theirs, come let us rise to where the powers pass, and let us be companions of the galaxy that bears the times, let us build a chamber that is a beginning and an end: there was not one like it and nothing equal to it will ever come to be on the earth, come let us make for ourselves a village that reaches to heaven, and dwell there in the place high above harms, let us make a wondrous ascent by means of our gathering, and by it let us go up from the earth into the air, let us leave the clouds and take dominion over a place above them, and let us leave the winds and then rise to the heights, let us make bricks and burn them with fire, and let us raise a building of stone that will not be destroyed.

St. Jacob of Serugh. In contrast to that, Abraham lived in the midst of pagan peoples, even his tribe worshiped the moon, but wisdom preserved him to be a father of all believers (Wis 10:5). By wisdom Abraham offered his son as a sacrifice to God, reckoning his love for God greater than his love for his only son, and so he enjoyed righteousness.

God gave man the mind as a divine gift that it befits him to sanctify for his edification in all aspects of his life. But the people of the land of Shinar abused the gift because they did not ask God's wisdom for their sanctification, and in pride they thought they were able to face God's disciplines by human ways. They wanted to set up a tower with its head in heaven, and they went down all the more to the abyss. A painful picture of him who rejects the wisdom of God and relies on his own human wisdom.

* See how evil are greatness and pride with wisdom! All were gathered and agreed. They magnified themselves, so God scattered them. Thus greatness scatters the company of all the boastful... The Lord came down to see their deed. Thus He prophesied beforehand of His coming down in the body for the sins of men at the end of time... He mentioned the coming down to the children of Israel to train them in it and lead them on step by step, so that they would not deny the true coming down in His incarnation.

St. Ephrem the Syrian. Here the wise man compares a people who relied in pride on their human wisdom, so they were scattered, with Abraham who believed in God and loved Him, and offered his only son as a burnt offering. Isaac returned with him, from whom came the One in whom all the nations are blessed.
* By faith Abraham did not hesitate when he offered his only son, in whom he had received the promises, for he reckoned that God was able to raise him up from the dead (Heb 11:17-19).

Thus the Apostle gives us a report of the thoughts of the believing man, that faith in the resurrection had been established at that time in Isaac. Therefore Abraham hoped for the raising of Isaac, and believed what would happen in the future and had not yet happened.
Now how can the children of Abraham not believe what is actually happening in Christ, when Abraham believed that it would happen, and that in Isaac?
Rather, I speak more clearly: Abraham knew himself to be a symbol of the image of the coming truth.
He knew that Christ would be born of his seed, He who would be offered a true sacrifice for the whole world and that He would rise from the dead.
Origen. By the wisdom of God, and not by his own abilities or understanding, Abraham perceived the things to come as though they were present in his life.
* When Abraham offered his son Isaac, he was a symbol of God the Father, while Isaac was a symbol of our Lord and Savior.
Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles

entries.section: 5. Its role in the life of Lot

paragraphs.text: 6 It is she who delivered the righteous man from the perishing ungodly; he fled from the fire that fell upon the five cities. 7 To this day a waste land that smoketh testifieth of their wickedness, and plants bearing fruit that never ripens, and a standing pillar of salt as a memorial of a soul that did not believe. 8 For those who neglected wisdom were not only deprived of knowing the good, but left to men a memorial of their folly, so that they could not hide the things in which they slipped. 9 But those who served wisdom she delivered out of every toil.
It was she who delivered the righteous man when the wicked perished, as he fled from the fire that fell upon the five cities. [6]
The righteous man here is Lot, and the five cities, the Pentapolis, which are in the plain, are: Sodom and Gomorrah and Admah, Zeboiim, and Bela or Zoar (Gen 14:2).

St. Jerome has a beautiful comment on the character of Lot, for he says that since Lot's faith was little he went to Zoar and so saved a small town from destruction, and if he had greater faith he would have saved more and larger cities.

Wisdom delivered Lot from the fire that fell and the smoke that rose from the five cities, from which none escaped except Zoar, which God spared so that Lot might dwell in it. And when his wife lost wisdom she looked back, and became a pillar of salt.

Philo the Jew of Alexandria mentions that even in his days the place still gave off smoke, and it is likely that it was at the southern end of the Dead Sea where a chain of mountains extends for a distance of 8 km, on most of which salt is piled up, and called the mountains of Sodom, and there are to this day some pillars of salt, one of which is called Lot's wife.

Lot lived in Sodom, whose people were marked by evils and corruption, and as Peter the Apostle says: "And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked: for that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds" (2 Pet 2:7-8). He was dwelling in their midst, but he was fleeing from them in his heart so as not to share in their iniquities. Therefore when Lot went out he never thought of looking back toward the people of Sodom. He fled from their evils, and consequently fled from the fire that fell upon them. St. Ambrose urged us to follow his example, fleeing from the love of the evil world and from indulgence in evil.
* Let us flee like Lot, who feared the crimes of the people of Sodom more than the punishments that came upon them.

* Certainly the holy man chooses to shut his house before the men of Sodom, and to flee from the contagion of their transgressions. When he dwelt with them he did not become acquainted with them, for he did not know their evils, and he fled from their shame. When he fled he did not look back toward them, since he did not wish to share with them.

He who withdraws from vices and renounces the way of life of his (wicked) fellow citizens is in a state of flight like Lot. Such a man does not look back, but enters the upper city through the paths of his thoughts, and does not withdraw from it until the death of the high priest who bears the sins of the world.

Truly He (our Christ the high priest) died once, but He dies for every person who is baptized into the death of Christ, so that we may be buried together with one another with Him, and rise with Him, and walk in newness of life (Col 2:12; Rom 6:4).

Your flight is good if your heart does not act upon the counsel of sinners and their way. Your flight is good if your eyes flee from seeing the cups and drinking vessels, so that they do not become fixed, longing for wine. Your flight is good if you do not answer the fool according to his folly (Prov 23:33) LXX. Your flight is good if your steps are far from the ways of the foolish. Truly man soon turns aside by evil counsels, but if you wish your flight to be good, let your ways be far from their words.

entries.section: 5. Its role in the life of Lot

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose. To this day a waste land that smoketh testifieth of their wickedness, and plants bearing fruit that does not ripen in its season, and a standing pillar of salt as a memorial of a soul that did not believe. [7]
Smoke: perhaps because of the haze or the light mist rising from the basin of the Dead Sea, or the heat because of the continental climate.

As for this plant, Josephus refers to it, and calls it the apple of Sodom, a plant that appears in that region and looks to the eye as if it can be eaten, but inside it is a black powder that cannot be eaten.
St. Ambrose says that Satan and Sodom are both behind man, so the believer must look forward, not backward, until he reaches the mountain with Lot and does not become a pillar of salt like his wife.
Origen sees in Lot a symbol of the soul earnest in its salvation which looks forward, while his wife symbolizes the body that wishes to hinder the soul from its spiritual longings and earnestness.

* When the soul walks toward salvation, the body looks back, and seeks pleasures. The Lord also said of this: "No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God" (Lk 9:62). He adds: "Remember Lot's wife." For truly she became a pillar of salt, appearing as a clear sign of folly. The salt represents the wisdom which she lost.

Origen. * God looks precisely at the real inner goal, like the wife of Lot, who alone with her whole will had inclined toward the evil of the world. He left her rigid and without feeling and made her like a pillar of salt, and left her without strength, unable to move, like a statue, but not without benefit, for she became (an example) so that those who have spiritual perception may be salted.

entries.section: 5. Its role in the life of Lot

paragraphs.text: St. Clement of Alexandria. And those who turned aside from wisdom were not only harmed by not knowing the good, but left behind them for the world a memorial of their folly, so that they cannot hide their stumblings. [8]

entries.section: 5. Its role in the life of Lot

paragraphs.text: But wisdom delivered her servants out of their toils. [9]

After mentioning examples of the work of wisdom in the lives of men from Adam to Lot, and the effect of being deprived of her, he gave in verses 8 and 9 a discourse on the danger of lacking wisdom, which arises from folly, and how wisdom delivered her servants from their toils.

On this pattern there came in the Constitutions of the Apostles a discourse of St. James the son of Zebedee, much like a prayer to God, in which he declares the blessings of the work of God's (wisdom) in some men of the Old Testament and the destruction of him who avoids her:

[You are the eternal knowledge, the perpetual insight, the unbegotten hearing, the natural wisdom... You subjected all creation to him (Adam) and gave him freedom to bring food for himself by his sweat and toil, while it is You who made the fruits of the earth sprout and grow and ripen... You called him to be reformed again and to loose the bonds of death, and You promised him life after the resurrection. Not him alone, but when he grew in abundance to an innumerable multitude, those who continued with You You glorified, and those who denied You You punished.
While You accepted the sacrifice of Abel (Gen 4) as that of a holy man, You rejected the gift of Cain, the killer of his brother, as that of a wretched and hateful one.

Besides this You accepted from Seth and Enosh (their gift), and translated Enoch, for You are the Creator of men and the giver of life and the support of the needy and the giver of laws and the rewarder of those who keep them and the chastiser of those who disobey them.

It was You who brought the flood upon the world because of the multitudes of the wicked (Gen 6-7), and saved righteous Noah from the flood by the ark (1 Pet 3:20) with eight souls, where was the end of a former generation and the beginning of a later one.

It was You who kindled a terrible fire against the five cities of Sodom and turned the fruitful land into a salt lake for the wicked who dwelt there (Wis 10:6; Gen 19; Ps 107:34). But You snatched Lot the holy man from the great burning.

It was You who delivered Abraham from the evil of his forefathers, and made him heir of the world, and revealed to him Your Christ, and appointed Melchizedek as a high priest to present worship to You (Gen 12 etc.).
It was You who compensated Your patient servant Job, the conqueror of the serpent, which represents evil.
It was You who made Isaac a son of the promise, Jacob a father of twelve sons...]

entries.section: 6. Its role in the life of Jacob

paragraphs.text: 10 It is she who guided the righteous man, when he fled from his brother's wrath, in straight paths, and showed him the kingdom of God, and gave him knowledge of holy things, and made him prosper in his labors, and multiplied the fruits of his works. 11 In the covetousness of those who oppressed him she stood by him and made him rich, 12 and defended him from his enemies, and kept him safe from those who lay in wait for him, and gave him victory in a hard fight, that he might know that godliness is mightier than all things.

It was she who guided the righteous man, fleeing from his brother's wrath, in straight paths, and showed him the kingdom of God, and gave him the knowledge of holy things, and made him prosper in his labors, and multiplied the fruit of his works. [10]

The wise man did not ascribe wisdom to Jacob when he used means of deceit to obtain the birthright and the blessing or to obtain a greater share from his uncle Laban, but he speaks of her when he met the wrath of his brother Esau with a spirit of humility and generous giving.
By wisdom he enjoyed the opened heaven and the comforting heavenly visions, in return for Esau's hatred of him and attempt to kill him.

He refers here to the dream of Jacob, fleeing from the face of Esau his brother (Gen 27:41-28:17), where he saw heaven as the "kingdom of God," an evangelical expression rarely used in the Old Testament. Jacob enjoyed an eschatological vision, where God reigns over the believers, and establishes from them His divine kingdom.
"Holy things": points to the heavenly sanctuary or to the heavenly ones who are holy in the Lord.

* Consider an ascetic (Jacob); he was running, fleeing from an exceedingly violent man, he was fleeing from his brother, and he found his help in a stone, and this stone is Christ. This stone is a help to all who suffer persecution, but to the unbelieving Jews it is a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence (Rom 9:33; 1 Pet 2:8; Isa 8:14; 28:16). There Jacob saw a ladder set up on the earth with its top reaching to heaven, and in heaven the Lord leaning upon it, and he saw angels ascending and descending (Gen 28:12-13). Look, he saw angels ascending, he saw Paul ascending. And he saw angels descending, Judas the traitor falling headlong. He saw angels ascending, he saw saints ascending from earth to heaven, and he saw angels descending, Satan and all his army cast down from heaven.

entries.section: 6. Its role in the life of Jacob

paragraphs.text: St. Jerome. And gave him victory over the covetousness of those who oppressed him, and made him rich. [11]

entries.section: 6. Its role in the life of Jacob

paragraphs.text: And defended him from his enemies, and kept him safe from those who lay in wait for him, and gave him victory in a hard fight, that he might know that godliness is mightier than all things. [12]

Here he refers to the period of his service to his uncle Laban, who exploited him and deceived him and was covetous to send him away empty. As for his enemies, they are Esau and his men or Laban and his brothers (Gen 31:23).
By the hard fight he means his struggle at the crossing of the ford of Jabbok, striving with God (Gen 32:22-29).
Jacob's weapon in his battle and hard fight is godliness, which is mightier than all things.

The wise man tells us of our father Jacob, who in the midst of his toils found a stone to put under his head. What is this stone but the wisdom of God incarnate, on whom we lean our heads that He may sanctify them, and lift our thoughts to heaven amid our troubles in this world? Thus "wisdom delivered her servants out of their toils" [9].

* The stone under his head was Christ. He had not put a stone under his head before, but only when the time came in which he was fleeing from his persecutor. When he was in his father's house and enjoyed the comforts of the body, he had no stone for his head. But he left his home poor and alone, went out with nothing but a staff, and immediately in that very night he found a stone and put it under his head.
St. Jerome. * We have not read of the blessed Jacob that he set out with horses or asses or camels, but we only read that he carried a staff in his hand...
Jacob showed his staff to take a wife for himself (Gen 32:10), and Christ carried the wood of the Cross to save the Church.
When Jacob slept he put a stone under his head and saw a ladder reaching to heaven, while the Lord leaned upon the ladder.

Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles. * The ladder set up on the earth and reaching to heaven is the Cross of Christ, through which He granted us to reach heaven, and indeed leads to heaven. This ladder contains various steps of virtues, by which we rise toward heaven. Faith and righteousness and purity and holiness and patience and godliness and all the rest of the virtues are the steps of this ladder.

St. John Chrysostom. God gave Jacob intelligence, and he was able to debate with his uncle who had deceived him, but Jacob was exposed to danger when his uncle pursued him with his relatives who were with him. Here human wisdom could not have preserved Jacob, but God Himself intervened, and warned Laban not to do Jacob harm (Gen 34:24 etc.).

* Wonderful is the goodness of the Lord. For when God saw Laban determined to fight him and to enter with the good man into battle, He said to him, as one asking him to review his intention: "Take heed that thou speak not to Jacob either good or bad" (Gen 31:25). He says to him: Do not try to trouble Jacob, not even with a harsh word, but take heed to yourself, review your evil attack, restrain your anger, bridle your raging thoughts... I ask you to note the compassion of God. Instead of God commanding Laban to return to his place, He was content to direct him not to use harsh and violent words with the good man. What is the reason for that? That the good man might learn and experience how far God's care for him extends.

Do you not see that if Laban had turned back, how could the good man and his wife have known this? God allowed Laban to go and bear witness with his lips to the words that were spoken to him by God... This truly is the sign of the creative wisdom of God, that He turns the enemies of the truth themselves into witnesses to the truth, so that they fight with their mouths on the side of the truth.

St. John Chrysostom. * Jacob, who purified his heart from all appearances, showing conduct full of peace, first sent away all his possessions and remained behind, and wrestled with God (Gen 32:23-25). For he who leaves worldly things draws near to the image and likeness of God. What is the wrestling with God but entering into a struggle for virtue, and he who strives with one stronger than himself comes to a better state by imitating God more than others? Since Jacob's faith and consecration were unconquerable, the Lord declared to him His divine mysteries by touching the hollow of his thigh (Gen 32:26). For of his seed the Lord Jesus was born of a virgin, and Jesus is not unlike God (the Father) nor less than He.

St. Ambrose. By divine wisdom Jacob strove with God and men and prevailed. He wrestled until the dawn, when the light of the Sun of righteousness began to rise upon him. The reward he received is the desire of the heart of every true believer, for he was no longer called Jacob, which means "he who pursues," but "Israel," which means "seeing," and as St. Augustine says: "a great name carrying a great blessing."

* The Lord says in the Gospel: "the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force" (Mt 11:12)... He says to Jacob: "Let me go, for the day breaketh," he answered him: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me." And He blessed Jacob; how? By changing his name... See, it is one man, on one side touched and withered (Jacob), and on the other side blessed to receive strength (the seeing of God).
St. Augustine. St. Cyril the Great sees that as long as we are in the night of this world we wrestle, but when the dawn of eternity comes there is no more room for wrestling but for seeing God.

* You see how he did not continue in the wrestling at the beginning of the day. In fact there is no wrestling for those who have already lived in the light. Those who have come to such greatness it befits to say: "O God, my God, I watch for thee from the light" (Ps 62:2) LXX. And also: "In the morning thou wilt hear my voice, I will wait for thee, and thou wilt see me" (Ps 5:4) LXX. When the light of righteousness, that is Christ, rises in our minds and presents His brightness in our hearts, then we wait as noble souls, and are made worthy of the divine care: "The eyes of the LORD are upon the righteous" (Ps 34:15). At dawn the wrestling ceases.
St. Cyril of Alexandria

entries.section: 7. Its role in the life of Joseph

paragraphs.text: 13 It is she who did not forsake the righteous man when he was sold, but kept him from sin, and went down with him into the pit. 14 And in bonds she did not leave him, until she brought him the scepter of the kingdom, and authority over those who held him in subjection, and showed those who accused him to be liars, and gave him everlasting glory.
It was she who did not leave the righteous man whom they sold, but rescued him from sin, and went down with him into the pit. [13]

Since Joseph committed himself to wisdom in a spirit of godliness, she delivered him from the pit, and rescued him from the enticements of Potiphar's wife and sustained him in prison, and brought him up to the throne, and gave him great glory!

Joseph did not learn human wisdom and magic, but by godliness he overcame the wise men and counselors and magicians, and became a witness to the work of the wisdom of God in a foreign land! He became by his conduct and behavior a teacher of wisdom to the elders (Ps 105:17-22).
What does the wise man mean by saying that "wisdom did not forsake the righteous man [13], and did not leave him [14]"?

When righteous Joseph was sold and when he was put in bonds, wisdom was with him, for he was a symbol of the Lord Christ who was sold as a slave through the betrayal of His disciple Judas, and was put in bonds when He was brought to trial. The life of this righteous man bears a wonderful image as a symbol of the Lord Christ in many respects; it is enough for me to mention what St. Aphrahat wrote as an example of what is found in the writings of the Fathers on this matter.
* Joseph was persecuted, and his brothers were the persecutors. Joseph was glorified, and his persecutors bowed down to him, and his dreams and visions were fulfilled.
Joseph the persecuted was a symbol of Jesus the persecuted.
Joseph's father clothed him with a coat of many colors, and Jesus' Father clothed Him with a body from the Virgin.
Joseph's father loved him more than his brothers, and Jesus is the dear beloved of His Father.
Joseph saw visions and dreamed dreams, and the visions and the prophets were fulfilled in Jesus.
Joseph was a shepherd with his brothers, and Jesus is the Chief Shepherd.

When his father sent him to visit his brothers they saw Joseph coming and planned to kill him, and when the Father sent Jesus to visit His brothers they said: "This is the heir; come, let us kill him" (Mt 21:38).
Joseph's brothers cast their brother into the pit, and Jesus His brothers brought down to dwell among the dead.
Joseph came up out of the pit, and Jesus rose from among the dead.

After Joseph rose from the pit he had authority over his brothers, and after Jesus dwelt among the dead His Father gave Him a great glorified name (Phil 2:9), that His brothers might serve Him and His enemies be subjected under His feet.

After Joseph's brothers recognized him they were ashamed and afraid and amazed before his greatness, and when Jesus comes at the end of time and declares His greatness His brothers will be ashamed and afraid and tremble before Him because they crucified Him.
Moreover Joseph was sold into Egypt on the counsel of Judah, and Jesus was delivered to the Jews by the hands of Judas Iscariot.
When they sold Joseph he did not answer his brothers a word, and Jesus also did not speak nor answer the judges who tried Him.
Joseph was delivered by his master to prison unjustly, and Jesus was condemned unjustly by the children of His people.
Joseph gave up two garments, one in the hands of his brothers, and the other in the hand of his master's wife, and Jesus gave up His garments and they were divided among the soldiers.

Joseph, when he was thirty years old, stood before Pharaoh and became lord of Egypt, and Jesus, when He reached thirty, came to the Jordan to be baptized and received the Spirit and went out to preach.
Joseph sustained Egypt with bread, and Jesus sustained the whole world with the bread of life.
Joseph took the daughter of the wicked unclean priest as a wife for himself, and Jesus betrothed to Himself the Church from the unclean Gentiles.
Joseph died and was buried in Egypt, and Jesus died and was buried in Jerusalem.
Joseph's bones his brothers brought up out of Egypt, and Jesus His Father raised from the dwelling of death and He put on His body and ascended with it to heaven in incorruption.

entries.section: 7. Its role in the life of Joseph

paragraphs.text: St. Aphrahat the Persian Sage. And in bonds she did not leave him, until she brought him the scepter of the kingdom, and authority over those who held dominion over him, and she showed those who found fault with him to be liars, and gave him lasting glory. [14]

Wisdom accompanied him in his bonds to bring him into glory, so that instead of being a prisoner he became a man of authority, supplying with provisions those who held dominion over him, and perhaps he means here Potiphar and his household, and the jailer and those with him, and also his brothers who sought to kill him and sold him as a slave.

Some looked at him as a criminal thrown into prison, and counted what befell him as a sign of his evil and of God's wrath upon him, but the wisdom of God (God the Word) revealed his righteousness, and declared that his sufferings and afflictions were only for his glory in this world as in the world to come, for "she gave him everlasting glory."
* See how it suddenly happened that the prisoner became king over all Egypt; he who was sent to prison by the captain of the guard the king raised to the highest rank.

His former master looked, and suddenly saw that the man whom he had thrown into prison as an adulterer was rewarded by receiving authority over all Egypt. Do you not see the importance of enduring trials with thanksgiving? For this reason Paul says: "tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope: and hope maketh not ashamed" (Rom 5:3-5). Note: Joseph endured affliction with patience, and patience gave him experience, and experience worked in hope, and hope did not make him ashamed.

St. John Chrysostom. * What is the meaning of the ring that was put on his finger (Gen 41:42)? It is only that we may understand that the position of the episcopate by faith was granted to him so that he might seal others. And what of the robe but that it is the robe of wisdom? This alone is the excellence in wisdom which the King of heaven gave him. The chain of gold appears to represent good understanding. And the chariot (Gen 41:43) also points to the glorious heights for which he was made worthy.

St. Ambrose. * "They brought him hastily out of the dungeon: and he shaved himself, and changed his raiment" (Gen 41:14), then it was possible for him to enter in to the king. So he who was bound in the prison of sin, and a captive in the lusts of the world, far from God, cannot come to Him until he comes out of that unclean prison, that is, leaves the doing of sin, and shaves the superfluities of the hair of his head, which are the thoughts of his mind that love sin, and changes his raiment, which is his evil deeds, for good works. He who has cleansed his heart of evil thoughts in this way, and changed his sinful works for righteous works, is worthy to enter in to Christ, the King of kings, and to partake of His precious Body and Blood.
St. Ephrem the Syrian

entries.section: 8. Its role in the life of the people

paragraphs.text: 15 It is she who delivered a holy people and a blameless seed from a nation of oppressors. 16 She entered into the soul of a servant of the Lord, and withstood dread kings with wonders and signs. 17 She rendered to the saints a reward of their labors, and led them in a marvelous way, and was a shelter to them by day, and a light of stars by night. 18 She brought them over the Red Sea, and carried them through much water. 19 But their enemies she drowned, and then cast them up from the depth of the abyss upon the shore; so the righteous spoiled the ungodly, 20 and sang praise to thy holy name, O Lord, and with one accord praised thy hand that fought for them, 21 for wisdom opened the mouth of the dumb, and made the tongues of babes to speak clearly.

He concludes the whole book with an extensive discourse by which he shows how divine providence preserved the people through the events of the Exodus, as the most important event in the history of the people, as a symbol of the exodus that the world enjoys through the Crucified One. The writer showed the divine providence through examples that carry contrasts. This chapter came much like a sermon or a group of expository sermons on the Book of Exodus.
It was she who delivered a righteous people and a blameless seed from a nation of oppressors. [15]
After speaking of the work of the wisdom of God in the lives of individuals, to reveal His concern for every person, he speaks of the divine wisdom which delivers the holy people.

God calls His people "a holy people," "a blameless seed," because He sanctifies His people and cleanses them from every sin. And He calls Egypt, which subjected them and humiliated them, "a nation of oppressors."

Truly the world does not cease to embitter the life of the true Church with injustice in cruelty (Ex 1:14), but God cherishes her as His holy suffering Church, which is without blame, and calls her: "Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee" (Song 4:7). For she will not hear this praise from the divine mouth unless she shares with her Bridegroom, the wisdom of God, His sufferings and His crucifixion.

* The Bridegroom says: "I will get me to the mountain of myrrh, and to the hill of frankincense" (Song 4:6)... after Christ tasted death for sinners (Rom 5:8). Human nature was delivered from the stain of sin after the Lamb of God took away the sin of the world and destroyed iniquity (Jn 1:29). Therefore the Song says "Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee" and adds to that the mystery of the passion, which myrrh symbolizes, and then mentions the mixture of aromatic herbs and incense, which point to the divinity of Christ. He who shares with Christ in the myrrh will obtain the fragrance of the aromatic herbs and incense, for he who suffers with Him will receive glory with Him (Rom 8:17). And when he is in the divine glory he will obtain perfect beauty and be very far from every hateful blemish. By Christ and through Christ you are separated from sin. He died and rose from the dead for us.

St. Gregory of Nyssa Thus the wisdom of God saved the people by accepting the crucifixion, so that the people might be crucified with Him, and rise with Him in surpassing glory, and the true believers might be made worthy of heaven.
Pharaoh humbled the people and forced them to labor in clay and in the building of three cities, enslaving them. In this he represents the work of the enemy of good with mankind, the sons of Adam.

* Pharaoh enslaved the children of Israel in building cities for himself. Pharaoh appointed taskmasters from among his soldiers over the children of Israel, urging them on to his works. And the devil appoints demons over the sons of Adam, urging them on to his evil works, the works of sin.
Pharaoh appointed his soldiers to enslave the children of Israel to the making of bricks, and the devil urges the sons of Adam on to lowly earthly works.

The Holy Scripture mentions that the children of Israel built great cities for Pharaoh (Ex 1:11)... And the demons urge the sons of Adam to set up great sins that are the root of all evils: the love of silver, the lusts of the flesh, and vainglory.
St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian Truly, what do we expect from the earthy heart of Pharaoh, filled with mire, except that he should issue orders to force the children of Israel into the work of clay?

* For Satan, who harms people and corrupts them, is intensely concerned that his subjects should not look up to heaven, but should bow down to the earth and make bricks of clay - within themselves - from the mud. And it is clear to everyone that what belongs to material pleasure is certainly composed of earth and water, and this applies to the one who is concerned with the lust for food or the lust for money and wealth.

The mixture of these two elements - earth and water - becomes clay. And those who long for pleasures are like those who long for clay; they keep filling themselves with it, and yet they are never filled, and the place that receives the clay becomes empty before the next pouring. In the same way the brickmaker keeps pouring more clay into the mold, and the mold is continually emptied. Everyone can easily understand the meaning of this figure by looking at the sensual side of the soul.

Whoever follows his desires and what he craves, if he achieves one desire and then turns with his desire to something else, finds himself empty again with respect to that thing; and if he is filled with it, he becomes empty again like an empty vessel, seeking something else, and so on.
