paragraphs.text: St. Ephrem the Syrian But that which is made an idol is cursed, both it and he that made it: he, because he made it; and it, because, being corruptible, it was called god. [8]

The wise man offers the mystery of the curse of both the material of the idol and its maker. The material in itself is not evil, nor is man as God's creature evil, for all that God created is good. The evil of the material lies in its use as an idol, which usurps the glory of God and which the devil inhabits to deceive men by it. And the evil of man is not in his body nor in his soul, but in the perversion of his will, in which he bears a will that resists the divine truth.
The world is beautiful and good, and the body is good and the soul is good; the deviation of any creature from the course for which it was created corrupts its being and makes it evil.

* “But that which is made an idol is cursed, both it and he that made it” (Wis 14:8) does not mean that what has no life in it is cursed in itself, but by the word “made” he means precisely the lifeless idol (in which Satan dwells).

entries.section: 1. The ship or the wooden idol?

paragraphs.text: Origen For God hates the ungodly and his ungodliness alike. [9]

God does not hate His creation, but He cannot bear what is not in harmony with His holiness. The wicked man who denies the faith, whether by his mouth or by his work, cannot enjoy fellowship with the Holy One unless he accepts sanctification by the Spirit of God.
Here God hates the evil will of the wicked man, as He hates evil itself.

entries.section: 1. The ship or the wooden idol?

paragraphs.text: So the thing made and the maker are punished. [10]

Often God allowed the prophets to destroy idols, as Moses the prophet did, who ground the golden calf to powder and scattered it (Ex 32:20). As for idolaters, God allows them to be disciplined in this world, and if they do not cease, their punishment will be the eternal fire of Gehenna.

entries.section: 1. The ship or the wooden idol?

paragraphs.text: Therefore there shall be a visitation also upon the idols of the Gentiles, because they have become an abomination in God's creation, and a stumbling block to the souls of men, and a snare to the feet of the foolish. [11]
Sadly, Solomon the wise himself, when he married foreign pagan women, worshipped their gods (1 Kgs 11:8); how much more are simple souls exposed to fall into this worship!

entries.section: 2. Fornication behind idolatry

paragraphs.text: 12 For the devising of idols was the beginning of fornication, and the invention of them the corruption of life. 13 For they were not from the beginning, neither shall they be for ever. The idea of making idols is the origin of fornication, and the invention of them is the corruption of life. [12]

Man was created bearing within himself a natural law that urges him to worship the living God, and he finds rest and peace in fulfilling this impulse; but when man turned his back to God and rejected His divine commandment, the lusts of his body rose against him and took possession of and ruled over his will. At the same time he wants to worship, so he exchanged the invisible God, who rebukes his conscience, for false gods that he sees and touches and appeases by every means, even by wounding his body or slaughtering his children, to quiet his conscience.

Idol worship is bound up with fornication. For on one side the relation of believers with God is like the relation of a bride with her bridegroom, so that if she turns her back to Him to be joined to pagan gods she has fallen into marital unfaithfulness. Therefore it was said of unfaithful Israel: “Where is the bill of your mother's divorcement?” (Isa 50:1). It was also said: “Take heed to yourself, lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and they go a whoring after their gods, and do sacrifice unto their gods, and one call you, and you eat of his sacrifice; and you take of their daughters unto your sons, and their daughters go a whoring after their gods, and make your sons go a whoring after their gods” (Ex 34:15-16). The origin of idolatry is the corruption of man's thought and unfaithfulness to God the Creator, which is counted as fornication of the soul that abandons its union with its Creator to be joined to accursed idols.
On the other hand, idolatry has often been bound up with bodily fornication, sometimes even in the temples of the idols themselves.

The connection of idolatry with fornication appears from what is recorded of the people's worship of the golden calf, for it was said: “the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play” (Ex 32:6). Here “play” means sexual caresses.
* (Idol worship) was discovered among men for no reason other than the existence of passions among those who imagined it.

* When the human soul had experienced various pleasures, and forgot divine things, and was the more delighted with the pleasures of the body that it set before its eyes, and cared for nothing but present things and contemplating them, it no longer thought that there is any good except temporal and bodily things. Therefore, having turned aside and forgotten that it was in the image of the good God, it no longer had the power by which it saw God the Word, after whose likeness it was created. But having withdrawn from itself, it began to imagine and fancy what has no existence.

* When the men of the former age lost their minds, and sank in passions and the fancies of bodily things, and forgot the knowledge of God and His glory because of the dullness of their minds, or rather the absence of their minds, they made for themselves gods of visible things, glorifying the creature rather than the Creator God, and deifying the things made rather than the Lord, their cause and Creator.
Pope Athanasius the Apostolic * He who serves vain gods is without doubt an adulterer away from the truth, for all vanity is fornication. Thus he sinks into fornication.

Tertullian * Blessed is Rachel, who hid the idols of the vain Gentiles and declared that their images were full of uncleanness. And let no one think that she offended against the honor of her father and her reverence for him as a father, because she sat while he stood (Gen 31:35). For it is written: “He that loves father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me” (Mt 10:37).

The woman who commits adultery does not cleave to her husband, and is not one flesh with him (1 Cor 6:15-16), but isolates herself and separates herself from him by her adultery. So every soul that does not cleave to God but walks in fornication by submitting to the worship of vain idols is separated from the Lord by the grievous defilement of holy things, when it ought to have cleaved to Him. And he who withdraws from the Lord perishes.
St. Ambrose

entries.section: 2. Fornication behind idolatry

paragraphs.text: They were not in the beginning, neither shall they be for ever. [13]

When man was created good and pure, purity was bound up with the worship of God the Creator from the beginning. But when corruption gained mastery over man, and he enslaved himself to bodily pleasures and fell into fornication, he turned aside from worshipping the Holy One and began to worship idols or creatures, and these will pass away one day.
Cleaving to the true, holy God brings us into immortality, where divine righteousness is, while indulgence in bodily lusts drives us to perdition and destruction, because they do not last.

entries.section: 3. Vainglory and idolatry

paragraphs.text: 14 For by the vain glory of men they entered into the world, and therefore shall they come shortly to an end.
They entered the world through men's love of vainglory, and therefore a speedy end was written for them. [14]

Besides fornication there is another motive for idol worship, namely the love of vainglory. For the worship of the humble God moves the soul to enjoy inner glory, but the worship of vain idols glorifies man and his handiwork.

It is as though the worship of the humble Holy One is bound up with humble souls, and the worship of idols and enslavement to the proud Satan is bound up with man's fall. We do not wonder at the warning of Holy Scripture: “God resists the proud.”

entries.section: 4. Immortalizing the dead and idolatry

paragraphs.text: 15 For a father afflicted with untimely mourning, when he has made an image of his child who was suddenly taken away, now honored him as a god, who was then a dead man, and delivered to those that were under him ceremonies and sacrifices. 16 Thus in process of time an ungodly custom, grown strong, was kept as a law, and graven images were worshipped by the commandments of kings. 17 Whom men could not honor in presence, because they dwelt far off, they took the counterfeit of his visage from afar, and made an express image of a king whom they honored, to flatter the absent as if he were present.

There is a father afflicted with untimely mourning, who made an image of his son who was suddenly taken away, and began to honor with the honor of a god him who yesterday was a dead man, and ordained for those under his hand mysteries and rites. [15]

The author gives an example of the origin of idol worship. A father who lost his young son made a statue for him as a memorial, and the remembrance turned into worship, and he devised for himself a particular system for worshipping the statue of his son.
It is natural that children and grandchildren should worship their ancestors (2 Macc 11:13), but the worship of dead children was also known among the Egyptians and others.
It is reported of Cicero the famous orator that he deified his daughter Tullia after her death.

entries.section: 4. Immortalizing the dead and idolatry

paragraphs.text: Then this wicked custom became firmly established with the passing of time, and was kept as a law, and by the commands of kings the carved images became objects of worship. [16]
The second example of the origin of idolatry is the kings' setting up statues to honor themselves, and then demanding that the people worship them.
The deification of rulers was spread by Euhemerus about 290 B.C.

entries.section: The worship of emperors

paragraphs.text: And men who could not honor them in their presence, because of the distance of their dwelling, portrayed their likeness from afar, and made a visible image of the king whom they honored, that by their zeal they might express flattery to the absent as though present. [17]

Among the chief evils of idol worship is the instilling of the spirit of hypocrisy, for the great and the people vied with one another to offer worship to the statues of kings out of flattery and adulation, regarding his statue as standing in his place.
* Let us reckon that all idol worship is worship offered to men...

Idol worship is condemned not because of the persons who are the object of worship, but because of its being practiced on behalf of demons. “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's” (Mt 22:21; Mk 12:17; Lk 20:25).

It is enough to set against this: “Render unto God the things that are God's.” What then remains for Caesar...? The Lord asked that they bring Him money, and asked whose image is this? And when He heard that it was Caesar's, He said: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's.”
* We pray to the eternal God, the true God, the living God, for the health of our rulers...

It is fitting for them to realize from whom they received their authority, that as men they know from whom they received life itself. They are convinced that He is the only God, and on His power they depend entirely...

To Him we Christians lift up our eyes and spread out our hands, being innocent, and with our heads uncovered because we have no need to be ashamed, and finally without anyone to prompt us, because we pray from the heart, and pray constantly for all our emperors. We ask for them a long life, a peaceful empire, a safe dwelling, strong armies, a faithful senate, a world at peace, and everything that this man and Caesar desire.
* We honor the Emperor as we are permitted to honor him, as a man who comes after God.
Tertullian

entries.section: 5. Flattery behind idolatry

paragraphs.text: 18 Also the singular diligence of the artificer helped to set forward the ignorant to more superstition. 19 For he, perhaps willing to please one in authority, labored with all his skill to make the likeness of the best fashion. 20 And so the multitude, allured by the grace of the work, took him now for a god, who a little before was but honored as a man. 21 And this was an occasion to deceive the world: for men, serving either calamity or tyranny, ascribed unto stones and stocks the incommunicable Name.
Then the ambition of the artist impelled even those who did not know him to spread his worship. [18]

Misuse of gifts: the artist who makes statues does not make them for kings as they are, but they labor to pour upon them a touch of beauty that is not found in the kings themselves. So art was turned into a snare to catch men into evil.

entries.section: 5. Flattery behind idolatry

paragraphs.text: And perhaps he wished to please the king, so he strained his art that the result might be more beautiful than the reality. [19]
With the skill with which the artist was endowed, what occupies him is not respect for his artistic gift but pleasing the king, for material or moral gain.

entries.section: 5. Flattery behind idolatry

paragraphs.text: So the crowd, allured by the splendor of his work, took for a god him whom a little before they honored as a man. [20]

The artist misused his gift, and offered his art to entice men to attribute divinity to a man. And God Himself warned us of this, saying: “I am the Lord: that is My name: and My glory will I not give to another, neither My praise to graven images” (Isa 42:8).

entries.section: 5. Flattery behind idolatry

paragraphs.text: And this became a hidden snare for mankind, that men enslaved by calamity or royal authority gave to stones and wood the incommunicable Name. [21]

The wise man counts the setting up of idols and the worship of them as a catastrophe, whose motive is often the love of power and temporal glory, so that emperors and the great set up their statues as objects of worship, to which the people give what is fitting for God alone.

entries.section: 6. Idolatry and deception

paragraphs.text: 22 Afterward it was not enough for them that they erred in the knowledge of God, but they live in the great war of ignorance, and those so great plagues they call peace. 23 For while they slay their children in sacrifices, or use secret ceremonies, or make revels of strange rites; 24 they keep neither lives nor marriages any longer pure, but one slays another traitorously, or grieves him by adultery. 25 So that there reigns in all men without exception blood, manslaughter, theft and dissimulation, corruption, unfaithfulness, tumults, perjury, 26 disquieting of good men, forgetfulness of good turns, defiling of souls, changing of kind, disorder in marriages, adultery and shameless uncleanness. 27 For the worship of idols not to be named is the beginning, the cause, and the end of all evil. 28 For either they are mad when they are merry, or prophesy lies, or live unjustly, or lightly forswear themselves. 29 For insomuch as their trust is in idols, which have no life, though they swear falsely, yet they look not to be hurt.

After setting forth the motives for the worship of idols, namely fornication and the love of vainglory, the immortalizing of the dead and flattery of emperors and the great, he tells us of the role of idol worship in deceiving men.

entries.section: a. Error of knowledge

paragraphs.text: Then it was not enough for them to err in the knowledge of God, but they plunged into the wide war of ignorance, and called such evils peace. [22]

If pagan worship puts weak creatures and lifeless, dead idols in the place of God, and offers them the worship and glorification fitting for God alone, what is more serious than this is that in doing so they deceive themselves, claiming to be in deep inner peace. For more serious than ignorance is that a man should suppose in his ignorance that he has wisdom, and in his deprivation of inner peace that he is possessed of peace.

Perhaps he means here that idol worshippers used to hold feasts and practice evils and abominations under the cover of joy and peace. The wicked look upon the children of God as though they were devoid of life, joy and peace. And they pretend to grieve for the believers because they are deprived of happiness.
The wicked theological thought of the pagans drives them to a life of licentious amusement.
* Christ is our peace (Rom 5:1). Therefore the way of peace is the way of Christ, which the wicked do not know.
Origen

entries.section: b. Insane customs

paragraphs.text: We saw the wise man looking with bitterness at idol worshippers because they were ignorant of the true knowledge of God, and in this ignorance they suppose that they enjoy happiness and peace. Now he adds a third factor, namely their performing shameful practices and rites unbecoming to them as men.
And with their rites that kill children, and their hidden mysteries, or their insane festivals with strange customs. [23]

By the word “rites” he means “ceremonies”; instead of the ceremony being an order fitting for man in God's holy creation, killing became among their important ceremonies, under the cover of offering sacrifices to the gods. Fathers lost their fatherhood and mothers their motherhood, and they agreed together to offer children as sacrifices to the pagan gods.
And if they were asked what lies behind this brutal act, they answered: It is a hidden mystery that none can understand.
Besides this brutal violence they practice strange customs on the days of their festivals, which often means perverse bodily practices.

Pope Athanasius the Apostolic gives us horrible examples of human sacrifices, of which we mention: 1. Some used to offer men as sacrifices to idols bearing the image of dead men, offering living creatures as sacrifices to dead creatures, and rational beings to motionless things. 2. The Taurians, a division of the Scythians, who lived in the Crimean peninsula in southern Russia. They used to seize those who had escaped from wrecked ships and offer them as sacrifices to their virgin, as they call her. So in cruelty and brutality they show that those whom their gods saved from drowning are slaughtered. 3. Some of the Scythians used to divide the spoils of war into groups, each group comprising a hundred men, and they chose one from each group and slaughtered him as an offering to their gods. 4. The ancient Egyptians used to offer human sacrifices to Hera. The Cretans and Phoenicians used to appease the face of Cronos by slaughtering their children. Even the ancient Romans used to offer human sacrifices in their worship of Jupiter Latius, the god who was regarded as protector of the Italian league composed of thirty Latin cities.

entries.section: b. Insane customs

paragraphs.text: They no longer keep purity in life, nor in marriage, but one kills another, or grieves him by adultery. [24]

When they deprive themselves of fellowship with the Holy One, they are joined to Satan, who cannot bear chastity and holiness, but wants every man to fall into defilement, even in marriage, practicing perverse and unseemly things.

Their rule becomes pleasure whatever the cost, so there is nothing to prevent a man from killing another to seize his wife or daughter. He may even rape her before his eyes, threatening him with death, and this is what he means by “grieves him by adultery.”

entries.section: b. Insane customs

paragraphs.text: Evil abounds, for there is blood and killing and theft and deceit and corruption and unfaithfulness and tumult and false witness. [25]

When man leaves the worship of the living God, his life turns into a chain of evils that does not stop, “evil abounds.” He cares nothing for the shedding of blood, or killing, or theft, or deceit, or corruption, or unfaithfulness, or tumult, or false witness.

entries.section: b. Insane customs

paragraphs.text: And confusion of values and ingratitude for grace, and defiling of souls, and sexual perversion, and disorder in marriage, and adultery and licentiousness. [26]
They live without any regard for human or social values, with denial of divine grace, and defilement of soul and body, and licentiousness, and so on.
Idol worshippers suppose that as free men it is their right to practice evils and perversions in unrestrained wantonness. They are rights that no one may deprive them of.

* Rachel, that is the Church or discernment, hid the idols (Gen 31:34), for the Church does not know statues and forms of idols in which there is nothing of the truth, but knows the true existence of the Trinity. Truly she destroys the darkness and declares the radiance of glory. Let us then forsake the darkness and seek the sun. Let us leave the smoke and strive for the light. Smoke is evil; for as smoke is to the eyes (Prov 10:26), so is evil to those who practice it.

entries.section: b. Insane customs

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose For the worship of nameless idols is the beginning, the cause and the end of all evil. [27]

The wise man sees that idol worship does not deserve to have a name, because it rejects the name of the Holy One, and that it is the source of all evil, and behind all corruption and dissolution and license, and indeed it is the goal of evil, in which man denies his Creator and worships the wicked enemy in one form or another.

entries.section: c. Rejoicing in evil

paragraphs.text: For those who worship them rejoice to madness, or prophesy lies, or live in injustice, or lightly bear false witness. [28]

After speaking of the effect of idol worship, from the lulling of the conscience to the rejection of fellowship with the holy God, and the practice of every sort of evils, he makes clear that the wicked cover evil with an atmosphere of joy, but it is not the calm inner joy, but “they rejoice to madness”; they claim prophecy, helped in this by the devil the liar, and they walk in a spirit of injustice and false witness. This was characteristic of the priests of the idols in particular.

* The father (Jacob) was commanded to dwell there in Bethel, and there he was commanded to make an altar to God who appeared to him (Gen 35:1). There he took the strange gods and buried them under the terebinth (Gen 35:4) in Jerusalem. There also Rachel was buried on the way to Ephrath, that is Bethlehem (Gen 35:19), and there Jacob set a pillar upon her grave (Gen 35:20). What great mysteries! There is the Church of God, where God appeared and spoke with His humble servants.

There the idols of the Gentiles are taken away and buried, for the faith of the Church shatters every practice of idolatry. I ask: why did he bury them under the terebinth? Surely because it is one of the unfruitful trees; so the gods of the Gentiles are there, where there is no fruit.
St. Ambrose Perhaps some may ask: How can idols prophesy, even falsely?

Holy Scripture links idol worship with false gods or demons, and counts their priests as false priests and their prophets as false prophets, because those who serve him and are moved in all their actions by Satan are called “a liar, and the father of it.” Therefore idols are called “false gods” as “the gods of the heathen are idols (demons)” (see Ps 96:5).

entries.section: c. Rejoicing in evil

paragraphs.text: For since their trust is in lifeless idols, they do not expect to be harmed when they swear falsely. [29]
As they prophesy falsely, they swear and bear false witness, for they do not fear the gods, because they are statues in which there is no spirit, and cannot harm them.
They worship them and are zealous for them, and resist him who worships the true God, but in their depths they do not believe in them.
St. Ambrose * He says: Let those whom you call gods tell you of past events or prophesy to you of future events (see Isa 44:7).
Father Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus

entries.section: 7. The punishment of idol worship

paragraphs.text: 30 Therefore shall justice overtake them for both: because they thought badly of God, giving heed unto idols, and swore unjustly, in deceit, despising holiness. 31 For it is not the power of them by whom they swear, but it is the just vengeance of sinners, that punishes always the offence of the ungodly.
There are two things for which they deserve that punishment come upon them:
Their evil thinking about God by following idols, and their deceitful oath falsely sworn, by despising holiness. [30]
Punishment comes upon idol worshippers for two things:
First: their rejection of the worship of the living God by accepting idols in His place.

Second: false swearing and contempt of holiness. Here, in speaking of the wicked life or wicked conduct, he concentrates on the lying tongue, which swears falsely, and the unclean, reckless life that cares nothing for holiness and purity and chastity.

entries.section: 7. The punishment of idol worship

paragraphs.text: For what always follows the transgression of the unrighteous is not the power of those by whom they swear, but the judgment upon sinners. [31]

He brings out here a point of the greatest importance, namely that though idolaters swear by false gods, false swearing is evil even if it is in the name of false gods, because lying in itself is sin whether with an oath or without it.
Arise within me, O wisdom of God,

entries.section: 1. Taking pride in the merciful God

paragraphs.text: 1 But You, our God, are gracious and true, longsuffering, and in mercy ordering all things. 2 For if we sin, we are Yours, knowing Your power; but we will not sin, knowing that we are counted Yours. 3 For to know You is perfect righteousness, and to know Your power is the root of immortality.
But You, our God, are good and true, longsuffering, and ordering all things in mercy. [1]

In the midst of his speaking of the idol worship which shattered man's thought with folly, and his life with abominations and lying with violence and cruelty, Solomon looked to God to see a joyful, shining picture. So he speaks of Him as “our God,” as though the pagans possess idols as their property, but they cannot possess or own them, for they are lifeless. But God is our God who possesses us as a people for Himself, takes pride in us, and we take pride in Him.

We saw that with corruption pagan worship was marked by violence and fierceness until it reached the offering of human sacrifices, but our God is good, true in His promises, longsuffering, the Upholder of all, ordering all things for our benefit and our eternal edification.

The author presents his discussion of the punishment of the wicked in the form of a prayer addressed to God (Wis 15:2-3), who is merciful and mighty, in contrast to the idols which are utterly unable to act.

David the prophet had already sung, saying: “For You, Lord, are good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon You... But You, O Lord, are a God full of compassion, and gracious, longsuffering, and plenteous in mercy and truth” (Ps 86:5, 15).

entries.section: 1. Taking pride in the merciful God

paragraphs.text: And even if we sin we are Yours, knowing Your power; but we will not choose to sin, knowing that we are counted as Yours. [2]

The author confesses that Israel sinned by turning aside to idol worship, but since he realizes that he is the people of God he finds the door of repentance open before him to enjoy God's mercies, believing in God's power to save even from idol worship. The secret of his falling into idol worship is two things:
First: his ignorance that he is God's own.
Second: his not realizing that God is perfect righteousness and the Almighty and the root of immortality.

In other words, what preserves us from sin, and what drives us to repentance when we have sinned, is our realization of our position in relation to God, that we are His own, beloved by Him and cared for by Him. The second matter is the truth of God's person, that He is our Father who does not withhold from us but gives Himself to us, and He is the supreme righteousness, the Almighty and the Giver of immortality. So while we constantly feel our weakness, our position gives us cleaving to Him and belonging to Him, and our knowledge of His truth gives us boldness to ask as befits His possibilities, to become an icon of Him, bearing His righteousness and trusting in His power and hoping for eternity.

* It was necessary that they should come up by means of the water in order to become alive, for they cannot enter the Kingdom of God unless they put off the state of death that they had before... For before a man bears the name “Son of God” he is dead, but when he receives the seal he casts off the state of death and enjoys life. The seal then is the water, into which they go down dead and come up alive.
Father Hermas * Truly we go down into the water full of sins and defilement, and come up bearing fruit in our hearts, bearing in our spirits the fear (of God) and hope in Jesus.

entries.section: 1. Taking pride in the merciful God

paragraphs.text: St. Barnabas For to know who You are is perfect righteousness, and to know Your power is the root of immortality. [3]

St. John the Beloved explains to us this phrase together with the preceding one, saying: “Behold, what manner of love the Father has bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God... Whosoever abides in Him sins not: whosoever sins has not seen Him, neither known Him... Whosoever is born of God does not commit sin; for His seed remains in him: and he cannot sin, because he is born of God. In this the children of God are manifest, and the children of the devil: whosoever does not righteousness is not of God” (1 Jn 3:1, 6, 9-10).

* We must hasten to know what way leads to the forgiveness of sins and the hope of the inheritance of the good things promised, for there is no other way but this: that you come to know this Christ, and be washed in the fountain (Baptism) of which Isaiah spoke for the forgiveness of sins (Isa 4:4), and so we begin to live in holiness.
Justin the Martyr * Since you were baptized into Christ, and have put on Christ, you have become subject to the Son of God... By this you become partakers of Christ.
St. Cyril of Jerusalem

entries.section: 2. Idolatry, the fruit of corruption and folly

paragraphs.text: 4 For neither did the mischievous invention of men's art deceive us, nor the painter's fruitless labor, a form stained with divers colors; 5 the sight whereof entices fools to lust, so that they desire the form of a dead image that has no breath. 6 Both they that make them, and they that desire them, and they that worship them, are lovers of evil things, and are worthy to have such things to trust upon.
For neither did what the wicked art of men invented lead us astray, nor the barren labors of painters, images smeared with discordant colors. [4]

In his book Contra Gentes (Against the Pagans) St. Athanasius the Apostolic says that evil had no existence; it is made by the evil will of man. God did not create evil, but man's withdrawal from God, who is wholly good, drove him to evil. This evil is the origin of idol worship, which had no existence, but came as a natural result of the evil brought into being by the evil will.

But the children of God, whose thoughts are lifted up to the heavens, however far the creativity of artists reaches, their hearts cannot be drawn to worship some idol. In their eyes there is no ground for comparison between the experience of heavenly things and the wicked inventions of men.
The inventions of men will not cease, but the children of God are firm in their hope in the Lord, holding fast to the Kingdom of their Father.

entries.section: 2. Idolatry, the fruit of corruption and folly

paragraphs.text: The sight of it arouses passion in fools, and makes them desire the form of a dead image without spirit. [5]

However great the artist's perfection, and however great the allurement, the idol is a dead statue with no spirit in it; how then does a living man enslave himself to a dead statue? It is fitting for man to take pride in what he has received, for there is no ground for comparison between the statue, whatever its allurements, and man, created in the image and likeness of God!

entries.section: 2. Idolatry, the fruit of corruption and folly

paragraphs.text: Those who make them, and those who desire them, and those who worship them, are lovers of evil, and worthy to have such things as their hopes. [6]
The wise man wonders how the lust for evil draws these classes, that is, the makers of statues and the lovers of statues, so that they acquire them and worship them.

* The idol worshipper is like a murderer. Do you ask: whom does he kill? There is an aggravated charge against him, for he does not kill a stranger, nor a personal enemy, but kills himself. By what nets is he caught? By his error. By what weapon? By rebellion against God.
* Idolatry embraces all crimes, and all crimes embrace idolatry.
Tertullian

entries.section: 3. A potter who makes gods

paragraphs.text: 7 For the potter, tempering soft earth, fashions every vessel with much labor for our service; yea, of the same clay he makes both the vessels that serve for clean uses, and likewise also all such as serve to the contrary; but what is the use of either sort, the potter himself is the judge. 8 And with misspent labor he molds a vain god of the same clay, he who was himself born of earth a little before, and after a short time returns to the same from which he was taken, when his life that was lent him shall be demanded. 9 Notwithstanding his care is, not that he shall have much labor, nor that his life is short, but he strives to excel goldsmiths and silversmiths, and endeavors to do like the workers in brass, and counts it his glory to make counterfeit things.
For the potter toils in kneading the soft clay, and forms everything of what we use.
Out of the same clay he makes the vessels designated for clean works and those designated for the opposite, all alike.
But the designation of each vessel of both classes goes back to the judgment of the maker of the clay. [7]

He spoke before of the carpenter (chs. 13-14), to whom God gave skill and art to make ships for the benefit of mankind, and who turned his skill to making dead idols that shatter and corrupt mankind. Now he speaks of the potter, for whom it is fitting, while kneading the clay, to remember how God created man from clay, so that he may glorify his Creator by his skill and work for the benefit of mankind, and not form a ceramic idol in folly, driving men to unclean practices in their worship of idols!

So it is fitting for both the carpenter and the potter to bear witness to the wisdom of God the Savior and Creator, but in folly they turned the thoughts of men from their Creator to worship wooden or ceramic idols.

The wise man does not attack carpenters and potters, for all who have skills can work and create for the edification of mankind, bringing out of wood household tools or tools of work, and out of clay clean and splendid vessels used in cooking or serving food and drink or for adornment, and so on.
For work in wood and clay and stones and metals is holy if the will of the workers is holy. To the pure all things are pure.
* All things that exist are good, because the Creator of all of them is wholly good.

St. Augustine * Creatures are not evil by nature; if they were evil God would not have created them, for “every creature of God is good,” as the Apostle Paul said (1 Tim 4:4); and God's commandment does not command us to reject good things and flee from them, but to manage them well. And no one is condemned for possessing wealth, but for boasting in it or for misusing it.

St. Basil the Great * Is not the world good? Is not the present life good? But if these draw me away from Christ I count all these things loss. Why? “For the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord.” For when the sun rises, sitting beside a candle is counted a loss. For loss rests on comparison, on the superiority of the other things... Notice how he calls everything loss, not in itself, but for the sake of Christ.

entries.section: 3. A potter who makes gods

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom And toiling to no purpose he makes of the same clay a trifling god, one born of clay a little while ago, who after a little while returns to the clay from which he was taken, when he is asked to repay the soul that was lent him. [8]

The wise man looks at the potter who spends all effort to bring out of clay a god to be worshipped by himself and by him who buys it from him. It is a toilsome effort, and a corruption of thought and of gifts as of life, for the potter to imagine that he is able to bring into being a god made by his hands.
Perhaps by his saying “repay the soul that was lent him” he means that Satan enters the statue and speaks and deceives by working miracles as the magicians did before Pharaoh, but only for a while.

* By these words (Isa 44:11) God teaches us how great is their folly, for they worship (the idols) as makers of good things... The makers of these which seem gods are men who have the same nature as those who worship them, and the man who makes them himself worships them as a god.

entries.section: 3. A potter who makes gods

paragraphs.text: Tertullian Yet he does not care that he shall die, and that his life is short, but vies with the goldsmiths and silversmiths, and imitates the workers in brass, and glories in forming counterfeit gods. [9]

The makers of idols compete in making statues, and each of them boasts that he has made a god or false gods. In their recklessness they boast of the work of their hands and count them great works, while they trade in religion and seek their own material gain.

entries.section: 4. The degradation of man

paragraphs.text: 10 His heart is ashes, his hope is more vile than earth, and his life of less value than clay, 11 forasmuch as he knew not his Maker, and Him that inspired into him an active soul, and breathed in a living spirit. 12 But they counted our life a pastime, and our time here a market for gain: for, say they, we must be getting every way, though it be by evil means. 13 For this man, more than all others, knows that he offends, in that of earthly matter he makes brittle vessels and graven images.
His heart is ashes, and his hope is more vile than earth, and his life more despicable than clay. [10]

Since Israel rejected the light of the Lord, He warns them by Isaiah the prophet not to imitate the pagan nations that ignored man's dignity and brought him down to the depths, saying: “Their land also is full of idols; they worship the work of their own hands, that which their own fingers have made: and the mean man bows down, and the great man humbles himself: therefore forgive them not” (Isa 2:8-9).

Truly what grieves the heart of God, who created man from the dust and breathed into him the breath of life, and gave him to be in His likeness and image, is that he has sunk to his origin, indeed to what is lower than this origin. By his disobedience to the Spirit of God and his welcoming the thoughts of the devil, making idols to worship, his heart became ashes, lower than dust and of less value. His hope became more despicable than the dust from which he was created, because dust does no evil.

* What a terrible thing it is when man leaves the easy yoke of Christ and His light burden (Mt 11:30), and submits to the yoke of demons and bears the weight of exceedingly sinful sin, after we have learned that the heart of idol worshippers is ashes, and their life no more than dust (Wis 15:10).

entries.section: 4. The degradation of man

paragraphs.text: Origen Because he ignored Him who fashioned him, and breathed into him an active soul, and inspired a living spirit. [11]

A grave contrast between the work of God who loves man and man who loves evil. God created man and formed him from the dust, but breathed into him the breath of life that gives him the spirit of working with power, to govern the world with holiness and righteousness; and the other supposes that he is able to raise up from dust a god without motion, without life.
God wishes to raise man's estate to dwell in heaven and enjoy fellowship in the glories, and man in his degradation wishes to submit to the dust and clay that has no life.

* He who was created in the image of God and received authority over all creatures on earth as his portion, fell by his folly from his royal position. And wanting to recover the honors, behold by his own will he honors the work of his hands, and bows down and prostrates himself and submits himself to the despotic authority of the demons.
Father Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus * Prostration before God lifts man up and increases his greatness, and bowing before idols lowers his estate and brings him down.
What degradation is greater than that man should leave his salvation, and set up enmity with the God of the universe, and at the same time bow before lifeless things, worshipping stones?

Truly God raised us by the honor with which He created us to something greater than the heavens, but Satan set it in himself to degrade those who obey him until they become beings without feeling or life. This is surely the reason for which the prophet declares: “The mean man bows down, and the great man humbles himself” (Isa 2:9).
St. John Chrysostom But he counted our life a worthless game, and our existence a market of profits, and said:

entries.section: 4. The degradation of man

paragraphs.text: “We must be getting by every means, though it be by evil.” [12]

While God wishes to raise man to a surpassing level, so that he may have a portion among the heavenly ones, and it has cost Him much, for He sent the fathers and the prophets and the Law and allowed events to prepare the way for the acceptance of His work of salvation. The matter of man's salvation and glorification is the concern of the Holy Trinity, and still occupies God the Trinity until we enter into glory. Sadly, man sometimes trifles with his salvation, and counts his life a worthless game.

While God prepares for us the eternal heavenly glories, behold man is occupied with material gains or temporal honors that he achieves even by unseemly ways such as injustice. For example, Demetrius the silversmith, who made silver shrines for Diana, brought the craftsmen no small gain (Acts 19:24), and caused the Apostle Paul many troubles.

The Christian, as he walks on earth in a spirit of responsibility and commitment in all that is entrusted to him, bears a heavenly touch in his thoughts as in his feelings and emotions, translated in his words and outward conduct. Our life is a divine school in which we learn and train for the heavenly life, in all directions of our life.
* I want you to keep your minds on these things continually (Col 3:1). For our concern with them frees us from the earth and transports us to heaven.
St. John Chrysostom * Though we are surrounded by the world, we do not give ourselves up to it.

Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus * The end toward which we strive, and which we aspire to reach with all care and diligence, is the blessed life with God in the immortal heaven. And nothing in the world equals this praiseworthy endeavor in honor and greatness for the rational creation.
* Direct your striving toward heaven, and profit from everything you meet on the course of your life on earth.

* Asceticism is the loosing of the bonds of this perishing material life, and release from human attachments so that we may prepare ourselves the more to be on the road that leads to God. It is the unhindered impulse to acquire and enjoy the exceedingly precious goods that are “more to be desired than gold, yea, than much fine gold” (Ps 19:10). In short, asceticism is a transfer from the human heart to the heavenly life, so that we may say: “For our conversation is in heaven.” Also it is the chief point, the first step toward being like Christ, who though He was rich, yet for our sakes became poor (2 Cor 8:9). For if we do not obtain this likeness it is impossible for us to reach the way of life according to the Gospel of Christ.
* While we drag our body on the earth like a shadow, we keep our souls in the company of the heavenly spirits.

entries.section: 4. The degradation of man

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great For he knows better than all men that he offends, because he makes from earthly matter brittle vessels and graven images. [13]
However great the folly of the potter, in his depths he realizes as he makes an idol for worship that he is sinning, and that what he makes is breakable and perishable.

entries.section: 5. Exchanging the Immortal for the dead

paragraphs.text: 14 And all the enemies of Your people, who hold them in subjection, are most foolish, and are more miserable than very babies. 15 For they counted all the idols of the heathen to be gods, which neither have the use of eyes to see, nor noses to draw breath, nor ears to hear, nor fingers of hands to handle; and as for their feet, they are slow to go. 16 For man made them, and he that borrowed his own spirit fashioned them: but no man can make a god like unto himself. 17 For being mortal, he works a dead thing with wicked hands: for he himself is better than the things which he worships: whereas he lived once, but they never. 18 Yea, they worshipped those beasts also that are most hateful, for being compared together, some are worse than others. 19 Neither are they beautiful, so much as to be desired in respect of beasts: but they went without the praise of God and His blessing.
Some see that he concentrated on Egypt when he referred to the pagan nations, because some of the Egyptians were among the worst idol worshippers.
He cast light on the error of the ancient Egyptians in their folly regarding the worship of idols that are lifeless and unable to act.
Perhaps the satire here against the idols rests on what is recorded in (Psalm 115:4-7; Psalm 135:15-18).
But all the enemies of Your people who rule over it are very foolish, and more wretched than the babies themselves. [14]

When man withdraws from God he becomes foolish and ignorant, and enslaves himself to what is mean; he becomes like a child, not in simplicity, but in lack of knowledge and lack of understanding and of studying matters seriously.

* Humor (or lack of seriousness) makes the soul pampered and idle, for it stirs up the soul excessively and often causes violent acts and creates wars, and what more than this? In short, do you not wish to be among men? Leave childish things!

St. John Chrysostom * Christ does not want us to be without understanding but wants us to understand all that is useful and necessary for our salvation in a perfect manner. For even Wisdom promises that she will give “to the simple subtlety, to the young man knowledge and discretion” (see Prov 1:4). And Wisdom is found in the Book of Proverbs as one who lifts up her voice and says: “Unto you, O men, I call; and my voice is to the sons of man. O you simple, understand wisdom: and you fools, be of an understanding heart” (see Prov 8:4-5)...

But how can a man be simple and wise at the same time? This the Savior makes clear to us in another place, saying: “Be therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves” (Mt 10:16); and in the same way the blessed Paul writes: “Brethren, be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be children, but in understanding be men” (1 Cor 14:20).

We must examine what it means to be children in malice, and how a man becomes so while being in mind a mature man. A child's knowledge is very little, and sometimes entirely lacking, so he is innocent of the corruption of evil, and it is our duty also to strive to imitate them in this matter by uprooting the habits of evil from us completely, so that we are looked upon as men who have not even knowledge of the way that leads to guile, having no perception of craftiness or deceit, but being simple and innocent, practicing kindness and a humility that is beyond price, and ready to bear anger and malice. By this we affirm that we bear the marks of those who are still children.

While our character is simple and innocent, it is fitting for us to be perfect in mind, so that our understanding is established firmly and clearly on Him who is by nature and in truth the Creator of the universe, God the Lord...

The chief perfection of the mind rests on faith, so that our understanding is not corrupt; and the second matter, adjoining this chief perfection and near to it and attending it, is the clear knowledge of the way of conduct that pleases God, which we learned by the Gospel, the perfect way that is without blame (here the saint distinguishes between those who walk the evangelical way of the Lord and those who are noble in conduct through philosophies that can deceive). He who walks this way practices a life of simplicity and innocence, and yet they know what (doctrinal) opinions they hold and what true works they practice. Such enter by the narrow gate, and do not reject the labors that are required for godliness in God and necessary to lead to the glorious life. So truly they advance to the wide abundance of the way of God and rejoice in His gifts, and win for themselves the Kingdom of Heaven through Christ, to whom with God the Father be praise and dominion, through Christ, with the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.

entries.section: 5. Exchanging the Immortal for the dead

paragraphs.text: St. Cyril the Great For they counted all the idols of the Gentiles gods, though they do not use their eyes to see, nor their noses to breathe the air, nor their ears to hear, nor the fingers of their hands to touch, and though their feet are unable to walk. [15]

It is strange that the Pharaohs, who excelled in knowledge of the art of embalming and astronomy and architecture and colors and sculpture, and so on, fell into worshipping statues that do not see nor breathe the air nor hear, and have no feeling when someone touches them, unable to move. The Pharaohs, full of vitality and activity, worship what is inert.

* How can one not pity them in this respect, when he sees them worshipping what is unable to see, and hears them praying to what is unable to hear, and beholds men like themselves who were born and have life and mind, but call gods those things that have no motion at all, indeed have not life itself? And the strangest of all is that those which they keep under their authority they serve as their masters.

St. Athanasius the Apostolic In his book “Against the Pagans” Pope Athanasius the Apostolic says that it would have been better for the idols not to have ears and eyes and noses and fingers, lest the idol worshippers be exposed in that their idols do not hear nor see nor smell nor touch.
For he who made them is a man, and he who molded them is a being who was lent a spirit.

entries.section: 5. Exchanging the Immortal for the dead

paragraphs.text: And it is not within the power of man to make a god like himself. [16]

The maker of these idols is the artist man, who with all the skill and art he has reached does not possess life. The breath of life in him is lent to him as a divine gift, and certainly one day he dies and his soul departs from his body; how then does such a being give immortal life to dead materials without life?!

entries.section: 5. Exchanging the Immortal for the dead

paragraphs.text: And since he is mortal, he makes a dead thing with wicked hands.
He himself is one of the things that he worships, for he was alive, but they were not alive. [17]

Man is a mortal being, unable to raise himself or return his soul to his body; how then do his hands reach out in iniquity to claim that he sets up a living god, made by his hands, who does not die? And how does he worship an idol of a man like himself, mortal or already dead?

* They hate the vile animals and wild beasts and birds and reptiles, and shrink from them, either because of their fierceness or because of their filthiness, yet they carve their images on stone or wood or gold and call them gods. But it would have been better for them to worship the living creatures themselves instead of worshipping their images in stones. But both cases are a vain pretense, for neither the matter nor the image is the cause of the divine indwelling, but it is the skill of the art that summons the divinity... But if the divinity is joined to the statues because of the art, what need is there also of the matter, so long as it is established in men? For if God reveals Himself only because of the art, and if the statues are worshipped as gods for this reason, it would be more correct to worship and serve man, who is the master of the art, because he is also rational and has intelligence.
St. Athanasius the Apostolic

entries.section: 5. Exchanging the Immortal for the dead

paragraphs.text: And they worship even the most harmful animals, and the most foolish of animals. [18]

entries.section: 5. Exchanging the Immortal for the dead

paragraphs.text: And there is not in them what is in the rest of the animals of fair and charming appearance, and they have lacked the praise of God and His blessing. [19]

It is a strange thing that man enslaves himself to animals, which are less than man and created for his service, how much more if he chooses from among them the harmful and fierce and ugly ones. As though, while he exalts himself against God the Creator and resists His commandment and even denies His existence, he is ready to submit to harmful and mean creatures!

We conclude our discussion of idol worship with what many of the Fathers pointed out, that man is formed according to the possibilities of him whom he worships. He who worships God the Creator enjoys immortality, and he who worships dead idols falls under death and destruction, and as Holy Scripture affirms, those who worship idols become like them: “they have walked after vanity, and are become vain” (Jer 2:5). “They went to Baal-peor, and separated themselves unto that shame; and their abominations were according as they loved” (Hos 9:10).

St. Athanasius the Apostolic sees that man in his wickedness sank down the more, so he mixed together dissimilar creatures, the rational with the irrational, like the gods of the Egyptians that have the head of a dog or the head of a serpent or the head of an ass, and Ammon the god of the Libyans who has the head of a ram. And some deified parts of the human body such as the head and the shoulder and the hand and the foot.
Why does Holy Scripture sometimes call idols gods?

* When Holy Scripture calls them gods, though they are not gods, it does not declare of them that they are gods in any sense, but in an added sense, though it shows that they are not gods at all. As David says: “All the gods of the nations are idols (demons)” (see Ps 96:5).

“There shall no strange god be in you” (Ps 81:9). In this he says: gods of the pagans, but the pagans are ignorant of the true God, and it calls the idols “other gods,” in order to repel their view that they are gods. But as to their reality, he says of them “idols (demons),” and Isaiah says: “Let all them be ashamed that blaspheme God and carve things that are profitable for nothing, I am a witness, says God” (see Isa 44:11). And Jeremiah also says the same: “The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth” (Jer 10:11).
St. Irenaeus
Your fatherhood keeps me and lifts me up to You!
* I look to You, O Wisdom of God; I see You the Sun of Righteousness, shining with the rays of love upon all mankind.
* I plunge into the sea of Your mercies and Your longsuffering.
So my depths are filled with Your tender fatherhood!
* Allow me, O Wisdom of God, to complain to You of myself.
For You created me a free lord, and a king, an ambassador of the King of kings.
And in my folly I drew my hand away from Your hands.
And I turned my eyes away from Your eyes, and my ear was occupied with the voices of the wicked enemy.
* I complain to You of my fathers who left You, O Source of wisdom, and descended from the heavenly life to the dunghill.
They exchanged You for idols that do not hear nor see nor smell nor move.
* How strange! They fear the wild beasts, and set up idols of insects and reptiles.
They set up idols for them, and adorn them with roses and precious stones and gold and silver.
They exalt themselves in pride and arrogance, and set up statues of emperors and kings, and offer them offerings and sacrifices even after the death of the emperors...
* How strange! You took clay and raised me from it, when You breathed into it a breath of life from You.
And behold the potter takes clay, and makes a ceramic idol for man to bow down to.
You raised us from the dunghill to sit in heaven with the heavenly orders, and by our corrupt will and in our full freedom we came down to bow to the dust!
Our fathers exchanged You, O eternal Holy One, for lifeless ceramic!
Did our fathers find happiness in humiliation before idols?
Does man love degradation and humiliation?
* Glory to You, O heavenly Wisdom of God!
You came down to us, and lived on our earth, that by Your Cross You might draw us again from the dust to the glories.
You emptied Yourself, and took our form, we slaves, that You might lift us from slavery to the glory of the children of God.
You opened to us, the earthly ones, the door of heaven, and called the heavenly orders to rejoice in us.
* You made us a wonder before the heavenly ones!
Behold all heaven awaits the day of Your coming on the clouds, to see all Your believers, the heavenly Queen, enjoying a marvelous and surpassing glory!

entries.section: 1. Return to the second contrast: between the quail and the frogs

paragraphs.text: 1 Therefore they were worthily punished by the like, and tormented by a multitude of insects. 2 But thy people, instead of that punishment, thou didst treat graciously by preparing quails, meat of a strange taste, wherewith thou satisfiedst their desire. 3 So that, while those, with their hunger, lost all desire for food through loathing of what thou didst send upon them, these, after a short want, partook of meat of a strange taste. 4 For it was meet that upon those oppressors inevitable want should come, and that these should only see how their enemies were tormented.
Therefore they were justly punished by the like of these, and were tormented by a multitude of insects. [1]

We saw in chapter eleven (Wis 11:16-20) the contrast between the plague of the Egyptians by the frogs, the gnats, the flies and the locusts, and the gift of the quail to the believers in the wilderness. The ancient Egyptians worshipped some insects and animals, so they were struck by their very gods.

This is what the wise man affirms here: “They were justly punished by the like of these.” What befell them was the fruit of these acts of worship, and God wished them to discover the truth of these false gods.

What they thought to be the source of their happiness became the source of their torment. This is the nature of sin: it carries its poison within it. He who thinks that he is enjoying its pleasure drinks its poison without knowing it.

When Moses the prophet was enraged against the people of Israel because they had worshipped the golden calf, he “took the calf which they had made, and burnt it in the fire, and ground it to powder, and strawed it upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink of it” (Ex 32:20). Some ask: why did he make them drink of the water in which the powdered golden calf was? He wished to assure them that what they had done, they drink of. For he who commits sin tastes its bitterness, and discovers that its pleasures are temporary and passing, hiding behind them the bitterness of death.
* Moses ground up the calf and made them drink it in the water of testing, so that all who had lived to worship the calf died by drinking it.

St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian St. Augustine sees that Moses the prophet ground up the calf and made the children of Israel drink so that they might be crushed by repentance for the sin they had committed. So God permitted the worshippers of the idols of insects to be disciplined by the plagues of insects, so that their life might be made bitter and they might be crushed and repent, and return to the true God.
But thy people thou didst not punish, but didst treat graciously:

entries.section: 1. Return to the second contrast: between the quail and the frogs

paragraphs.text: So that, to satisfy their keen appetite, thou didst prepare for them meat of a strange taste, that is, the quail. [2]

The people murmured against God and His prophet Moses, and asked for flesh in the wilderness, so He sent them quail, a bird like the partridge, which came migrating until it was weary of flying, so that its course was near the surface of the sea, and when it set out toward the camp, the people caught it very easily. The Lord smote them with a very great plague (Num 11:33) because of their murmuring.

Here he does not mention the murmuring, nor the great plague that was for their discipline, but he mentions that God does not leave His believers in need or hunger, and that the people could have eaten and given thanks to God for His gift instead of continual murmuring. The hearts of the ancient Egyptians were bound to the idols as gods, so their bodies, their animals and their crops were struck. So they became afflicted and hungry, in great distress, although they were in the fertile land of Egypt. Whereas the hearts of the believers were bound to God, so they were satisfied with the manna that came down from heaven, and with the quail sent to them in the midst of the wilderness, even though those who murmured against God fell under discipline.

The psalmist says: “The people asked, and he brought quails, and satisfied them with the bread of heaven” (Ps 105:40), and St. Augustine comments on this psalm that the people comprised two groups, one group that believed and trusted in God, and God was pleased with them, and another group that bore weariness and murmuring against God. The former ate and rejoiced, and the latter were smitten by God for their murmuring.

Here he speaks of those who trusted in God, whom the mixed multitude of the Egyptians did not drive to the lust for eating flesh (Num 11:4), nor did they remember with the rest of the people what they used to eat as slaves in Egypt, the (small) fish, and the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick (Num 11:5). These enjoyed the quail and the manna as delicious and wonderful food.

entries.section: 1. Return to the second contrast: between the quail and the frogs

paragraphs.text: So that those, though hungry, lost all desire for food, because of the loathsomeness of what was sent upon them, while these, after a short want, shared meat of a wonderful taste. [3]

For the worshippers of idols in their hunger lost the desire for food, since their houses were filled with the stench of the dead frogs, and their bodies were struck by the bites of the gnats, their animals by boils, and their crops by the locusts. Everything became loathsome to them. But those who trusted in God enjoyed the wonderful food in the wilderness.

entries.section: 1. Return to the second contrast: between the quail and the frogs

paragraphs.text: For it was meet that upon those oppressors inevitable want should come, and that these should see how their enemies were tormented. [4]

The portion of the unjust enslavers was not wealth, honor and authority, but want, that is, extreme poverty, hunger and need, a thing from which there is no escape, that is, there is no way to flee from it.

In contrast to this, while the believers enjoyed divine gifts in the wilderness, they remembered the plagues that had befallen their enslavers, and so they marveled at the work of God’s wisdom with them.

When the children of Israel saw what had befallen those who unjustly opposed them, they offered a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God, who had kept them from these plagues and brought them out into the wilderness, where they practice praises and experience true joy and rest.

entries.section: 2. The third contrast: the locusts and the bronze serpent

paragraphs.text: 5 For when the terrible fury of wild beasts came upon these, and they were destroyed by the bites of crooked serpents, 6 thy wrath endured not to the end, but they were troubled for a little season for a warning, having a sign of salvation, to put them in remembrance of the commandment of thy law, 7 for he that turned himself toward it was saved, not by that which he saw, but by thee, O Saviour of all. 8 And in this thou didst prove to our enemies that thou art he who delivereth from all evil, 9 for them the bitings of locusts and flies killed, neither was there found any remedy for their life, for they were worthy to be punished by such. 10 But thy sons not even the teeth of venomous dragons overcame, for thy mercy came and healed them. 11 For they were pricked that they should remember thy words, and were quickly saved, lest falling into deep forgetfulness they should be deprived of thy goodness. 12 For neither herb nor mollifying plaister restored them to health, but thy word, O Lord, which healeth all things. 13 For thou hast power of life and death: thou leadest to the gates of hell, and bringest up again. 14 A man indeed killeth through his malice, but he cannot bring the spirit again that is gone out, neither release the soul that is received.
Even when the dreadful fury of wild beasts came upon these, and the bites of the crooked serpents destroyed them, thy wrath endured not to the end. [5]

Without partiality, when the people fell into murmuring and returned in their hearts to the land of bondage, desiring the perishable food (Num 11:5), He gave them the desire of their hearts and sent them quail. They ate greedily and gluttonously and did not offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God, so by their continual murmurings they made themselves worthy of the deadly serpents; but when they returned to Him, He removed the plague from them by setting up a bronze serpent, which is a type of the Cross.

It is written in the Book of Numbers: “And the people spake against God, and against Moses, Wherefore have ye brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? for there is no bread, neither is there any water; and our soul loatheth this light bread. And the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people; and much people of Israel died. Therefore the people came to Moses, and said, We have sinned… And the Lord said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole… And it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived” (Num 21:5-9). Those who returned to God in repentance through Moses found the bronze serpent, and so enjoyed new life.

entries.section: 2. The third contrast: the locusts and the bronze serpent

paragraphs.text: But they were troubled for a little while for a warning, having a sign of salvation, to put them in remembrance of the commandment of thy law. [6]

Discipline by the fiery serpents was necessary, so that God might warn them, showing them how grave their situation was. But God commanded that the bronze serpent be set up as “a sign of salvation,” so that they might remember the divine Law, which presents to them prophecies and types of the salvation promised to Adam and his sons.
Thus God turned even their evils to good, so long as they seek to return to Him and to know His divine mysteries.

* Tell me, did not God command through Moses that no images or likenesses be made of anything in heaven or on earth? And yet did He not Himself ask Moses to make the bronze serpent in the wilderness? Moses made it as a sign by which those bitten by serpents are healed. In doing this, was not Moses free from any sin? In this, as I said before, God declared through Moses a mystery by which He breaks the power of the serpent that drove Adam to sin. He promises that He will save from the bites of the serpent (that is, from evil works, idolatry and other sins) all who believe in Him, who died by this sign, which is the Cross.
St. Justin Martyr * The serpent struck Adam in Paradise and killed him. And it also struck Israel in the camp and destroyed it.
As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up (Jn 3:14).

Just as those who looked with their bodily eyes at the sign that Moses fixed on the pole lived bodily, so also those who look with spiritual eyes at the body of the Messiah nailed and hung on the Cross and believe in Him shall live spiritually.
This was proclaimed through the bronze serpent, which by nature does not suffer, so that He who by nature cannot die might suffer on the Cross.

St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian * It is a great mystery, the healing from the serpent. What does it mean, healing from a serpent by looking at a serpent? It is healing from death by faith in one who is dead! Yet Moses was afraid and fled from the serpent (Ex 4:3). What does it mean that Moses fled from that serpent? What is this, brethren, but what we know was fulfilled in the Gospel? Christ died, and the disciples were afraid and withdrew from that hope in which they had been.

entries.section: 2. The third contrast: the locusts and the bronze serpent

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine For he that turned himself toward it was saved, not by that which he saw, but by thee, O Saviour of all. [7]

Some may ask: how does the Lord Christ say, “And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up” (Jn 3:14)? Is the Lord Christ being likened to the serpent, or does the deadly serpent signify the Lord Christ, the giver of life? The answers of the Fathers of the Church came many and mutually harmonious:

First: the Lord Christ bore the sins of the world (Jn 1:29), so the Lord Christ took our place, and accepted to bear our death in order to raise us to His life. For in the Crucified we see what the Lord Christ bore on our behalf, the fruit of our sins, that He might kill it by His death.
Second: St. Augustine sees that the lifted-up serpent is dead, and it is a symbol of the death which the Lord Christ accepted by His own will in order to kill our death.
Third: St. Gregory of Nazianzus sees that the children of Israel looked at the bronze serpent, dead and lifted up on a pole, and so perceived that by the Cross death died and became motionless!

Fourth: Origen has a marvelous comment concerning the Cross, for he sees in it two realities: the first is apparent, namely that Jesus Christ, in His love for mankind and His obedience to the Father, was lifted up on the Cross by His own will. The second is hidden, namely that the one who was crucified and lost his movement and authority is the devil, since the handwriting that was against us was nailed to the Cross, and principalities and powers were spoiled of their authority and were made a show of openly in a bitter defeat (Col 2:14-15). So the serpent that was lifted up represents, on the one hand, the Lord Christ who bears our sins, and on the other hand, the ancient serpent whom the Lord Christ nailed with His Cross and stripped of its authority over the believers.

entries.section: 2. The third contrast: the locusts and the bronze serpent

paragraphs.text: * Perhaps you ask: for what purpose did Christ not say plainly, “I shall be crucified,” but directed his hearers to an ancient type (the serpent)? We say to you: first, that you may know that the sayings of the Old Testament agree with the New, and that those are not strange to these. Second: that you may know that Christ did not come into the world unwillingly. Besides these two reasons, that you may know that the Lord suffered no harm from the reality of these (sufferings), and that these sufferings, for many, proceed out of salvation. So that no one may say: how can those who believe in the Crucified be saved if death itself laid hold of Him? Therefore He leads us to the ancient story. For if the Jews by looking at a bronze image of the serpent escaped death, how much more shall those who believe in the Crucified enjoy, for good reason, greater benefits. For the crucifixion does not take place through the weakness of the Crucified, or because the Jews are stronger than He, but because “God so loved the world” [16], therefore His living temple (His body) hastened to the Cross.
St. John Chrysostom * What are the serpents that bite? The sins that proceed from the death of the body.
What is the serpent that was lifted up? The death of the Lord on the Cross. As death came by the serpent, it was symbolized by the image of a serpent.

The bite of the serpent is deadly, and the death of the Lord is life-giving. When one looks at a serpent, the serpent loses its power. What is this? When one looks at death, death loses its power. But whose death? The death of Life…
By the death of Christ (the Life) death died.
The death of Life slew death, the fullness of life swallowed up death.
Death was dissolved in the body of Christ.
Therefore we say at the Resurrection, as the victors sing: “O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?” (1 Cor 15:54)…
There is a difference between the symbolic image and the real thing: the symbol gives temporary life, and the reality of which it is the symbol gives eternal life.

* To present a type of His Cross, Moses, at the command of the merciful God, lifted up the image of a serpent on a pole in the wilderness, in the likeness of the sinful flesh which had to be crucified in Christ, who was typified (Jn 3:14). It was to look at this Cross that the psalmist purposed when he said: “Mine eyes fail for thy salvation, and for the word of thy righteousness” (Ps 119:123), because He made Christ Himself “sin for us, in the likeness of sinful flesh, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (Rom 8:3; 2 Cor 5:21).
For the sake of declaring the righteousness of God he says that his eyes have failed from looking with zeal and fervor, while he remembers human weakness, looking to the divine grace in Christ.

St. Augustine * That bronze serpent was hung up as a remedy for the bites of serpents, not as a type of Him who suffered, but of the opposite. It healed those who looked at it, not because they believed that it lived, but because it was slain, and with it was slain the one subject to it, for it deserves to perish. And what inscription suitable to it shall we inscribe? “O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?” (Hos 13:14; 1 Cor 15:55). You have been cast down by the Cross. You have no longer a soul; you have died motionless, though you retain the form of a serpent raised on a pole!
St. Gregory of Nazianzus And in this thou didst prove to our enemies that thou art he who delivereth from all evil. [8]
For those the bitings of locusts and vermin killed, and no remedy was found to preserve their life, for they were worthy to be punished by such. [9]

By the ten plagues God did not display His power, for He is not in need of human glory, but He showed His people their possibilities, in that they enjoy the power of God through their faith. And at the same time He showed the weakness of the gods of the Egyptians, unable to protect them even from the locusts or the gnats (flies).

* “He spake, and the locusts came, and caterpillers, and that without number, and did eat up all the herbs in their land, and devoured the fruit of their ground” (Ps 105:34-35). The trees were destroyed by the hail and the fire, and the gardens and the crops by the locusts and the caterpillers (the young locusts before they have wings), for it wasted not only the fruit but even the plant itself.
Father Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus Whereas the teeth of venomous serpents did not overcome thy sons, for thy mercy came upon them and healed them. [10]

The wise man stands in amazement before two scenes: an unbelieving people struck with insects and perishing, because they did not believe in the Physician who heals souls; and a believing people struck with venomous serpents and healed, because they believed in the Savior who gives victory over the powers of darkness.

If feeble insects cause destruction while the fangs of venomous serpents do not prevail over the believers, this is not a natural matter; rather, healing is accomplished according to the riches of God’s grace, His surpassing mercy and His wonderful salvation. This is the mystery of the Cross!
Concerning the bronze serpent, it is not the serpent that gives healing, but “thy mercy came and healed them” (Wis 16:10).
For they were pricked that they should remember thy words, and were quickly delivered, lest falling into deep forgetfulness they should neglect thy goodness. [11]

The Lord commanded Moses the prophet to lift up the dead bronze serpent on a pole, so that when the believers look at it they may remember God’s promises of salvation. He hastened and healed them, lest they fall into the depth of forgetfulness and lose their hope in the promised salvation.
And neither herb nor ointment healed them, but thy word, O Lord, for it healeth all. [12]

He did not give them medicinal herb or ointments for healing, not to prevent them from using medicines, but lest they ascribe their healing from the bites of the serpent to medicines and not to the word of God and His promise of salvation.

St. Basil the Great presented to us in his “Long Rules,” question number 55, a long and engaging discourse on the Christian view of medicine and physicians, and on whether it is permissible to have recourse to the art of medicine and to use medicines while keeping the practice of godliness. I translated it, arranged it and published it in the book “What do the Fathers say about sickness?” I quote a little of it here.

* All the arts (crafts) are a gift to us from God, remedying the deficiencies of nature. So He gave us agriculture, because the harvest which the earth gives us without cultivation is not sufficient for our needs. And the craft of weaving, because the use of clothing is necessary for modesty and for protection from the wind. In the same way as regards the craft of building, and so also as regards the craft of medicine. For since our body is exposed to various pains, some attacking from outside, and others from within because of the food we eat, and since the body suffers from surfeit as well as from lack of food, therefore the art of medicine is granted by God, who directs all our life, as a pattern for the healing of the soul, to lead us to remove what is superfluous and to obtain what is lacking.
* We would not have needed the toil of the farmer if we were living in the delights of Paradise; so also we would not have sought the art of medicine for healing if we were immune from sickness.

So it was at the time of creation before the fall, as a gift from God. But after we were driven out of that place, and heard the words: “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Gen 3:19), then with toil and exhausting hardship we established the craft of agriculture to remove the misery that followed the curse that had come.
