And God gave us the knowledge and understanding for this craft, when we returned to the earth from which we were taken and were bound to a body full of pains, and were cast into the judgment of corruption because of sin.
For the same reason we became subject to sickness, and God gave us the craft of medicine for the treatment of the sick, even if only to a certain degree.

* The herbs that are used for the treatment of every sickness did not grow in the earth spontaneously, but it is clear that it is the will of God that they should grow from the soil to serve our needs. Our enjoyment of the natural benefits latent in the roots of herbs, their flowers, leaves, fruits and juice, and even in some minerals and products of the sea, is necessary for bodily health, and they are regarded like food and drink.
St. Basil the Great * The art of medicine is not a hindrance to godliness, but you must practice it with the fear of the Lord.

Father Barsanuphius By saying: “it healeth all,” he makes clear that if a certain people benefited by bodily healing from the deadly serpents by looking at the bronze serpent, then it is a type of the Cross, which offers salvation to the whole world. “God so loved the world, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life” (Jn 3:16).
For thou hast power of life and death: thou leadest down to the gates of hell, and bringest up from it. [13]

As the wise man looks at the One hung on the Cross, he sees Him not only as the Physician who can heal all men, but as the Almighty, the giver of life and resurrection, and the Judge who carries His believers to eternal glory while the gates of Gehenna are opened before the unbelievers, since they chose of their own will to withdraw from the giver of life. God breathes into us the spirit of power and victory, so that neither the devil nor death has authority over us. “Thou leadest down to the gates of the realm of the dead, and bringest up from it.”
A man can kill by his wickedness, but he cannot bring back the breath that has gone out, nor set free the soul that is held fast! [14]

Man by his free will delivered himself over to death by sin, but he is unable to recover the lost Paradise or true life; but God alone can raise the dead, bodily or spiritually, and restore man to something greater than he was in the garden of Eden.
If a man thinks that he has authority to kill by his wickedness and injustice, does he have authority to bring the slain back to life?

entries.section: 3. The fourth contrast: the hail and the manna

paragraphs.text: 15 For it is not possible for any one to escape thy hand, 16 for the ungodly, who denied to know thee, were scourged by the strength of thine arm, and were pursued with strange waters, hail and rains, and consumed with fire. 17 And what is most strange, the fire was more intense in the water, which quencheth all things, for the world fighteth for the righteous. 18 For sometime the flame was mitigated, that it might not burn up the living creatures sent against the ungodly, but that they might see and perceive that God’s judgment pursued them; 19 and sometime it burneth even in the midst of water above the power of fire, that it might destroy the fruits of an unrighteous land. 20 Instead of which things thou feddest thine own people with angels’ food, and didst send them from heaven bread prepared without their labour, able to content every man’s delight, and agreeing to every taste. 21 For thy substance declared thy sweetness unto thy children, and serving to the appetite of him that took it, tempered itself to every man’s liking. 22 The snow and ice endured the fire, and melted not, that they might know that fire burning in the hail and sparkling in the rain destroyed the fruits of the enemies. 23 But this, again, forgot its own strength, that the righteous might be nourished. 24 For the creature that serveth thee, who art the maker, is made more intense for the punishment of the unrighteous, and is relaxed for the benefit of such as put their trust in thee. 25 Therefore even then was it altered into all fashions, and was obedient to thy grace, that nourisheth all things, according to the desire of them that had need, 26 that thy children, O Lord, whom thou lovedst, might know, that it is not the growing of fruits that nourisheth man, but that thy word preserveth them that put their trust in thee. 27 For that which was not destroyed of the fire, being warmed with a little sunbeam, melted away, 28 that it might be known that we must prevent the sun to give thee thanks, and at the dayspring pray unto thee. 29 For the hope of the unthankful shall melt away as the winter’s hoar frost, and shall run away as unneedful water.
It is impossible to escape from thy hand. [15]

Often man in his pride thinks that he is able to lord it over his brother, to oppress and persecute, and that there is no law that can restrain him. These were the feelings of Pharaoh and his counselors and men, as they mocked and humbled the Hebrews. These did not perceive that God is the Almighty, and that “it is impossible to escape from his hand.”

Pharaoh made the plan firm to destroy Moses and the people of God: the sea before them, the army behind them, and the mountains on both sides, while they had no weapons, no military experience and no fortresses in which to take refuge. But God made for His people a way of salvation in the midst of the sea, and that very way became the total destruction of Pharaoh.

entries.section: 3. The fourth contrast: the hail and the manna

paragraphs.text: For the wicked, who denied to know thee, were scourged by the strength of thine arm, pursued by unusual rains, and hailstones, and harsh tempests, and consumed by fire. [16]

Pharaoh defied God Himself, for in a spirit of domination and violence he said to Moses that he did not know the Lord, but only knew his own authority and material gains, without any regard for God, the Creator of all, or for showing kindness to his brethren in humanity.

God let nature itself answer the wicked Pharaoh. Egypt does not know hail, and yet, contrary to nature, He disciplined the pagan Egyptians with hail. And what is astonishing is that hail and fire (lightning) do not occur together, but the two opposites worked together by divine permission for discipline…
By this nature stopped the mouth of the arrogant Pharaoh, to declare to him that he had lost all reason and wisdom, by resisting the wisdom of God.

entries.section: 3. The fourth contrast: the hail and the manna

paragraphs.text: And what is most strange, in the water which quencheth all things, the fire grew more intense, for the universe fighteth for the righteous. [17]
Water is used to extinguish fires, but what happened to Pharaoh was that whenever the hail fell the flames grew more intense, so the two opposites agreed together to discipline him.

entries.section: 3. The fourth contrast: the hail and the manna

paragraphs.text: And the flame was sometimes quieted, lest it should burn up the animals that were sent against the wicked, but that they might see and understand that a divine judgment pursued them. [18]

The wise man stood in amazement, for the natural phenomena that rose up in an unnatural manner against the unbelieving pagans worked together. Note that the fires did not burn the insects and animals sent for their discipline, as though everything had joined together against the unbelievers to drive them to faith.
The unnatural factors removed from the wicked any possibility of imagining that what was happening was by chance; rather, they came to carry out a divine judgment against them for their discipline.

entries.section: 3. The fourth contrast: the hail and the manna

paragraphs.text: And sometimes it burneth even in the midst of water above the power of fire, that it might destroy the produce of an unjust land. [19]

When fires break out, especially in an agricultural land, people’s dream becomes the falling of rain able to put out the fires. But what happened was that in the midst of the hail the fires grew more intense in their flaming, and the losses increased.

* “He gave them hail for rain, and flaming fire in their land. He smote their vines also and their fig trees; and brake the trees of their coasts” (Ps 105:32-33)… The clouds changed their natural role, and sent hail instead of rain, thunderbolts and whirlwinds accompanied by hail, and water and fire. Although by nature the one is contrary to the other, no confusion occurred between them. The fire did not melt the frozen water or the hail, nor did the fire put out the flame. Besides their leaving the natural resistance of each to the other, they brought a severe punishment on the Egyptians, to condemn their enslavement and their disrespect for their nature (as human beings). For though they were men, they oppressed their fellows in humanity with cruel bondage. Therefore even their vines and their fig trees and all kinds of plants were utterly destroyed by the fire and the hail.

entries.section: 3. The fourth contrast: the hail and the manna

paragraphs.text: Father Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus But thy people, instead of this, thou didst feed with angels’ food, and didst present to them from heaven bread prepared, which they did not labour for, bread that supplied every delight and suited every taste. [20]

While nature rose up against the wicked and did not keep to the natural factors, so also, contrary to the laws of nature, it worked on behalf of the believers, offering them manna from heaven, a thing of which mankind had never heard before.
The manna is considered the food of angels (Ps 78:25; 105:40), because it points to the heavenly sweetness that each person tastes according to what he desires.

* “Each one tasted the manna in his mouth according as he longed” (cf. Wis 16:20)… In any case, this can be realized for the believers and not for those who murmur against God, those who certainly would not seek other food, since the manna gave them a taste according to what they wished.

entries.section: 3. The fourth contrast: the hail and the manna

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine For thy substance declared thy sweetness unto thy children, and satisfying the desire of him that took it, was changed to what every man would. [21]
There is a rabbinic tradition that the manna had a special flavor which each person experienced according to what he desired, so that each person found in it a sweet taste suited to his wish.

* Would then that we hasten to receive the heavenly manna. This manna grants a taste to every mouth according to what it desires. Hear also the Lord saying to those who approach Him: “As thou hast believed, so be it done unto thee” (Mt 8:13). So also if you receive the word of God which is preached in the Church with perfect and devout faith, the word becomes for you according to what you desire. For example, if you are sad, it comforts you, saying to you: “A broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Ps 51:19). If you are exulting in your coming hope, it lavishes joys upon you, saying: “Be glad in the Lord, and rejoice, ye righteous” (Ps 32:11). If you are in anger, it gives you calm, saying: “Cease from anger, and forsake wrath” (Ps 37:8). If you are in pain, it heals you, saying: “The Lord healeth all thy diseases” (cf. Ps 103:3). If you are consumed by poverty, it comforts you, saying: “The Lord raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the needy out of the dunghill” (cf. Ps 113:7). So the manna of the word of God gives a taste to your mouth according to what you wish.

Origen Here we stand in wonder before God’s indulgence of His believers, for not only does He give them what is for their satisfaction, growth and progress, but He gratifies every believer, giving him what he desires so long as it is for his good and benefit.
When the believer is in the bosom of God, and feels that he is carried on the everlasting arms, everything becomes sweet in his throat, it satisfies his needs, and he lacks nothing at all.

entries.section: 3. The fourth contrast: the hail and the manna

paragraphs.text: The snow and ice endured fire and melted not, that it might be known that the fruits of the enemies were consumed by fire blazing in the hail and flashing in the midst of the rains. [22]

A marvelous picture of God’s surpassing love for man, for He moves nature even against its laws to serve man, so He permits the fire to blaze in the midst of the hail and the heavy rains. Man is the object of God’s care, so He lays out a plan for him and gives him a message, and turns all things to his good if he loves God (Rom 8:28).

entries.section: 3. The fourth contrast: the hail and the manna

paragraphs.text: Whereas this fire forgot even its own power, that the righteous might be nourished. [23]

As though nature, in its longing to serve man, the object of God’s love and care, is ready to disregard its characteristics and forget its properties, to work for the benefit of the righteous believers, even contrary to its laws.

entries.section: 3. The fourth contrast: the hail and the manna

paragraphs.text: For the creation, which serveth thee who art its maker, is strained for the punishment of the unjust, and is relaxed for the benefit of those who trust in thee. [24]

Nature does not work blindly according to its laws; rather, while keeping the natural laws, which are the work of God, it moves and reacts according to the Creator’s plan, so it works for the benefit of the righteous believers of the Lord, and is harsh upon the unbelievers for their discipline, to the extent that the Creator permits.

The fire that could not melt the manna when the believers cooked it in the wilderness did not hurt the insects and animals sent to discipline the pagan Egyptians during the plagues. The fire that did not burn the three holy youths in Babylon is the one that killed the soldiers who cast the youths into it, and is the one that harmed the Egyptians and their crops and their plantings during the plagues.

entries.section: 3. The fourth contrast: the hail and the manna

paragraphs.text: Therefore then it was changed into every form, and was in the service of thy gift that nourisheth all, according to the desire of those who had need of it. [25]
In His wisdom God created man to govern the world with righteousness and holiness, for when he is bound to his Creator, God moves nature to work in his service according to what he asks and desires.

entries.section: 3. The fourth contrast: the hail and the manna

paragraphs.text: So that thy sons whom thou lovedst, O Lord, might know that it is not the produce of the fruits that nourisheth man, but thy word preserveth those who trust in thee. [26]

The Holy Scripture is accustomed to call the believers the beloved of the Lord. They are the object of His love and care. Therefore what nature offers them is from the hand of God, according to His word or His divine promises.

entries.section: 3. The fourth contrast: the hail and the manna

paragraphs.text: For that which the fire did not destroy was melted away when warmed by a little sunbeam. [27]

The wise man marvels as he looks at the manna sent to them from God, for it does not endure the rays of the sun even in the early morning. If a man was late in his sleep he could not gather manna, for he would find it melted by the rays of the sun. And at the same time that he gathers the manna he cooks it, and the heat does not melt it nor spoil it, but it becomes fit for eating.

entries.section: 3. The fourth contrast: the hail and the manna

paragraphs.text: So that it might be known that we must rise before the sun to give thee thanks, and meet thee at the rising of the light. [28]

The wise man urges us to rise early to God, so that He may be the beginning in all the days of our life, and before every work He may have the first place in our hearts, and He pours out upon us the riches of His surpassing gifts. For he who does not hasten before sunrise cannot gather the manna, and remains hungry all his day; for God satisfies the soul with heavenly food when it rises early to Him.

* Concerning the place (of prayer): “I will therefore that men pray every where” (1 Tim 2:8). Concerning the direction (of prayer) it is written in the Wisdom of Solomon: “That it might be known that we must prevent the sun to give thee thanks, and meet thee at (before) the rising of the light” (Wis 16:28).

entries.section: 3. The fourth contrast: the hail and the manna

paragraphs.text: Origen For the hope of the ungrateful shall melt away like the winter frost, and shall run away like water that is of no use. [29]

The wise man sees in those who rose early to gather the manna before sunrise the class of those obedient to the divine commandment with thanksgiving to God, the maker of good things; and as for those who in negligence wait until the sun rises, like those who do not believe the divine words, they are ungrateful and deniers of kindness. The former find delicious food offered to them freely, which may be called “the bread of angels,” and the latter find the manna turned to water like frost in the cold of the wilderness, good for nothing, for it cannot be gathered for drinking nor does it water plants, because the wilderness is a desert.

* What greater thing does (the Lord) ask of us than that we ask Him that we may be thankful in return for this tender care of His? Let us then obey, and keep this in everything. For there is nothing that ruined the Jews like their ingratitude; plagues upon plagues befell them for no other reason than this. Indeed, over and above these plagues, their souls perished and were corrupted. “For the hope of the unthankful shall melt away as the winter’s hoar frost” (Wis 16:29). For it paralyzes the soul and kills it as happens with bodies.
St. John Chrysostom
Who satisfies me but you, O Wisdom of God?
* With the greatness of the gifts and abilities of my fathers the Pharaohs, they bowed down to idols of animals and insects, and so they drank of the very cup which they had filled.
They tasted bitterness from the plagues of the frogs, the gnats, the flies and the locusts.
Their houses were turned into tombs full of stench.
Their bodies found no rest, but pains and torment.
And their life became full of uncleanness; their crops the locusts ate, so they found no food for themselves.
* Grant me to cleave to You in the midst of the wilderness of this world.
I do not ask for bread or flesh; You are my satisfaction and my feast!
You are my joy and the exultation of my heart!
* My soul groans, because You grant me every fullness, while I see many of my brethren in humanity deprived and in ruin!
* Who heals me but You, O Physician of souls and bodies?
The unbelievers could not endure the plagues of feeble insects.
They perished because of the gnats and the flies, and went hungry because of the locusts.
But the believers, the bites of the deadly serpents could not destroy them.
They looked at the bronze serpent and were healed.
Let me look at Your Cross, and perceive that the powers of darkness have been stripped of their authority.
Death died, and it became impossible for it to move.
The bites of the deadly serpents were turned into a living witness to Your mercy.
You are the wonderful Physician of my soul.
You are the heavenly, saving medicine!
Who heals me but You, O Savior of the world?
* O the riches of Your wisdom and Your love for me!
For my sake You created nature with all its laws, seen and hidden.
You prepared it for my service, for I am Your beloved, and the object of Your care.
And for my sake also You permit its laws to be broken, at one time to satisfy my needs, and at another to discipline me.
All Your works are love and surpassing care.
By fire coming down from heaven to burn Sodom and Gomorrah, so that the believers may learn purity and fear uncleanness and abominations.
And You permitted the fire to become dew, so that the three holy youths might walk in it.
* How marvelous! When the fires fell upon the Egyptians for their discipline, they longed for rains to fall to put them out.
So rains fell, and even hail, but they did not put out the fires; rather they made them blaze the more.
* The fire could not melt the hail that fell upon the wicked, nor spoil the manna which the believers gather to cook.
It was not possible for the manna to endure the heat of the rays of the sun in the early morning, while it endured the blazing fires for its cooking.
* What shall I render to You, O my Creator?
For You move everything for my edification!
To You be glory, O You who are rich in love!

entries.section: 1. Darkness that exposes evil

paragraphs.text: 1 For great are thy judgments, and cannot be expressed; therefore unnurtured souls have erred. 2 For when the wicked thought to oppress the holy nation, they, being shut up in their houses, the prisoners of darkness and fettered with the bonds of a long night, lay there exiled from the eternal providence. 3 For while they supposed to lie hid in their secret sins, they were scattered under a dark veil of forgetfulness, being horribly astonished, and troubled with apparitions.
For great are thy judgments and cannot be expressed; therefore souls that were not disciplined have erred. [1]

entries.section: 1. Darkness that exposes evil

paragraphs.text: For when the wicked supposed that they would have dominion over the holy nation, they became prisoners of darkness, bound with a long night, shut up under their roofs, exiled from the eternal providence. [2]

The plague of darkness that came upon the Egyptians came before the final plague, “the slaying of the firstborn,” as though it were the last divine warning directed against the wicked so that they might discover what they were and reassess the situation.
By this plague the greatness of God’s wisdom appeared, for the following reasons:

First: by falling under this plague they perceive the inner darkness that had settled in their hearts and thoughts. Their souls had erred and had paid no heed to the preceding successive plagues, so they became like those in wandering and error, and the features of the true way were lost to them, because they had rejected the divine light. Rightly was it said of them: “Therefore unnurtured souls have erred.”

Second: they live in delusion, and do not perceive the truth, so they think that they are possessors of authority, that there is none who can stand before them or repel their assaults upon a defenseless, enslaved people.
Third: they mock this defenseless people, and do not perceive that at that time they represent a holy nation.

Fourth: these cruel men did not perceive that they were being cruel only to themselves, for they were “prisoners of darkness,” bound and in a long night, upon which perhaps no morning light will dawn because of their stubbornness.
Fifth: by their violence and cruelty they became prisoners without iron fetters, in a prison made by their own sins: “shut up under their roofs.”
Sixth: since they are without mercy they deprive themselves of God’s mercy and kindness, “exiled from the eternal providence.”

These six facts are the making of the sinner who persists in violence, injustice and cruelty: an inner darkness in the depths of the soul; reliance on an imaginary authority that has no existence; failure to perceive the potential of those whom they treat cruelly, and to recognize their true reality; they take themselves captive in darkness without hope of enjoying a shining light; they imprison themselves in a prison made by the work of their own hands; and finally they deprive themselves of the divine mercies.

Pharaoh and his men thought that they were possessors of authority with none to restrain them, so they paid no heed to the divine command issued to them through the man of God, Moses. And instead of responding to it, in stubbornness strict orders were issued to treat the people of God with cruelty and violence. And since they persisted in this even after suffering many disciplines, they were struck with the plague of darkness. Here the wise man portrays the Egyptians in prison and darkness, unable to carry on their daily work, and no light was found except in the land of Goshen (today’s Sharqia governorate). Instead of their enslaving the Jews, they imprisoned themselves in their own houses in the midst of pitch darkness, and even the gift of the shining of the material sun left them. It was not possible for their god, as they were worshipping the sun (the god Ra), to deliver them from the darkness.
Their houses were turned into an unbearable hell, where phantoms assailed them, and their strength was dissolved by fear.

God, the lover of mankind, makes His sun to rise on the evil and on the good (Mt 5:45), and out of His love also He permits this gift to be taken away at times, so that when the wicked man loses the tangible light he may perceive that he has lost the divine light in his depths, and that the evil darkness has dominion over his heart, his mind and his senses! Thus he appears as one who has lost the divine providence (Wis 17:2).
* Surely this darkness of the heart is in itself a punishment, that is, blindness of heart, because they abandoned the light of wisdom they fell into graver and graver sins.
St. Augustine Origen sees that the darkness points to the plague of ignorance with which the wicked man is struck.

* Who was able to break the plague of ignorance, the destroying darkness? Not a prophet, nor an apostle, nor any righteous man! But rather there was need of the power of a God who comes down from heaven, able to die for us all, that by His death we might have a defense against Satan.

entries.section: 1. Darkness that exposes evil

paragraphs.text: Origen They supposed that they would remain hidden in their secret sins; they were scattered under the dark veil of forgetfulness, being in great terror, troubled with phantoms. [3]

When man commits sin, he thinks that he is acting with wisdom or cunning, and that there is none who can discover his matter. And with the passing of time he reckons that what he did has been folded away by time and has become forgotten. But even if his matter is not discovered among men, and he does not fall under a civil or criminal penalty, he falls under a penalty in his depths. For a great terror comes upon him and a dread of phantoms that pursue him. This is one of the curses that come upon him who falls into evil, as he tries to flee, scattered among many ways, with no enemy behind him following his tracks. The enemy of the sinner is within him, terrifying him, and none can rescue him from it except God Himself, if he returns to Him in repentance. Its remedy is to drive out fear by fear, for the fear that comes without hope from committing sin is removed by the fear of the Lord, which fills the soul with hope in the Savior of the world, the lover and sanctifier of sinners.

It is written among the curses that come upon him who is determined to rebel and disobey the divine commandment: “The Lord shall send upon thee cursing, vexation, and rebuke, in all that thou settest thine hand unto for to do, until thou be destroyed, and until thou perish quickly; because of the wickedness of thy doings, whereby thou hast forsaken me” (Deut 28:20). If the fruit of the Spirit is love mingled with joy (Gal 5:23), as the Holy Spirit carries the soul as though to heaven to taste eternal joy while it is still in the midst of the world’s troubles, cares and trials, then the work of sin, especially disobedience, is the deprivation of man of this heavenly atmosphere. For by disobedience man turns his back on God, the source of true joy, so he casts himself into the hell of anxiety and disturbance, bearing a spirit of rebuke and ingratitude in every work to which his hand reaches. He drives himself by himself to inner ruin.
The enemy of good is bound to the night and darkness, because he cannot bear the true light. All his works are evil and deceptive, therefore they are counted darkness.
* The deception of the enemy is night, as Paul said: [We are not of the night, but of the day] (cf. 1 Thess 5:5-8).
St. Mar Isaac the Syrian St. John Chrysostom criticizes the worshippers of idols because they destroyed the light that was in them (the natural law), so they became in darkness.

* This is the gravest accusation against the pagans (that they left God), and the second is that they worshipped idols (Jer 2:13)… The pagans tried to reach heaven, but since they destroyed the light that was in them, and instead trusted in themselves, in the darkness of their thinking, they looked for the immaterial in bodies and gazed at the unlimited in created forms, and by this they lost their harmony with the light.

St. John Chrysostom * Surely this darkness of the heart was a punishment and a recompense; by this recompense, which is blindness of heart because of abandoning the light of wisdom, they fell into graver and graver sins.
St. Augustine

entries.section: 2. No escape from the deadly terror

paragraphs.text: 4 For neither did the corner that held them keep them from fear, but noises as of waters falling down sounded about them, and sad visions appeared unto them with heavy countenances.
For the inner chambers that kept them did not shield them from fear, for loud noises resounded about them, and phantoms with appalling faces appeared to them. [4]

In some translations it reads: “the nests in which they lodged did not shield them from terror.” So he likens them to young birds lying in nests, thinking that they are protected among the branches of the trees, with none to approach and harm them.

What was the refuge that the Egyptians thought able to cover them from what they were committing, except their feeling that they were possessors of authority and that they were above the law?! This feeble refuge was not able to protect them from the terror within them, and the loud noises resounding about them, and the phantoms that terrified them in the midst of the pitch darkness.

The matter did not stop at the loss of light and the dominion of darkness over the wicked, but God permitted the apparitions of demons to terrify them in the midst of the darkness, so that they might perceive that they had refused to belong to God and had accepted by their own will sonship to the devil.

* If someone constantly thinks about what pleases God and what does not please Him, it may be said of him that the fear of God is always before his eyes. But such a person needs to be tested and to learn diligently in the law of God, so that he may not fear where there is no cause for fear. For the fear of God must always be set before our eyes - not the eyes of the body, for what we are speaking of here is something unseen and immaterial, but the eyes of the mind, where the perception and understanding of the fear of God is clear, and by this, as we said before, we discover what we must fear and what we must not fear. For he who fears God does not fear the rulers of this world.
Origen The Egyptians failed to find a refuge for themselves from the darkness; there was need of the intervention of the Holy Spirit to be delivered from it.

* We must ask the Lord Himself, the Holy Spirit Himself, to remove every cloud and all the darkness that hinders the sight from our hearts, which have been hardened by the defilement of sins, so that we may behold the knowledge of His wonderful spiritual law.
Origen To be rid of the darkness, it befits us to overcome the love of the world, so that we may be occupied with the heavenly things and see them.
* No one who has overcome (the love of the world) and been made worthy of the world to come is blind in understanding, because his eyes are enlightened.
St. Didymus the Blind

entries.section: 3. Nothing to dispel the darkness

paragraphs.text: 5 No power of the fire, however strong, could give them light, neither could the bright flames of the stars enlighten that horrible night. 6 Only there appeared unto them a fire kindled of itself, very dreadful; for being much terrified, they thought the things which they saw to be worse than the sight they saw not.
And no fire, however strong its power, gave light, nor did the shining of the stars illumine that murky night. [5]
The darkness was a plague for discipline, therefore all their attempts to kindle a fire or lamps, however strong they were, ended in failure.
Even with the splendor of the stars, it was not able to illumine the murky night that had come upon them.

It was an unnatural darkness; no artificial or natural lights could dispel it. As though the darkness were crying out in a loud voice: there is no salvation for you by any means except by returning to God, the true Light, who alone is able to dispel your inner darkness.
And nothing shone for them but masses of fire that kindled of themselves, and cast terror.

entries.section: 3. Nothing to dispel the darkness

paragraphs.text: And when this sight passed away from them, they were still trembling, reckoning that what appeared to them was more dreadful than it was. [6]

Masses of fire appeared to them, not to give them light but to terrify them. Perhaps these masses represented fiery evil spirits, but without radiance and unable to give light, or they were from the inspiration of their imaginations. They were in great perplexity, for the pitch darkness terrified them, and the masses of fire did not remedy the matter, but rather inflamed their hearts the more with terror.

Perhaps these masses of fire were the work of magic, for the magicians tried to resist the darkness, which was a divine discipline, by producing masses of fire that gave them light. But the masses appeared and were unable to dispel the darkness and remove the fear and terror, which terrified the Egyptians all the more.

Since the creation of Adam the enemy of good has exerted every effort to imitate God and His angels so as to catch man in his nets by deception. Here the enemy of good tried - through magic - to appear as masses of fire, so as to assure the Egyptians that he is God.
* This is Satan’s habit, to imitate the things that belong to God. He raises up false prophets who resist the true prophets, and he also appears in the form of an angel to deceive men.

Father Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus * If we have Christ in our hearts, He gives us light. Therefore if the perception of knowledge removes ignorance, and if we leave unseemly works and do what is upright, then we are in the light, and we walk faithfully as in the day.
Origen

entries.section: 4. The inability of magic to remove the darkness

paragraphs.text: 7 Then the art of magic was put down, and their vaunting in wisdom was reproved with disgrace, 8 for they that promised to drive away terrors and troubles from a sick soul were themselves sick of fear, worthy to be laughed at.
The trickery of their magic art was powerless, and its claim to wisdom was silenced with disgrace. [7]

entries.section: 4. The inability of magic to remove the darkness

paragraphs.text: For those who promised to drive away fears and troubles from the sick soul, these a ridiculous fear made sick. [8]

They chose to submit to the powers of darkness, and despised taking refuge under the wings of God (Ps 91:4), so they could not be delivered from the frightening voices of the demons or stop their moving about them. In vain they tried to light a lamp in their houses to protect them from the darkness of the devil, because “Except the Lord keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Ps 127:1).

The demons saw the Egyptians resorting to kindling fires to give them light, so they hastened to frighten them by showing themselves as flaming fires in the air, moving before them, and the Egyptians were very afraid.

The Egyptians were skilled in magic and relied on it, so that Pharaoh and his counselors thought that they were able to resist Moses and Aaron by means of the magicians. And behold, the demons that play a principal role in magic were unable to rescue them from the plague of darkness that came upon them by divine permission, and instead of offering them help, the demons became an object of greater terror.

entries.section: 5. Terror of animals and serpents

paragraphs.text: 9 For though no terrible thing did fear them, yet being scared with beasts that passed by, and hissing of serpents, they were overcome.
For though there was no terrible thing to frighten them, the passing of animals and the hissing of serpents alarmed them. [9]
How marvelous! Those who used to worship some insects and creeping things, now the little creatures and serpents terrified them in the midst of the darkness.

entries.section: 6. Terror of the air

paragraphs.text: 9 So they perished for fear, and denied that they saw the air, which could of no side be avoided. 10 For wickedness, condemned by her own witness, is very timorous, and being pressed with conscience, always forecasteth grievous things. 11 For fear is nothing else but a betraying of the succours which reason offereth, 12 and the expectation from within, being less, counteth the ignorance more than the cause which bringeth the torment.
So they perished from the terrifying fear, and refused even to look at the air, which cannot be avoided. [10]

Everything around them, even the air, turned into a source of terror for them, for the inner terror is reflected upon man’s senses, so he thinks that everything around him is exceedingly terrifying and frightening, and he wishes to close his eyes, for he cannot bear to look even at the air he breathes.

entries.section: 6. Terror of the air

paragraphs.text: For wickedness is a mark of cowardice, when it is condemned by its own witness, and under the pressure of conscience it keeps magnifying difficulties. [11]

The wise man presents to us a grave truth, namely that terror comes upon man from within, through his wickedness and the crookedness of his heart and its turning away from God, the source of his peace; for sin begets anxiety, and the righteousness of God begets peace and joy.

entries.section: 6. Terror of the air

paragraphs.text: For fear is nothing but the abandonment of the helps of reason. [12]

The wise man reveals the cause of fear in the life of the wicked: it is not from events that befall them, nor from circumstances surrounding them, but from their losing the soundness of their minds, so there is no help that can give them rest.
* Darkness points to the sins of the flesh, which are practiced through worldly enticements… But to take up the armor of light (Rom 13:12) is to practice good works.

entries.section: 6. Terror of the air

paragraphs.text: Father Ambrosiaster The weaker the expectation of help, the greater the sense of ignorance of what brings the torment. [13]
The wicked lose their hope of enjoying balance of mind, for there is no help for the reason, and consequently bitter torment comes upon them through their ignorance of what they are.

entries.section: 7. The darkness of death or the prison of the grave

paragraphs.text: 13 For they that slept the same sleep that night, which was intolerable, and which came upon them out of the bottoms of inevitable hell, 14 were partly vexed with monstrous apparitions, and partly fainted, their heart failing them; for a sudden fear, and not looked for, came upon them. 15 So then whosoever there fell down was straitly kept, shut up in a prison without iron bars.

entries.section: 7. The darkness of death or the prison of the grave

paragraphs.text: But they, in that night which was truly powerless and which came from the depths of the realm of the dead, were sleeping the very same sleep (of death). [14]

Their life was turned into a bitter night, as though it were not the work of nature, like an eclipse of the sun, but issued from hell, to turn their life into hell, as they said. And with their great terror they became like those who slept in the grave and lay down.

entries.section: 7. The darkness of death or the prison of the grave

paragraphs.text: And at one time dreadful phantoms pursued them, and at another their strength was dissolved by the faintness of their souls, because of the sudden and unexpected fear that came upon them. [15]
Finally, their terror has three sources: the phantoms that pursued them, the dissolving of their hearts and their complete collapse, and their failure to perceive what would befall them after that.

entries.section: 7. The darkness of death or the prison of the grave

paragraphs.text: And so whoever fell there, whoever he was, was kept shut up in a prison without iron. [16]

They were in a terrifying prison; they shut themselves up by themselves in their houses, fearing to move inside the house or to go out of it, lest they strike against something in the intensity of the darkness and fall to the ground. The darkness bound them as with chains on their hands and feet, so they were unable to move, so that perhaps they might perceive the state of captivity that had come upon their souls without their knowing.

The wicked shut themselves up in the prison of darkness that has no iron. They are terrified by the fear that comes from the inability of their minds to supply them with peace. “They were more grievous unto themselves than the darkness” (Wis 17:20).

entries.section: 8. Bound with one chain of darkness

paragraphs.text: 16 For whether he were husbandman, or shepherd, or a labourer in the field, he was overtaken, and endured that necessity, which could not be avoided; for they were all bound with one chain of darkness. 17 Whether it were a whistling wind, or a melodious noise of birds among the spreading branches, or a pleasing fall of water running violently, 18 or a terrible sound of stones cast down, or a running that could not be seen of skipping beasts, or a roaring voice of most savage wild beasts, or a rebounding echo from the hollow mountains, these things made them to swoon for fear.

entries.section: 8. Bound with one chain of darkness

paragraphs.text: For whether he was a farmer or a shepherd or one who did a work of the wilderness, he was suddenly seized and fell into the inevitable doom. [17]

The darkness came upon them suddenly, so those who were in farming, or tending sheep, or practicing any work in the wilderness were not given a chance to go to their houses, but remained groping in the midst of the darkness, not knowing how to move.
For they were all bound with one chain of darkness.

entries.section: 8. Bound with one chain of darkness

paragraphs.text: For the whistling of the wind, the singing of birds on the spreading branches, and the rhythm of rushing water. [18]

entries.section: 8. Bound with one chain of darkness

paragraphs.text: And the crashing of tumbling stones, the unseen running of leaping animals, the roaring of the most savage beasts, and the echo resounding in the hollows of the mountains, all this paralyzed them with fear. [19]

What added to the terror was that while they were in the captivity of darkness, everything around them increased their anxiety: the sound of the branches of the trees, the rushing water and the tumbling stones, even the animals which in their terror of the darkness ran uncontrolled in a state of hysteria, and so on. All this deprived them of every possibility of reassurance! Their hearts were dissolved, because all nature was in revolt against them, and they feared the attack of the raging beasts of prey. Therefore they stayed in their places in the wildernesses, like those bound with one chain, none daring to move to find a companion in his distress.

entries.section: 9. None to share their darkness

paragraphs.text: 19 For the whole world shined with clear light, and none were hindered in their labour. 20 Over them only was spread a heavy night, an image of that darkness which should afterward receive them; but yet were they unto themselves more grievous than the darkness.

entries.section: 9. None to share their darkness

paragraphs.text: For the whole world was illumined by a bright light, and carried on its works without hindrance. [20]

The whole world was enjoying the gift of God, that is, the existence of day and night: men practice their works in the day through the light of the sun and rest at night, but these became in a perpetual night in the midst of a nature in revolt, with their utter inability to practice any work. The darkness struck them with a kind of paralysis, although their limbs were able to move.
But over them alone was spread a heavy night, an image of the darkness prepared to receive them, but they were more grievous unto themselves than the darkness. [21]

Had the darkness come upon all mankind, there would have been something of consolation in it, for it would be a general and universal distress; but its coming upon them and not upon others is a severe calamity, making them expect the coming of what is harsher than that.

* Behold the mercy and the judgment. Mercy for the elect, who obtain the righteousness of God, and judgment upon the others, who are blind. But the former believe because they wish to believe, while the others did not believe because they do not wish it. Therefore mercy and judgment come according to their (men’s) will.
St. Augustine
Enlighten my depths, and dispel all darkness in me!
* My depths within me cry out to You, O true Light.
Sin has corrupted my whole being.
Pitch darkness has reigned and settled in my depths.
I am no longer able to see.
I have become like a dead man in a grave, without movement.
My soul has turned into great bitterness!
Who can dispel my darkness but You?
* The enemy entered and reigned.
He turned my life into an unbearable hell!
I thought in sin there was pleasure and enjoyment, and behold, I am in misery and deprivation.
Phantoms have reigned over my soul.
And the sense of deprivation has shattered me.
* The darkness corrupted my life; I feared everything around me, as though the whole world had become hostile to me.
My depths were filled with deadly phantoms!
I am no longer able to draw my breath.
* Am I, then, in a prison?
It is the making of my evil will.
Are my soul and my body, then, bound with chains!
I have turned as though into a lifeless thing.
All vitality has been lost to me; I have lost all ability to move.
* I made every effort but to no avail.
Who can set me free but You?
Come, O true Light.
Shine in my depths, that I may perceive Your love!
I see You stretching out Your hands to embrace me.
I perceive Your wonderful longing toward me!
I cling to You, for You are my all.
Your light shatters every trace of darkness.
Your light lifts me up to Your heavens!
Your light renews my life!
* Now I cry out rejoicing:
Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil!
* Yes, shine, O Light, upon every man.
Dispel the darkness of the devil, and establish Your Kingdom in every soul.
Lift every heart to Your heavens, that it may enjoy Your splendor!
Let the heart of every man be enlarged, that he may love the light for all the world!

entries.section: A. Divine light

paragraphs.text: 1 But thy saints had a very great light, whose voices they hearing, and not seeing their shape, because they also had not suffered the same things, they counted them happy. But thy saints had a great light, and those who heard their voices without seeing their forms counted them happy that they had not suffered the torment. [1]

Most of the ancient Egyptians excelled in the sciences, the arts and culture. But, sadly, they fell into idolatrous worship and the evil customs and unseemly conduct that follow it, so they became by their own will children of darkness, therefore the plague of darkness came upon them. Now, as he speaks in contrast of the divine light that the believers enjoy, he calls them saints.

What occupies the heart of the writer is not the saints’ enjoyment of the light of the sun, but of the divine light, the light of the Sun of righteousness, who offers them a crossing to the heavenly life in the midst of the tribulations of this world.

For they were sanctified and set apart for God. And they were worshipping God, for they had light in their region, moving about in complete freedom, practicing their life with joy and gladness of heart.

The wise man highlights the inner light shining in the hearts of the saints, namely the light of divine love. For as they practiced their daily life with earnestness and diligence and worshipped the Lord in the midst of the great light, their pagan neighbors sensed their movements but did not see them. Yet the saints bore no malice or hatred or desire for revenge, nor did they move to trouble them whether by word or conduct. The wicked felt the great difference between their misery and the joy of the saints who fear God, and between their own hard hearts and the longsuffering of the saints toward them. They were thanking the saints and asking their forgiveness for what had come from them.

* If the Son alone were not the true Light, and the creatures shared with Him in this characteristic also… why do the saints cry out with a loud voice, asking God: “O send out thy light and thy truth” (Ps 43:3)…? If man has no need of the Word who enlightens, for what purpose do the saints ask Him to enlighten them, if He is not able to help them?
So then, the Only-Begotten Son is different in nature from the creatures, since He is the Light who gives light to those who are without light…
If we need light from another, then we are plainly not the true light. Therefore we do not have the same nature as the Word, who by nature surpasses us without measure.

entries.section: A. Divine light

paragraphs.text: * The light is not responsible for the sickness of the unenlightened, for as the light of the sun shines on all, and the blind man does not benefit from it without our blaming the sun, but we blame the sickness that afflicted the eyes, so the Word enlightened, but the sick creation did not receive the light. So it is with the true Light, the Only-Begotten Son, who enlightens all, but “the god of this world,” as Paul says, “hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them” [4].

St. Cyril the Great * Since we know that Christ is the true Light (Jn 1:9), in whom there is no vanity (1 Tim 6:16), we learn this: that it is necessary for our life also to be enlightened by the rays of the true Light. But the virtues are the rays of the Sun of righteousness (Mal 4:2) sent forth to enlighten us, through which we cast off the works of darkness (Rom 13:12) so that we may walk honestly as in the day (Rom 13:13), and reject the hidden things of shame. When we do everything in the light we become the very light which shines upon others (Mt 5:15-16), and it is a distinctive kind of light. And if we know Christ as “sanctification” (1 Cor 1:30), in whom every work is firm and pure, let us prove by our life that we ourselves are true partakers of His name, in harmony in deed and word with the power of His sanctification.

St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa * If life is equivalent to “the light of men,” then no one in the darkness is alive, and no one alive is in the darkness, but everyone who is alive is also in the light, and everyone who is in the light is alive. Therefore he alone who is alive is a son of light, and a son of light is he whose works shine before men (Mt 5:16).

* Paul says that he was formerly “darkness, but now light in the Lord” (1 Cor 2:14-15). Thus darkness can be turned into light. It is not difficult for one who perceives the possibility of every man changing to what is worse or what is better.

* It is possible for him who has the light of men and shares in its rays to accomplish the works of light and to know the light of knowledge (Hos 10:12 LXX) because he is enlightened. But we must also take into consideration the state of the opposite, that is, that both the evil works and what is called knowledge that is not according to the truth, these have the foundations of darkness.
Origen

entries.section: B. A unique sun that does no harm

paragraphs.text: 2 But they thanked them that they did not hurt them, they who had formerly wronged them, and begged their pardon for having been their enemies. 3 Instead of which thou gavest them a burning pillar of fire, both to be a guide of the unknown journey, and an harmless sun to entertain them honourably.
And they thanked them that they did not harm them, after having been wronged, and asked their forgiveness for their enmity toward them. [2]

entries.section: B. A unique sun that does no harm

paragraphs.text: Instead of the darkness thou gavest these a pillar of fire, a guide on a journey they had not known, and a sun that does not harm in their glorious wandering. [3]

A joyful look of the wise man, as he sees the saints - in his expression - in the midst of the wilderness as guests of God Himself, leading them as a pillar of light that sends forth His joy into them even in the midst of the night. A divine hospitality on the wilderness road which they had not known, so that the wilderness was turned into a joyful heaven, not only under the care of angels, but of the Lord of the angels Himself!

By saying “does no harm” he means that the material sun, with its great importance, if it lasts a long time, may harm whoever is exposed to it with what is called “sunstroke.” Perhaps the Jews suffered from the sun. For on the one hand, the Egyptians pressed them with many pressures to worship the god Ra, “the sun.” And on the other hand, as soon as it rose they began the works of forced labor and suffered the injustice under which they had fallen, and remained so until sunset, so the sun was bound with humiliation, violence and suffering from injustice.

entries.section: C. The light of the divine Law

paragraphs.text: 4 For they were worthy to be deprived of light and imprisoned in darkness, who had kept thy sons shut up, by whom the incorruptible light of the law was to be given unto the world.
But those deserved to lose the light and to be imprisoned in darkness, because they imprisoned thy sons, by whom the incorruptible light of the Law was to be given to the world. [4]

The pagan Egyptians were imprisoned in the prison of darkness, because they imprisoned the sons of God, from whom comes the Lord Christ, the eternal, incorruptible Light, who shines on those who sit in darkness!

While the wicked imprison themselves in a prison of their own making, the wise saints enjoy a great light: “Thou gavest these a pillar of light, a guide on a journey they had not known, a sun to entertain them honourably that does no harm” (Wis 18:3).

The writer sees in the people’s going out of Egypt to the Promised Land their enjoyment on the way of receiving the Law on Mount Sinai through Moses the prophet, as a light that guides mankind to the enjoyment of the incarnate Word of God, the Sun of righteousness.

* Scripture enlightens the eyes of the soul, so read it, O wise man, and be filled with love of it. For from the reading of the Holy Scriptures the sun rises upon the minds that feed upon them with discernment.
God has placed the Holy Scriptures in the world as a lamp of light that illumines its darkness. He who loves himself is enlightened by reading and walks by its guidance.
Approach the Scripture with love, contemplate its beauty. You will not benefit without love, for love is the entrance to understanding.
Scripture demands your love; if you do not love it, do not read it. It speaks to you, and if you grow weary in reading it, it deprives you of its hints.
You must love it, open it, read it and contemplate its beauty, otherwise do not read it, for if you do not love it you will not benefit from it.

St. Mar Jacob of Serugh * Whether man is saved or perishes, the Gospel remains in its power. Light, even if it blinds someone, is light. And honey, though bitter to the sick, is still sweet. So the Gospel has a sweet fragrance for all, even if those who did not believe in it perish.

* If a man is lost he blames only himself. The sweet perfume is said to suffocate swine. The light blinds the weak. It is in the nature of good things not only to set right him who clings to them, but also to shatter him who resists them; so their power works.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: A. He who kills is killed

paragraphs.text: 5 And when they had determined to slay the babes of thy saints, and one child was cast out, and saved, in reproof thou tookest away the multitude of their children, and destroyedst them altogether in a mighty water.

* Likewise the Egyptians became unable to distinguish between night and day, and came to live in an unchanging darkness (Ex 10:21-23). But nothing unusual happened to the Hebrews. So it was with all the other things: the hail, the fire, the boils (blisters), the flies of the cattle, the gnats and the cloud of locusts, each of which had its natural effect upon the Egyptians. And the Hebrews learned of the disasters that befell their neighbors by hearing, since nothing similar had happened to them. Then the distinction between the Egyptians and the Hebrews became sharper in the plague of the death of the firstborn (Ex 11-46; 12:29-31). The Egyptians were struck with shock, and began to lament the loss of their dearest children, while the Hebrews continued to live in complete calm and safety, and their salvation was assured by the shedding of blood (Heb 11:28). And at every house entrance the two doorposts and the lintel connecting them were marked with blood.

St. Gregory of Nyssa After the nine plagues that came upon Pharaoh and his people, and that did not come upon the people of God, but sustained them in their severe distress, the decisive night came. In this night the balances were completely changed. It was in Pharaoh’s plan to exterminate the people of God, and he thought that none could escape from his hands. He had issued his order to kill all their male children, so that they might become a company of women without men; the women would work as maidservants for the Egyptians, and in the long run there would be no Hebrew offspring, so that the company would have no existence at all.

In this night what happened suddenly and in moments was that all the Egyptians lost their firstborn! They were subjected to a plague that was not in their reckoning or in the reckoning of anyone at all, which turned the land of Egypt into a general lamentation, with none to comfort and none to help!

entries.section: B. A divine plan

paragraphs.text: 5 And when they had determined to slay the babes of thy saints, and one child was cast out, and saved, in reproof thou tookest away the multitude of their children, and destroyedst them altogether in a mighty water. 6 Of that night were our fathers certified afore, that, assuredly knowing unto what oaths they had given credence, they might afterwards be of good cheer. 7 So of thy people was accepted both the salvation of the righteous, and destruction of the enemies. 8 For wherewith thou didst punish our adversaries, by the same thou didst glorify us, whom thou hadst called.

And when they resolved to kill the babes of the saints, and a single child of them was saved after having been exposed to this, thou didst take away the multitude of their children to punish them, and didst destroy them all together in the sweeping water. [5]

They killed the innocent children, and enslaved all to their service, and thought that there was no defender for those who have neither power nor army. But heaven does not leave the rod of sinners to rest upon the righteous.
They killed the innocent children, and the fruit of that was the killing of their firstborn in one night!

Although all the children were exposed to being killed, one of them was exposed to it and was cast into the river. But the means that was for destruction became the means of salvation, for Pharaoh’s daughter drew him out and brought him up in the palace, and did not know that he was the leader prepared by God to free the Hebrews from the bondage of Pharaoh. In the water in which Pharaoh’s armies were drowned this child-leader came out.
And that night was made known beforehand to our fathers, so that their souls might be cheered, knowing with certainty in what oaths they had put their trust. [6]

God had told Moses the prophet beforehand what would happen, so what happened was not the offspring of chance, as some sometimes think. The element of surprise for the wicked increased the severity of the distress, and the saints’ perceiving beforehand what would happen gave them greater confidence in the work of God, and turned their life into a life of rejoicing, thanksgiving to God and praise.
Their souls were cheered, for they perceived the certainty of God’s faithfulness in His calling of His believers.

entries.section: B. A divine plan

paragraphs.text: So thy people expected the salvation of the righteous and the destruction of the enemies. [7]
The people did not sleep that night, for they were awaiting in faith and confidence that what God had declared would surely be fulfilled: salvation for the righteous, and destruction for the wicked!

entries.section: B. A divine plan

paragraphs.text: For by that by which thou didst punish our enemies, it became for us the occasion of our glory by thy calling us. [8]

The people rejoiced and praised, not out of a desire for revenge upon those who opposed them, but because of their pride in the fulfillment of God’s true promises that He is a refuge for His believers and a support to them.
The wicked bring the plagues upon themselves, and what is destruction for them becomes salvation for the righteous.

entries.section: C. Sorrow turned into praise

paragraphs.text: 9 For the righteous children of good men did sacrifice secretly, and with one consent made a holy law, that the saints should be alike partakers of the same good and evil, the fathers now singing out the songs of praise. For the holy children of the righteous were sacrificing secretly, and agreed together to establish this divine law, that the saints should share alike in blessings and in dangers, and from that time they were chanting the songs of the fathers. [9]

By the righteous saints he means Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and others of the fathers, for the people had received from their fathers the offering of sacrifices to the Lord. And when they were forbidden, they offered them secretly. For they perceived the importance of this law concerning the offering of animal sacrifices, so they insisted with one accord that they would not stop offering them.
Here he presents to us some features of this enslaved people, fallen under forced labor:
First: they insisted on living and worshipping as they had received from their fathers, so that they might enjoy the love of God and the fulfillment of His promises to their fathers.
Second: in the midst of humiliation they bore one spirit, so they agreed together to offer worship with one mind, having received its rites from previous generations.
Third: that they would practice a common life in enjoying blessings together and bearing distresses.

Fourth: this society, alienated and fallen under slavery, was marked by a spirit of hope and rejoicing, for they were in fact, before the appearance of Moses to take up the leadership, chanting the praises or songs of the fathers.

Moses the prophet did not tell us of this splendid picture in the Book of Exodus, because what concerned him was the revelation of the righteousness of God working for salvation, and His surpassing divine providence. The writer highlighted that they were in fact, before the salvation took place in that night, chanting the songs of salvation, in the spirit of the community, in living hope.

entries.section: D. Comprehensive discipline

paragraphs.text: 10 But on the other side there resounded an ill-according cry of the enemies, and a lamentable noise was carried abroad of children that were bewailed. 11 The master and the servant were punished after one manner; and like as the king, so suffered the common person.
And the discordant clamor of the enemies answered, and the voice of those weeping for their children with wailing spread in every direction. [10]

The disaster came upon all the Egyptians; it was a collective discipline, no house was without a firstborn of theirs who died, especially since society at that time was distinguished by the large family system. So in one house more than one firstborn would die, since married brothers were accustomed to live together in a large house!
With the unity of dwelling and the unity of trial, there was no communal sharing of consolation, for there was no person whose family was not struck by this distress.

While the righteous in the midst of their distress were chanting together in one spirit in harmony among themselves, as in harmony with their fathers, behold the unbelievers were uttering dreadful discordant voices and bitter cries because of the killing of their firstborn. The lands of Egypt were filled with the sound of wailing because of the death of their sons. And although the disaster that befell them was shared, the voices were a noise without harmony.

The Church, even in the midst of her sufferings, enjoys unity in the Spirit by the work of the Holy Spirit, but the wicked, even if they agree to resist the Church, utter conflicting voices in which there is no harmony.

entries.section: D. Comprehensive discipline

paragraphs.text: And the same punishment struck the slave and the master, and the son of the people and the king suffered the same torment. [11]

Pharaoh distinguished himself from the men of his palace, and the men of his palace from the Egyptian people. And the exploitation of the Hebrews as slaves came for the benefit of the rich classes. But since all bore feelings of hatred and gloating, and perhaps the people shared in enslaving and exploiting the Hebrews, behold the trial that came for their discipline was one. God wished man to perceive that all mankind is equal in the eyes of God. For with God there is no partiality to one who has authority or to a master or to a rich man.

entries.section: E. A bitter death

paragraphs.text: 12 They all together had innumerable dead with one kind of death, neither were the living sufficient to bury them: for in one moment the noblest offspring of them was destroyed.
They all died one death, so they had corpses without number, so that the living were not sufficient even to bury them, for in a moment the dearest of their offspring was destroyed. [12]

The royal orders were issued to the two midwives to kill secretly the children of the Hebrews at their birth, and the divine order was issued to discipline the wicked by the killing of the firstborn in one night with one stroke.

From the multitude of the dead there was not found a sufficient number of young men to carry the dead and bury them, so the hearts of the people were broken as the corpses lay before them, with inability to bury them.

* Then the angel arrives to strike Egypt, which had not been initiated into the mystery, nor partaken of the Passover, nor been sealed with blood, nor been under the protection of the Spirit, the unbelieving enemy; he struck her in one night and deprived her of her children. For the angel attacked Egypt, after he had passed among Israel and saw it sealed with the blood of the lamb, and he subdued stiff-necked Pharaoh with mourning, and wrapped him, not with a dark garment or a torn cloak, but with the whole of Egypt, completely torn and weeping for her firstborn.

All Egypt was drowned in sorrow and the plagues, shedding tears and beating her breast, and she came to Pharaoh in mourning, not only in her clothing but also in her soul; torn, not only in her outer garments but also within.

And you could see a new sight: here those who beat their breasts, and there those who uttered cries of pain, and in the midst Pharaoh in mourning, sitting on sackcloth and ashes, wrapped in a darkness that held him like a mourning garment, and girded with the whole of Egypt as with a mantle of mourning.
Egypt was around Pharaoh like a mantle of lamentation…

If you give heed, amazement will seize you at the matter of an incredible calamity. Here is what surrounded the Egyptians: a long night, and a darkness that light could not penetrate, and a death that felt its way, and an angel that destroys, and hell devouring their firstborn.
But what is more strange and more dreadful, you must learn. In the darkness that held them, the insatiable death was hiding, and that darkness the wretched Egyptians were groping…
But the death lying in wait seizes the firstborn of the Egyptians at the command of the angel.

What a strange mystery that cannot be explained! For the slaying of the lamb was in fact the salvation of Israel, so the death of the lamb became the life of the people, for the blood frightened the angel.
Melito, bishop of Sardis

entries.section: F. Confession of the truth

paragraphs.text: 13 For whereas they would not believe any thing by reason of the enchantments; upon the destruction of the firstborn, they acknowledged this people to be the sons of God. 14 For while all things were in quiet silence, and that night was in the midst of her swift course, 15 thine Almighty word leaped down from heaven out of thy royal throne, as a fierce man of war into the midst of a land of destruction, 16 and brought thine unfeigned commandment as a sharp sword, and standing up filled all things with death; and it touched the heaven, but it stood upon the earth.
And after they had refused, because of the art of magic, to believe anything, they confessed at the destruction of the firstborn that thy people is a son of God. [13]

The Egyptians relied on the arts of magic, and with every plague Pharaoh would ask the magicians to act, and in vain they exerted effort for the deliverance of Pharaoh and his people. With this inability Pharaoh continued in his stubbornness, resisting God with his pride, until his throne was completely shaken by the plague of the firstborn (Wis 18:12).

entries.section: F. Confession of the truth

paragraphs.text: And while a quiet silence enveloped all things, and the night was in the midst of its swift course. [14]

The writer compares the state of the Egyptians in the first half of the night and the second half. For half of the night passed in great stillness, and with surpassing swiftness, until the sentence of discipline was issued at midnight.

entries.section: F. Confession of the truth

paragraphs.text: Thine almighty word leaped from heaven, from the royal throne, like a fierce warrior into the midst of the doomed land, [15]
bearing thy inevitable command like a sharp sword.

entries.section: F. Confession of the truth

paragraphs.text: And standing, it filled every place with death, and it touched heaven and trod the earth. [16]

At midnight a battle of a unique kind was declared, between men on earth who think that they are possessors of authority, and have military capabilities, and that they are able to lay plans for battle, and the Word of God the Almighty in heaven, where the divine throne is.
He portrays the Word of God, who issued the order of discipline, as the Almighty who cannot be bounded. His head is in heaven and His feet are on the earth. Who can stand before Him?

entries.section: G. Increasing fears

paragraphs.text: 17 Then suddenly visions of horrible dreams troubled them sore, and terrors came upon them unlooked for. 18 And one thrown here, and another there, half dead, shewed the cause of his death. 19 For the dreams that troubled them did foreshew this, lest they should perish, and not know why they were afflicted. Then suddenly visions of terrifying dreams troubled them, and unexpected fears came upon them. [17]

It is hard for a man to imagine a whole country in which almost every house holds a lamentation for the firstborn of the family. And what stirred the situation the more was that, as they found no word of consolation, nor strength to gather the corpses and bury them before they rotted and caused plagues, they did not know what would come after this plague.
As though their fears of what was coming covered even their grief for their firstborn.
The wise man sees that the plague of the firstborn by the angel was accompanied by the appearance of demons who troubled them, so they perceived the weakness of their gods (Wis 18:17-18).

entries.section: G. Increasing fears

paragraphs.text: And each one was struck down here and there, between living and dead, and he would declare for what cause he was dying. [18]
The country turned into a state of chaos, each one running here and there, asking what was the cause of this grave disaster.

entries.section: G. Increasing fears

paragraphs.text: For the dreams that troubled them foretold this, lest they should perish not knowing why they suffered this torment. [19]
It appears that God permitted them dreams in that night, that perhaps they might repent and return before this destruction took place.

entries.section: H. Discipline without partiality

paragraphs.text: 20 Yea, the taste of death touched the righteous also, and there was a destruction of the multitude in the wilderness: but the wrath endured not long. But the trial of death touched the righteous also, and the stroke fell upon a great number of them in the wilderness.
But the wrath did not last long. [20]

A group of Levites who envied the priests in the service of God in the tabernacle of the congregation, Korah and Dathan and Abiram and others, two hundred and fifty men in number, murmured against the restriction of the priesthood to Aaron and his seed. They presumed and offered incense, and the earth was cleft and swallowed them up with their families. The people did not fear God, but murmured against Moses and Aaron. Without partiality God permitted a plague to spread that destroyed fourteen thousand of them, and in tender fatherhood Moses and Aaron interceded for the people that God might lift the plague from them.

entries.section: I. Fatherhood and intercession

paragraphs.text: 21 For the blameless man made haste; he took to him the shield of his ministry, even prayer, and the propitiation of incense, and withstood the wrath, and so brought the calamity to an end, declaring that he was thy servant. 22 So he overcame the destroyer, not with strength of body, nor force of arms, but with a word subdued him that punished, alleging the oaths and covenants made with the fathers. 23 For when the dead were now fallen down by heaps one upon another, standing between, he stayed the wrath, and parted the way to the living. 24 For in the long robe was the whole world, and in the four rows of the stones was the glory of the fathers graven, and thy Majesty upon the diadem of his head. 25 Unto these the destroyer gave place, and was afraid of them: for it was enough that they only tasted of the wrath.

For a blameless man hastened to protect them, and went with the shield of his ministry, which is prayer and the propitiation of incense, and stood before the wrath, and put an end to the calamity, showing that he was thy servant. [21]

Because of the corruption of a group of Levites a plague spread that destroyed many, but the figure of Moses stands out as a father who gathers all the people in his arms, and carries them in his heart and intercedes for them. His figure shone like a splendid star in the eyes of the heavenly beings, indeed in the eyes of God, who seeks souls enlarged with love. As He asked his brother Aaron to offer incense to God for the people.

entries.section: I. Fatherhood and intercession

paragraphs.text: So he overcame the destroyer, not by the strength of the body nor by the work of arms, but by the word he subdued the punisher, reminding him of the oaths and covenants made with the fathers. [22]

As though Moses had entered into a battle with the wrath of God against His people. His weapon was love with prayer in a spirit of humility and trust in God’s promises and in what He had sworn to the fathers in His covenants with them. He conquered by this marvelous spiritual weapon!

entries.section: I. Fatherhood and intercession

paragraphs.text: And while the dead were piling up one upon another, he stood in the midst and turned back the wrath, and cut off its way to the living. [23]

Moses the prophet stood in the midst of the corpses and spread out his hands that by living faith and sincere love he might stay the wrath of God, and preserve the living from the plague that had come.
Perhaps he speaks here of Aaron the high priest, who shared with Moses in the petition.

entries.section: I. Fatherhood and intercession

paragraphs.text: For upon his long robe was the whole world, and the glorious names of the fathers were engraved on the four rows of stones, and thy majesty was upon the diadem of his head. [24]

What adorns the priesthood of Aaron is that he was wearing a garment down to the feet representing the whole world, wrapping himself with all mankind to ask in love for the whole world. For the priest is a father to all mankind, who will not cease praying for all men.

entries.section: I. Fatherhood and intercession

paragraphs.text: When the destroyer saw this he drew back and was afraid, and it was enough that they had merely tasted the wrath. [25]
The destroying angel drew back and was afraid when he perceived God’s good pleasure in Moses’ love for his people and Aaron’s service on their behalf.

entries.section: Discipline me, and deliver me not over to death!

paragraphs.text: * My God, You are the Sun of righteousness, shine upon me, and all darkness in me will be dispelled, and pour out Your splendor upon my soul.
You discipline, but You give life and do not destroy!
* Take away from me the darkness of sin, and turn my sorrows into joys!
You permit the death of the body, but only for a time, while my soul enjoys life with You always.
I do not fear the death of the body, for by You it rises glorified, and shares with my soul its eternal splendor!
* Grant me, with Moses the prophet and Aaron, the spirit of fatherhood!
So that I may have no work greater than prayer for all mankind.
Stretch out the hands of my soul to embrace all.
I cry out saying: lift Your wrath from all mankind!

entries.section: A. Divine wrath without mercy

paragraphs.text: 1 As for the ungodly, wrath came upon them without mercy unto the end: for He knew beforehand what would become of them, 2 how that, having given them leave to depart and having hastened to send them away, they would repent and pursue them. 3 For whilst they were yet mourning and making lamentation at the graves of their dead, they took up another foolish counsel, and pursued as fugitives those whom they had urged to be gone. 4 For the destiny whereof they were worthy drew them unto this end, and made them forget the things that had already happened, that they might fulfil the punishment which was wanting to their torments, 5 and that Thy people might pass a most wonderful way, but they might find a strange death.
As for the wicked, wrath without mercy came upon them to the end, for He knew beforehand what they would do. [1]

In the ten plagues the chastening, however severe it seemed, carried mercy, for the Lord was giving an opportunity for repentance. Now that the cup of evil was full, Pharaoh and the men of his army cast themselves into the midst of the sea and perished, having shut against themselves the doors of the divine mercies.

entries.section: A. Divine wrath without mercy
