paragraphs.text: That after they had given them leave to depart and had hastened to send them away, they would change their mind and pursue them. [2]

Before the plague of the firstborn the Egyptians knew that this people was the son of God (Wis 18:13), and they realized that there was no room for resisting them, so they permitted them to go out, and even asked them to hurry to depart from Egypt. But their wicked hearts refused this; they went back on their decision, regretted it, and set their minds to pursue them.

entries.section: A. Divine wrath without mercy

paragraphs.text: For while they were still mourning and lamenting at the graves of their dead, another foolish thought occurred to them, and they began to chase those whom they had urged to depart, as one chases fugitives. [3]

The wise man presents a new cause for their evils. Besides their knowing that this people was the son of God, and besides their asking them to hurry out, they left the graves of their firstborn, and instead of lamentation a foolish thought came to their minds, namely to pursue those whom they had allowed to go out. This reveals a heart full of hatred and malice: they do not care about the firstborn who died, but what occupies them is killing those who had served them and done them good.

entries.section: A. Divine wrath without mercy

paragraphs.text: And a just destiny drew them to this extreme limit and led them to forget what had passed, that they might fulfil what was lacking of the torments of their punishment. [4]

Since they thought foolishly according to the wickedness of their will and the corruption of their hearts, they themselves drove themselves to destruction as the fruit of their corruption, and thus justice was fulfilled in them. They forgot the ten plagues as though they had not been enough, and so they threw themselves into a deadly blow.

entries.section: A. Divine wrath without mercy

paragraphs.text: And Thy people might experience a most wonderful journey, while those would meet a strange death. [5]

By their evil thinking and wicked conduct they cast themselves into a shameful death, while the people of God enjoyed a marvelous crossing, which became a lesson throughout the generations and a symbol of the crossing of all humanity through the destruction of the devil by the Cross.

entries.section: B. Nature serving God's plan

paragraphs.text: 6 For the whole creation, each in its own kind, changed its nature and served Thee according to what was appointed for it, that Thy children might be kept without harm. 7 As namely, a cloud overshadowed the camp; and where water stood before, dry land appeared; a smooth way in the Red Sea, and a green field out of the deep of a great abyss.
And the whole creation, according to its own nature, was fashioned again anew and submitted to Thy commands, that Thy children might be kept safe. [6]

All things worked for the good of the children of God, even the evil of the wicked, and also the movement of nature, which proceeded not according to its own laws but according to the divine commands.

entries.section: B. Nature serving God's plan

paragraphs.text: And they saw a cloud overshadowing the tent, dry land rising out of what had been water before, the Red Sea becoming a way without obstacle, and the rushing waves becoming a green meadow. [7]
Nature moved to work by divine commands for the preservation of the children of God.
First: in their crossing the camp, that is, the whole people and the ark, was overshadowed by divine clouds, like one under the wings of God.
Second: a way appeared in the midst of the water, dry and parched, fit to walk upon, although it had been covered by the waters for such a long time.
Second: the waters moved from every side and stood to become like walls protecting those who walked on the new way.
Fourth: there were no waves to terrify the people, but they were turned into green meadows, in which those walking in the midst of the sea took delight as though they were strolling.

entries.section: C. A joyful celebration in the midst of the waters

paragraphs.text: 8 There the whole nation passed over, covered by Thy hand, seeing marvellous wonders, 9 and they roamed at large like horses, and leaped like lambs, praising Thee, O Lord, their Savior, 10 being mindful of what had happened during their sojourn in a strange land, how the earth brought forth flies instead of the offspring of cattle, and the river overflowed with a multitude of frogs instead of fishes. 11 And at the last they saw a new kind of fowl, when desire led them to ask for delicate food, 12 for quails came up from the sea for their comfort.
In it they crossed as one nation, sheltered by Thy hand, and witnessing marvellous wonders. [8]

A glorious crossing that embraced the whole nation at once, for they had no need of ships to carry them and divide them into groups, and they did not fear the dangers of drowning or of pirates of the sea.
As they walked they saw a multitude of signs and wonders without number.

entries.section: C. A joyful celebration in the midst of the waters

paragraphs.text: They grazed like horses and leaped like lambs, praising Thee, O Lord, their Deliverer. [9]

It was not a crossing full of dangers, nor of anxiety about their condition or what they would be in the wilderness. Rather the crossing was turned into a joyful celebration, in which hearts delighted in dancing like horses, and souls were like joyful lambs walking in a pasture without care, and their mouths did not cease from praising God, the giver of marvellous salvation.

entries.section: C. A joyful celebration in the midst of the waters

paragraphs.text: For they remembered what had happened in their sojourn, how the earth brought forth gnats instead of cattle, and how the sea overflowed with a multitude of frogs instead of aquatic creatures. [10]

The procession turned back in its memory to contemplate everything: priests, Levites, and people, how nature was moving, and still moves, on their behalf. The earth brought forth gnats for those who enslaved them, not cattle, and the waters sent them frogs, not fishes!

entries.section: C. A joyful celebration in the midst of the waters

paragraphs.text: And at last they saw a new way of producing birds, when their desire urged them to ask for choice foods. [11]

A wonderful and unique journey: when they craved the taste of meat, what was impossible happened. From where would they bring meat in a dry wilderness? Yet the quails came migrating, as by divine command, flying toward them near the surface of the sea, as though they had been born from the waters of the sea. The people had no need of nets to catch them; rather they came as though into their very hands, advancing of themselves that the people might enjoy eating them.

entries.section: C. A joyful celebration in the midst of the waters

paragraphs.text: And the quails came up from the sea to satisfy them. [12]

entries.section: 2. A comparison between Egypt and Sodom

paragraphs.text: 12 But upon the sinners vengeance came, with the ancient signs which were the violence of the thunderbolts. And they suffered justly what their wickedness deserved, 13 for their treatment of guests was more hateful. For those would not receive strangers whom they knew not, but these made slaves of guests who had done them good. 14 And not only so, but there is another visitation upon them, for those received strangers only unwillingly, 15 but these received guests with feasting and joy, and made them partakers of their rights, and afterward afflicted them with the most grievous torments. 16 So they were stricken with blindness, like those at the door of the righteous man, when a dreadful darkness compassed them about; and each one groped about seeking the entrance of his own door.

But punishments came upon the sinners, not without having been signaled beforehand, by violent thunderbolts; and justly they suffered because of their wickedness, for they showed the most extreme hatred toward strangers. [13]

He compares the evil of Sodom with the evil of the Egyptians, with regard to what the people of Sodom did when Lot received two angels as guests, and what the Egyptians did when Pharaoh received Joseph and all his family. The people of Sodom deserved that thunderbolts from heaven should fall upon them, because they hated two strangers (or two angels who came in the form of two men).
Others refused to welcome strangers whom they did not know.

entries.section: 2. A comparison between Egypt and Sodom

paragraphs.text: But these made slaves of guests who had done them good. [14]

If an excuse is given to the people of Sodom for refusing to receive strangers, what excuse can the Egyptians offer for forcing into servitude those who had done them good in their time of distress and in the tending of their flocks?

entries.section: 2. A comparison between Egypt and Sodom

paragraphs.text: And besides this, there is a visitation (punishment) awaiting those because they received strangers in a hostile manner. [15]
Punishment awaited the people of Sodom, because they received strangers in a spirit of enmity without cause.

entries.section: 2. A comparison between Egypt and Sodom

paragraphs.text: But these, after receiving with celebration those who shared in their rights, burdened them with terrible works. [16]

From a new viewpoint the wise man compares the Egyptians with the people of Sodom. The former received the believers (Joseph and his family) with great welcome, in honor of Joseph who had saved them from the famine. But after Joseph they wronged them, oppressed them, and enslaved them, and forced them into harsh labors. As for the people of Sodom, they received two angels in the form of two strange men, but the reception was against their will, for they were struck with blindness, and the two angels went to Lot’s house. The people of Sodom also did wrong to the two guests, but they did not know them.

entries.section: 2. A comparison between Egypt and Sodom

paragraphs.text: So they were struck with blindness, like those at the door of the righteous man, when a great darkness compassed them about and each one went groping for the entrance of his house. [17]

entries.section: 3. A new harmony

paragraphs.text: 17 For the elements changed their proportions one to another, as in a harp the name of a sound changes in the melody, while the sound remains; and this is plain to him who considers those events. 18 For earthly things were turned into watery, and things that swam moved upon the earth, 19 and fire had power in the water, greater than its natural power, and the water forgot its quenching nature. 20 On the other hand, the flame did not hurt the flesh of the corruptible living creatures that walked in it, and did not melt the heavenly food, easy to melt like ice. The elements were changing one into another, just as the change of notes on the harp changes the nature of the rhythm while the sound remains, and this is plain from a close consideration of what took place: [18]

entries.section: 3. A new harmony

paragraphs.text: God transforms the elements of His will like one playing on the strings of a harp to bring forth a sweet melody on behalf of the world. The wise man sees that the events as a whole, whether in Egypt before the Exodus, or during the Exodus, or during the crossing of the Red Sea, or in the wilderness after the Exodus, are like the strings of a unique and marvelous divine harp, of different notes yet harmonious, bringing forth a wonderful symphony that bears witness to the care of God, the Almighty and the Savior of His children. For earthly creatures were turned into watery ones, and the swimming creatures moved upon the earth. [19]

One of these notes moves nature by a law contrary to nature, so that the procession of the whole nation became like fish crossing in the midst of the sea in safety, like sea creatures swimming in the midst of the waters rejoicing. Human beings, the inhabitants of the earth, became like water creatures, and the people came out of the sea to walk in the wilderness as sea creatures that had been transformed into land creatures.

entries.section: 3. A new harmony

paragraphs.text: And the fire, even in the water, kept its natural power, and the water forgot its power of quenching the fire. [20]

Another delightful string: when the fire came down with the hail, the flame of the fire was not quenched by the water but burned the more, for the water forgot its nature that quenches fires! And on the contrary, the flame did not consume the bodies of the weak animals that were roaming in it, and did not melt the heavenly food that resembled ice, which melts quickly. [21]

A third string in harmony with the two preceding ones: the fires that came down with the hail did not destroy the insects that had been sent to chastise the wicked, as though they had agreed with the fires to work together in harmony for the chastisement, or as though they had received a new nature that the fires could not destroy.

The fourth string is what happened with the manna, which resembles ice: the rays of the sun melt it, so that those who were late in going out to gather it might not gather it, yet the fires were not able to melt it while it was being cooked.

entries.section: 4. Conclusion

paragraphs.text: 20 For Thou, O Lord, didst magnify Thy people in all things, and glorify them, and didst not neglect them, but wast their helper in every time and place.
For Thou, O Lord, in everything didst magnify Thy people and glorify them, and didst not disdain to help them in every time and place. [22]

The conclusion of the book is a wonderful hymn of praise that calls every believer to witness the greatness of God’s love for His Church, the surpassing greatness of God’s love that she may share His heavenly glory, and His delight to uphold her in every generation and in every place!
Let me be united with You, O Wisdom of God!
* Let me be united with You, O wonderful Wisdom, who fill me with love for You and for humanity.
You remove from me the corruption of my nature, and renew me by Your Holy Spirit.
* You turn affliction for me into eternal glory!
I cross the sea with Your people as in the waters of Baptism.
You open for me a way in the midst of the waves.
You turn all that is around me into a harp of love.
So I join with nature in bearing witness to You.
I bear witness to You that You are the God of the impossible!
* Finally, work in me, O Wisdom of God, and make of me Your ambassador and a steward of heaven.
You make of me a sign and a wonder before the heavenly ones.
They see dust having become heaven.
They see corruption having been turned into incorruption.
They see an inhabitant of the earth become the object of their wonder in heaven!
